Second Readings 2026-129 An Order to accept the provisions of M.G.L. c. 140 sec. 139- Councilor Haggstrom and Councilor Redfern Sponsors Summary: This order accepts the provisions of Massachusetts General Laws Chapter 140, Section 139(c), which allows municipalities to waive dog license fees for residents aged 70 and older. By adopting this local option, the City of Amesbury would eliminate the annual dog licensing fee for qualifying senior residents while still requiring compliance with all licensing and vaccination requirements. This waiver would apply only to individual dog license fees and would not apply to late fees or kennel licenses. The measure is intended to support senior residents while encouraging continued compliance with local dog licensing requirements and protecting public health. 2026-130 An Order to authorize the Mayor to accept and expend a grant of $25,000.00 through the FY27 Field Demonstration Project. -Mayor Sponsor Summary: The Massachusetts Councils on Aging has awarded the Amesbury Council on Aging $25,000.00 through the FY27 Field Demonstration Program. The funding will support modernization of the kitchen located at the Costello Center, including the replacement of outdated and nonfunctioning kitchen equipment and related improvements to enhance nutrition services, accessibility, safety, and programming for older adults. 2026-131 An Order to approve payment from the FY27 general fund operating budget for the below listed prior year invoices-Mayor Sponsor Summary: The listed invoices below are for operating expenses related to supplies or services rendered in prior fiscal years but for which funds were not encumbered by the corresponding city department at fiscal year-end. This order requests payment be made to the listed vendors from the corresponding department’s current year (FY27) operating budget in accordance with M.G.L. c.44 s. 64. OTI handsets look a bit like a TV remote control, but instead of pushing buttons to changes channels, voters push the buttons to vote: the 1 button for Yes, or the 2 button for No. Selections are displayed on each the handset screen and wirelessly transmitted to a computer then counts votes. The voting tabulation computer then displays the results for the Moderator to announce. Typically, nothing but these totals is permanently recorded, so votes remain private and are not tied to the voter’s identity. Voter Check-In Voters attending the town meeting check-in with the Town Clerk. As voters check-in they receive a handset for use during that session. Each voter registration position is staffed by team members hired by the Town Clerk. As each voter arrives, they approach any available station. Their name is identified in the registration system, attendance is confirmed. © 2026 Option Technologies International LLC • 4303 Vineland Rd, F2. • Orlando, FL 32811 • Tel: • 407.872.3333 . 1 Overview of Electronic Voting for Town Meeting Test Votes Each meeting session typically begins with one or more “test votes” to get everyone comfortable with the voting procedures. The Moderator will pose a question like “Will the Red Sox win the pennant this year?”, and everyone will have 60 seconds to vote. During this interval, voters will be able to change their votes should they wish to do so. The system counts only the last button pushed by the voter: the 1 button for Yes, and the 2 button for No. When the 60-second interval is over, the Moderator will announce that the test vote is complete, and shortly thereafter announce the results. © 2026 Option Technologies International LLC • 4303 Vineland Rd, F2. • Orlando, FL 32811 • Tel: • 407.872.3333 . 2 Overview of Electronic Voting for Town Meeting Voting Process Before each vote, the Moderator summarizes the motion or amendment being decided. He or she will then announce the beginning of a 60 second interval during which each voter enters their vote. During this period and a “voting light” near the Moderator is typically illuminated. If desired, voting questions may be projected on a public screen with a countdown time. Voters enter their votes and receive a personalized confirmation message on the handset display (“OK”). If a voter accidentally pushes the wrong button, they may change their vote by pushing the correct button. If a voter does not want to participate in a particular vote, they don’t push any buttons during the 60 second voting interval. When the 60-second interval is over the Moderator will announce that the vote is complete; shortly thereafter the Moderator will announce the results from a display next to his or her lectern that is connected to the voting tabulation computer. © 2026 Option Technologies International LLC • 4303 Vineland Rd, F2. • Orlando, FL 32811 • Tel: • 407.872.3333 . 3 Overview of Electronic Voting for Town Meeting Handset Return Voters are asked to keep their handset with them during the meeting. When they leave the meeting - either during a session or at the close of a session – they are asked to place their handset in one of the plastic bins at each of the exits. After all voters have departed, the handsets are sanitized, sorted, and put away in storage cases. This is typically done by the check-in team members. Electronic Voting Help Desk OTI recommends a volunteer help desk in a central location for each open town meeting session. Assistance is available for voters who may be confused or need a replacement handset. All handsets are tested before each session of Town Meeting, and the probability of a handset failing is very low. However, if the voter has trouble for any reason, they may go to the Help Desk; they are provided with a paper ballot to record their current vote and are issued a new handset. This is an unusual circumstance but a best practice. Voters who are physically unable to use a handset to vote, are asked to inform the check-in team. They are typically seated in an area where their votes will be manually recorded and counted by Tellers. These votes are conveyed to the Town Clerk to be appended to the electronic tally. OTI offers special braille handsets for visually challenged voters. Safety Handsets use radio signals to transmit votes to transceivers attached to the voting tabulation computer. The radio energy is used by a handset to convey your vote wirelessly is less than 1% that of a typical cell phone. text: By Town Clerk's Office at 2:24 pm, Sep 24, 2026 TOWN OF CARLISLE Zoning Board of Appeals 66 Westford Street Carlisle, MA 01741 978-369-9702 Public Hearing Notice In accordance with the provisions of MGL Chapter 40A Sections 10 and 11, notice is hereby given of a public hearing by the Carlisle Zoning Board of Appeals remotely on Zoom starting at 7:30 pm, September 28, 2026, for the application of Sean McLaughlin requesting a Variance pursuant to Carlisle Zoning Bylaw Sections 4.3.2 and 7.5, for 18.1 feet of relief from the 40-foot setback requirement to allow construction of a detached barn. The property is located within the Residence B District at 391 Maple Street, Map 13, Parcel 84-1. A copy of the application, file number 2601, and any accompanying information may be viewed at the Planning Office located on the second floor of Town Hall, 66 Westford Street, during business hours Monday through Thursday, 8:30 am to 4:30 pm, and Friday, 9:00 am to 12:00 pm. Any person interested or wishing to be heard on the application should appear at the time and place designated or submit written correspondence to the Board of Appeals. Email correspondence should be sent to nbeland@carlislema.gov Noelle Beland, Planning and Land Use Coordinator Carlisle Zoning Board of Appeals

Approve minutes of August 4, 2026 B. Public Hearing: Case 406-4-DR: Petitioner: Paul Topham A Petition was filed pertaining to an Appeal of a Denial by the Building Commissioner for a Building Permit pursuant to Section 290-5-2.2 A and C of the Carver Zoning By-law, for property located at 66 Pond Street in Carver, MA (Assessors' Map 106, Lot 4-DR) so as to construct an accessory dwelling unit in a Residential Agricultural District. Per Section 290-2-2.6 B (1) of the By-law, the habitable area of the proposed construction shall not exceed one-half the gross floor area of the principal dwelling or 900 square feet, whichever is smaller. C. Correspondence (if any) D. Adjournment

MO-10 Mayor's appropriation of Thirty-one thousand three hundred forty-two and 00/100 dollars ($31,342.00) to the following named account: Police Special Account for Building Renovations from available funds in the Stabilization Fund. 11 A favorable Finance & Budget Committee report: Be it Ordered that a city audit when completed be referred to the City Council for a public hearing. 12 A favorable Finance & Budget Committee report: Be it Ordered that an independent audit be done for the Health Insurance and Dental Insurance. 13 A favorable Finance & Budget Committee report: Be it Ordered that the Golf Course meet with the Finance and Budget Committee for a full financial report. 14 An Ordinance Committee report: BE IT ORDAINED by the City Council that the Code of the City of Chicopee for the Year 1991, as amended, be and is hereby further amended as follows: 275-71 Renewable Energy By adding the attached definition Renewable Energy Storage Language and Battery Energy Storage System Language to Sections 275-71(a)(4), (b)(l), (c)(2), (d), and change 275-71(h) to 275-71(i), 275-71(i) to 275-71(j), and add 275-71(h)- Battery Energy Storage Systems (BESS). *Proposed additions noted in Bold* A. Definitions. As used in this section, the following terms shall have the meanings indicated: General Definitions Adverse Visual Impact: When an undertaking alters directly or indirectly the viewshed from a property in a manner that would diminish that property's perceived value. Site Plan Review Authority: Refers to the body of local government designated by the municipality to review site plans. For the City of Chicopee the Site Plan Review Advisory Committee (SPRAC) serves as the Site Plan Review Authority. Special Permit Granting Authority: A body of local government designated by the municipality to grant special permits. In the City of Chicopee the city council holds such authority. Zoning Enforcement Authority: The board charged with enforcing the zoning bylaws. For the City of Chicopee the Building Commissioner serves as the Zoning Enforcement Authority. Definitions (Energy Storage Systems) ANSI: American National Standards Institute Battery ar Batteries: A single cell or group of cells connected electrically in a series, in parallel, or a combination of both, which can charge, discharge, and store energy, electrically. For the purposes of this section, a Battery or Batteries utilized in commercial products are excluded from these requirements. Battery Energy Storage System (BESS): One or more containers or cabinets on a lot containing batteries and related equipment, assembled together, capable of storing electrical energy in order to supply electrical energy to the power grid at a future time. This includes all accessory equipment on said lot necessary for energy storage including but not limited to inverters, transformers, cooling equipment, switching gear, metering equipment, transmission tie-lines, and other power interconnection facilities and/or a project substation, but does not include public utility owned and operated interconnection equipment, regardless of location, or other interconnection equipment to be located on the real property of the public utility or within its right of way, determined to be necessary by the public utility to facilitate the BESS interconnection with the power grid whether for bringing power to the BESS or for returning it to the power grid, a stand-alone 12-volt vehicle battery, or an electric motor vehicle. It may be a primary use or an accessory use to a renewable energy generating facility (solar or wind), power generation facility, electrical substation, or other similar uses. Cell: The basic electrochemical unit, characterized by an anode and a cathode, used to receive, store, and deliver electrical energy. Commissioning: A systematic process that provides documented confirmation that a battery energy storage system functions according to the intended design criteria and complies with applicable code requirements. Energy Storage Systems (ESS), Accessory: ESS store energy for industrial and general uses utilizing various technologies. Accessory use ESS are considered part of the principal use for zoning purposes including allowable locations. To be considered as accessory, ESS shall be designed with appropriate storage capacity to serve the principal use only and not the electric power grid; Energy Storage Systems (ESS}, Stand Alone: ESS store energy for industrial and general uses utilizing various technologies. Chemical batteries are a type of ESS that are installed as a standalone use. Nationally Recognized Testing Laboratory (NRTL/: A U.S. Department of Labor designation recognizing a private sector organization to perform certification for certain products to ensure that they meet the requirements of both the construction and general industry OSHA electrical standards. NFPA: National Fire Protection Association Definitions (Photovoltaic Systems) Greenfield: An area of agricultural or forest land, or some other undeveloped site. Photovoltaic System (also referred to as Photovoltaic Installation): An active solar energy system that converts solar energy directly into electricity. Rated Nameplate Capacity: The maximum rated output of electric power production of the photovoltaic system in watts of Direct Current (DC). Solar Energy: Radiant energy received from the sun that can be collected in the form of heat or light by a solar collector. Solar Energy System, Grid-!ntertie: A photovoltaic system that is connected to an electric circuit served by an electric utility. Solar Energy System, Ground-Mounted: An Active Solar Energy System that is structurally mounted to the ground and is not roof-mounted; may be of any size (small-, medium-or large-scale). Solar Energy System, Large-Scale: An Active Solar Energy System that occupies more than 40,000 square feet of surface area (equivalent to a rated nameplate capacity of about 250kW DC or greater). Solar Energy System, Medium-Scale: An Active Solar Energy System that occupies more than 1,750 but less than 40,000 square feet of surface area (equivalent to a rated nameplate capacity of about 10 - 250 kW DC). Solar Energy System, Off-Grid: A photovoltaic solar energy system in which the circuits energized by the solar energy system are not electrically connected in any way to electric circuits that are served by an electric utility. Solar Energy System, Roof-Mounted: An Active Solar Energy System that is structurally mounted to the roof of a building or structure; may be of any size (small-, medium-or large-scale). Solar Energy System, Small-Scale: An Active Solar Energy System that occupies 1,750 square feet of surface area or less (equivalent to a rated nameplate capacity of about 10 kW DC or less). Definitions (Wind Systems) Building Integrated Wind Energy System: A building-mounted wind energy conversion system that has a manufacturer's rating of 10 kW or less and projects no more than fifteen (15) feet above the highest point on the rdof and shall not be considered a small wind energy system in terms of area and setback requirements. This definition also covers, for the purposes of this zoning provision, other wind energy systems primarily used for land-based applications which may be permanently mounted and operated on a building. Utility-Scale Wind Energy Facility: A commercial wind energy facility, where the primary use of the facility is electrical generation to be sold to the wholesale electricity markets. Wind Energy Facility: All of the equipment, machinery and structures together utilized to convert wind to electricity. This includes, but is not limited to, developer-owned electrical equipment, storage, collection and supply equipment, service and access roads, and one or more wind turbines. Wind Turbine: A device that converts kinetic wind energy into rotational energy to drive an electrical generator. A wind turbine typically consists of a tower, nacelle body, and a rotor with two or more blades. B. Purpose: The purpose of this section is to: 1. Promote the use of renewable energy systems, including the creation of new large-scale ground-mounted solar photovoltaic installations, wind energy facilities, and Battery Energy Storage Systems (BESS). 2. Provide standards for the placement, design, construction, operation, monitoring, modification and removal of such installations that address public safety and minimize impacts on scenic, natural and historic resources and residential viewsheds. 3. Ensure adequate financial assurance for the eventual decommissioning of such facilities. C. Applicability. 1. All renewable energy installations shall be installed in compliance with the requirements of Chicopee City Code Chapter 275 - 71; state and federal law, and the standards and procedures established by Chicopee Electric Light (CEL) or Western Massachusetts Electric Company (WM ECO). This requirement pertains to physical modifications that alter the type, configuration or size of installations pre-existing this ordinance and those installations permitted in accordance with this ordinance. This section also pertains to physical modifications that materially alter the type, configuration or size of these installations or related equipment. 2. Nothing in this chapter should be construed to prevent the installation of accessory roof mounted solar photovoltaic installations, Wind Energy Facilities, or BESS. D. Process. The following identifies those uses that are allowable and those that may be allowed only by special permit. The City Council is the special permit granting authority in accordance with Chicopee City Code, § 275-9. The construction and operation of all solar photovoltaic installations and wind energy facilities shall be consistent with all applicable local, state and federal requirements, including but not limited to all applicable safety, construction, electrical, and communications requirements. All buildings and fixtures forming part of a solar photovoltaic installation, wind energy facility, or BESS shall be constructed in accordance with the State Building Code, the [standards] of the National Fire Protection Association (NFPA). E. Utility Notification. 1. For installations that do not require a special permit: Prior to issuance of building and/or electrical permit, the installation owner or operator must enter into an interconnection agreement with the utility company that operates the electrical grid for which the installation connection is proposed. Proof of the interconnection agreement shall be presented to the Building Department with the permit application. Projects that are not designed to connect to an electrical grid are exempt but must comply with all other relevant requirements. 2. For installations requiring a special permit: No special permit applications shall be accepted unless installation owners provide written proof that they have notified the utility company that operates the electrical grid for which the installation connection is proposed. F. Solar. 1. Production for On-Site Use The following conditions shall apply to all installations designed to convert solar energy into a power source for residential, commercial, business and industrial uses where the primary purpose of the system is to generate power for those uses. These uses are permitted in any zoning district within the city. a. Visual Impact: All solar conversion installations shall be designed and located to minimize adverse visual impacts, defined as "an undertaking that alters directly or indirectly the viewshed from a property in a manner that would diminish that property's perceived value." Adverse visual impacts can be mitigated through a variety of actions in design, construction and maintenance. The removal of the natural or existing vegetation is the single most noticeable visual impact of a project and shall be held to a minimum to achieve community acceptance. Clearing only what vegetation is necessary for the construction can eliminate or reduce the need to mitigate. However, proper sight distances, clear zones and horizontal clearance requirements must be considered. All abutting property shall be visually screened from the project through any one or combination of the following: location, distance, plantings, existing vegetation (located on the same parcel as the installation) and fencing (not to exceed six feet). b. Pole Mounted Installations: If solar conversion installations are mounted on a pole or other apparatus separate from a principal or accessory structure, said apparatus must comply with accessory structure regulations within their respective zoning districts and be set back from adjoining property lot lines at a ratio of 1' apparatus height to 0.5' of setback or a minimum of the underlying setback requirement,. c. Rooftop Installations: Rooftop solar conversion installations that are not flush mounted must not exceed the overall building height limits of the underlying district. Height is measured to the highest protruding point of the solar energy system at its fullest extension, not to exceed 5' above the roof line. d. Wall-Mounted Installations: If solar conversion installations are mounted on building walls/facades, said installations must comply with minimum setback requirements as detailed within the property's respective zoning district. e. Utility Notification: Written proof that CEL or Eversource is in discussions with the applicant regarding an interconnection agreement must be submitted with all permit applications. No building or electrical permits will be issued until the installation owner or operator enters into an interconnection agreement with the utility company that operates the electrical grid for which the installation connection is proposed. Proof of the interconnection agreement shall be presented to the Building Department with the permit application. Projects that are not designed to connect to an electrical grid are exempt but must comply with all other relevant requirements. Reasonable efforts, as determined by the City Council with guidance from the Planning Department, shall be made to place all utility connections from the solar photovoltaic installation underground, depending on appropriate soil conditions, shape, and topography of the site and any requirements of the utility provider. Electrical transformers for utility interconnections may be aboveground if required by the utility provider. 2. Production for Off-Site Use The construction of a solar energy system intended for off-site generation as set forth in Chicopee City Code Chapter 275-6 and shall comply with all requirements set forth herein. a. 275-66: Burnett Road: Regulations promulgated in Chapter 275-66, which regulate new development on Burnett Road and appurtenant streets, shall not apply to solar energy projects proposed for the Burnett Road area of the City. b. Screening: Structures must be shielded from view and/or located to avoid adverse visual impacts as deemed necessary by and in the opinion of the Site Plan Review Advisory Committee. 1. Landscaping: (a) Plantings intended to provide screening shall be evergreen, installed at a minimum of 6' in height measured from the top of the root ball to the tip of the plant and spaced to create a visual barrier. (b) Deciduous buffers: deciduous or mixed deciduous and evergreen buffers shall be a minimum of 40' wide and are counted as part of the setback. 2. Natural features: Natural features and features designed to appear as natural features may be employed as visual barriers. Existing vegetation (located on the same parcel as the installation) must be at least 40' in width and adequately dense to provide sufficient screening. 3. Fencing: Fences shall be installed at a minimum of 6'and shall be solid in appearance. c. Setbacks: The purpose of setbacks is to mitigate adverse impacts on abutting properties. For large-scale, ground-mounted solar photovoltaic installations, front, side and rear setbacks shall be as follows: 1. Minimum of 50'. 2. Every

ANR-1 ii) Stormwater Committee Request: Documentation Requirement EPA Construction General Permit (CGP) From: To: Cc: Subject: Date: Nancy Goulart Kerrie Easterday; David Phillips; Lisa Caledonia Tom Ferry Construction General Permit (CGP) Thursday, August 20, 2026 11:30:15 AM Kerrie and Lisa, Please ask your respective boards/commission if they would consider adding as part of the application, a requirement that evidence of an approved CGP has been received from the EPA such as the permit number and date issued. I base this request on the advice I received from W&S (Jim) regarding questions I have on an existing project. "Regarding the NOI issue…For projects in Massachusetts disturbing one acre or more, the project operator generally files an NOI directly with EPA. EPA does not automatically file the CGP authorization with the municipality, and the permit number does not generally have to be shown on the approved plans unless specifically required by the municipality. For an MS4 community like Dighton, the Town could require the applicant or contractor to provide documentation of EPA CGP coverage, including the NPDES permit/authorization number, before land disturbance begins. I don't believe the Town's current regulations or permit procedures require this. Perhaps the easiest way to ensure NOI approval by permit applicants is to require notification to the Town by the applicant as a condition of approval. Maybe this is something that the Town would want to consider." If we had this requirement, the town would have assurance that the applicant has EPA approval, resolve questions about whether a SWPPP is required, and provide information that I think would improve communication amongst boards, commissions, committees. The SWC could add space for this information on its SW Permit Application for projects that do not fall under either Planning, Zoning, or the Con. Com. Thanks. From: To: Subject: Date: Daniel G Higgins Kerrie Easterday; Christopher Cunha; Jeff Carvalho; Joseph Figueiredo, Clerk; Leonard Hull Re: Construction General Permit (CGP) Monday, August 24, 2026 11:02:57 AM My understanding is that in the event the disturbance is greater than an acre, EPA generally requires getting a CGP from them but there are exceptions and in some cases waivers that EPA can grant. I think this is a good idea but with two changes: 1. "If" a CGP is required to be issued by the EPA then we need evidence of an approved permit from EPA. If it is exempt per EPA or they get a waiver then we don't need anything. We can of course require proof of EPA's decision. 2. We would need that evidence before construction can begin, not as part of the application with the Town. Application site plans can get revised multiple times before a final design is proposed. Requiring it already be approved when applying with us might mean multiple EPA filings and huge delays. This is actually what W&S is saying: "require before land disturbance begins" and "as a condition of approval". They are not suggesting pre-approval by EPA before ever approaching the town. Vitacco, Town Administrator Re: Principal Assessor Date. September 23, 2026 In accordance with the Town of Dighton Hiring Policy, the Town Administrator worked with the Human Resources Coordinator and the Board of Assessors to develop a list of candidates to present to the Board of Assessors for appointment to the position of Principal Assessor. The Town of Dighton received four candidates for the position of Principal Assessor. At a special meeting scheduled on September 1, 2026, the Board interviewed three candidates and at their next regularly scheduled meeting on September 9, 2026 the elected Board of Assessors voted unanimously to appoint Lisa Tetreult to the position of Principal Assessor. Ms. Tetreault has over fifteen years of municipal government experience in the assessing field. She has most recently been the Assistant Assessor for the Town of Eston, and between the years of 2018 — 2024 worked as the Senior Clerk for the Town of Dighton Assessing Office. Ms. Tetreault is in possession of the required credentials for the position including Massachusetts Department of Revenue course 101 and the Massachusetts Association of Assessing Officers (MAAO) Course 200. She also completed MAAO courses 5 and 6. In their interview of Ms. Tetreault, the Board determined she has the skill set and temperament to perform the essential tasks of the position. The Principal Assessor position is unique in that it requires appointment by both the Board of assessors and Board of Selectmen. Submitted for your approval. PRINCIPAL ASSESSOR JOB DESCRIPTION Position: Principal Assessor Department: Assessing Department Appointing Authority: Board of Assessors Reports to: Board of Assessors Works Under the Direction of: Board of Assessors Salary/Hourly Rate: $70,000.00 - $85,000.00 DOQ Hours: 35 hours per week; Monday through Thursday; May be required to work some night meetings and to attend Town Meetings Affiliation: Non-Union Benefitted Position: Yes POSITION DEFINITION This position serves under the general direction of the Board of Assessors and is a key member of Dighton’s Financial Team. The Assessor has the responsibility for the professional, administrative, and supervisory work related to the valuation of all residential, industrial and commercial real estate and personal property within the Town of Dighton in accordance with the Department of Revenue (DOR) regulations and related Massachusetts General Laws. ESSENTIAL FUNCTIONS The position is responsible for functions of a: highly technical nature requiring considerable judgement, independent thinking, and initiation. These functions include but are not limited to: e Overseeing the classification of all real and personal property on an annual basis and for the administration and management of MA DOR Re-Certifications every 5 years e Determining the total value of all real and personal property within the Town on an annual basis e Committing real estate, personal property, auto and boat excise amounts to the Tax Collector in order to produce tax bills for the Town e Responsible for reviewing and decision-making on all applications for all exemptions approved by voters including elderly, veterans, blind and hardship cases with the aid of professional clerical staff e Collecting and preparing all data and documentation for cases to be tried at the Appellate Tax Board and retaining expert appraiser, attorney, and rendering expert testimony in defense of contested assessments as needed © Determining the amount of the Overlay Account needed for each fiscal year and past fiscal year retentions as well as determining the amount of Overlay Surplus © Conducting statistical analysis of property values and their relation to recent sales data and other trends in the market with aid of professional staff e Managing all data dealing with transactions on all real and personal property records, assessments, exemptions, abatements and motor vehicle excise taxes © Negotiate PILOT and TIF agreements when necessary e Supervising, training and directing appraisal and administrative staff ® Supervising the work of professional contract employees for revaluations, large scope appraisals and legal defense at the Appellate Tax Board e Participating in regular budget planning, review, analysis and forecasting as a key member of Dighton’s Financial Team that includes the Town Administrator, Town Accountant and Treasurer-Collector e Developing, proposing and administering Assessors’ Department budget on an annual basis e Participating in afternoon or evenings required to attend Board of Assessors, Board of Selectmen and other related meetings e Prepares and posts meeting agendas e Takes and transcribes meeting minutes for Board of Assessors’ meetings e Assisting in the preparation of the Tax Recap Sheet, Tax Rate(s) and providing supporting documentation for the submission to the Department of Revenue (DOR/DLS) ® Performing other related duties as required SUPERVISION Works under the direction of the Board of Assessors. RECOMMENDED MINIMUM QUALIFICATIONS EDUCATION AND EXPERIENCE e Bachelor’s Degree and/or five years of real and personal property appraisal experience e Requires travel to properties within the town and have the ability to measure and list all Residential, Commercial and Industrial property e Completion of Massachusetts Association of Assessing Officers (MAAO) Courses 101 and 200 within six months of appointment e MAAO designation may be required within 3 years ADDITIONAL REQUIREMENTS Valid Driver’s License. Strong mathematical skills. Must be bondable. Licensed Massachusetts Realtor is a plus. KNOWLEDGE, ABILITY AND SKILLS Comprehensive knowledge of up-to-date appraisal principles and practices, including all applicable Massachusetts General Laws. Familiarity with Massachusetts General Laws relating to municipal finance. Knowledge of all related regulations and requirements promulgated by the Massachusetts Department of Revenue regarding assessment and tax administration. Working knowledge of CAMA appraisal system software; office practices and procedures; knowledge of GAAP and required computer applications such as VADAR and Excel. General knowledge of the organization, operations, and procedures of local government helpful.

The language does not make any substantive changes to the Open Meeting Law other than extending the expiration date of the temporary provisions regarding remote meetings from March 31, 2025 to June 30, 2027. Interdepartmental Transfer $9,540.00 from the Reserve Fund to Auditor Salary to cover additional hours for FY26 back-log and stay on track with FY27 tasks on schedule 3 Information           Planning & Community Development 50 Payson Avenue, Suite B19 Easthampton, MA 01027 Allyson Manuel, Director amanuel@easthamptonma.gov (413) 529-1400 DATE: August 13, 2026 TO: City Council FROM: Planning Department RE: Ferry St Improvements - Order of Taking ___ Dear City Councilors, Attached is a packet of information that constitutes the Order of Taking necessary for the City to acquire temporary and permanent easements associated with planned improvements to the Ferry Street and Parsons Street intersection. This packet also includes a vote to compensate land owners for each individual taking. We are requesting that the City Council hold a public hearing and consider voting on this matter at their September 16, 2026 meeting. The City was awarded an FY2025 HousingWorks grant to address public safety and accessibility concerns at the Parsons Street and Ferry Street intersection. This grant funds work to improve vehicle sightlines and to increase pedestrian safety and connectivity by creating a new sidewalk on the south side of Ferry Street. In order to accomplish these improvements, an existing retaining wall will be relocated several feet back from the roadway. Additionally, two crosswalks with rapid-flashing beacons will be installed on Ferry Street. These improvements require the City to acquire permanent and temporary construction easements on a total of eight properties. The City has communicated with all affected property owners since April 2026 and recently acquired appraisals for the permanent and temporary easements. Owners of two properties donated their easements to the City and Just Compensation Reports for the remaining properties were sent to owners in July 2026, along with notification of the City Council public hearing. The project design plans and easement plans are posted on the Planning Department website (https://www.easthamptonma.gov/978/Ferry-Street-HousingWorks-Infrastructure). The City’s team includes the City Planner, City Engineer and DPW Director, the design consultant (VHB), the City’s appraiser (Crowley and Associates), and the City Solicitor. The requested action from City Council includes voting on the Order of Taking to take the easements and an appropriation of $50,810 to pay property owners from the Parsons & Ferry Intersection Capital Project account. The following information is included in this packet: 1. Resolution 2. Order of Taking a. Exhibit A - Order of Taking with Exhibits b. Exhibit B - Chart of Payments c. Exhibit C - Donations 3. Stamped Plan of Easements, dated April 2026 4. Draft vote language We anticipate that the City Planner and/or Senior Planner will be present at any City Council subcommittee meetings as well as the full City Council meeting on September 16, 2026 to answer any questions. Please feel free to contact me if you have any additional questions. Sincerely, Johanna Stacy AICP Senior Planner A RESOLUTION TO ACQUIRE BY EMINENT DOMAIN TAKING CERTAIN REAL PROPERTY IDENTIFIED ON A PLAN OF LAND ENTITLED: “Owned by the City of Easthampton Easthampton, Massachusetts Hampshire County Layout Plans Showing Location of Easements For the Purpose of Reconstructing Parsons Street At Ferry Street For the City of Easthampton” Whereas: The City of Easthampton, Massachusetts (“City”) desires to expand and reconstruct all or portions of Ferry and Parsons Streets as shown on a plan of land entitled “Owned by the City of Easthampton Easthampton, Massachusetts Hampshire County Layout Plans Showing Location of Easements For the Purpose of Reconstructing Parsons Street At Ferry Street For the City of Easthampton” dated April 23, 2026 by VHB, Inc. and stamped by Christopher C. Danforth, PLS to be recorded in the Registry of Deeds for Hampshire County, Massachusetts (“Plan”), which Plan is expressly incorporated herein by reference (collectively “Property”); Whereas: It is necessary for the City to acquire by eminent domain taking permanent and temporary easements over certain parcels of land as shown on the Plan and as further detailed in Exhibit A to the Order of Taking (collectively “Order”) such Order to be recorded in the Registry of Deeds for Hampshire County, Massachusetts; and Whereas: Chapter 40, Section 14; Chapter 79, Section 1 et. seq.; and Chapter 82, Section 24 of the Massachusetts General Laws, and other applicable statutes, and of any and every power and authority to it, granted or implied, and the Charter for the City allow the City to acquire easements over real property by eminent domain for municipal purposes; and Whereas: The City Council has determined it is in the best interests of the City to obtain the Property shown on the Plan and detailed in the Order for the purpose of reconstructing and expanding Ferry and Parsons Streets, public ways in the City; and Whereas: The Mayor of the City is authorized to enter into all agreements and execute any and all instruments, as may be necessary, on behalf of the City to affect said taking; and Whereas: The Clerk of the City Council be authorized to execute all instruments relative to the taking, as may be necessary, on behalf of the City to affect said taking; and Whereas: To meet said purchase, exchange or taking of the Property, it is necessary to appropriate funds in the amount of up to $50,810 from the Parsons & Ferry Intersection Capital Project account or to accept the donation of certain easements or other property rights with the approval of the City Council. I move that the City Council for the City of Easthampton, Massachusetts vote to: 1. Appropriate up to $50,810 from Parsons & Ferry Intersection Capital Project account (052) to pay the cost of acquisition, by conveyance, exchange or eminent domain taking, the real property described in the “Order of Taking” for Parsons Street At Ferry Street for the purposes described in Exhibit A to this Vote. (“Order of Taking”). 2. Approve and adopt the Order of Taking with all Exhibits. 3. Award eminent domain damages for the properties affected by the Order of Taking in the amounts detailed in Exhibit B to this Vote. 4. Accept the donation of certain real property rights by the record owners of properties affected by the Order of Taking as described in Exhibit C. 5. Authorize the Mayor of the City, as necessary, to enter into all agreements and execute any and all instruments relative to taking of the real property described in the Order of Taking, as may be necessary, on behalf of the City to effectuate said eminent domain taking(s); and alternatively the Clerk of the City Council is authorized to execute any and all instruments relative to the taking of the Property, as may be necessary, on behalf of the City to effectuate said eminent domain taking. 6. Section numbers correspond to agenda packets and are not an indication of the order of the agenda Page 1 of 1 Town of Erving Select Board Public Meeting Participation Guidance The Select Board welcomes residents to communicate questions, comments or concerns. Participants at Select Board meetings are notified that the meetings are both video and audio recorded, and comments provided will become part of the record. While offering public input, it is important that the Select Board is also allowed enough time to conduct their other business. The following guidelines have been established to make the best use of time at Select Board meetings. 1. To request time on the Select Board agenda, persons must contact the Town Administrator at (413) 422-2800, Ext.1102 or at SBRequests@erving-ma.gov by noon on the Tuesday before the meeting. a. Requests will be submitted to the Chairperson for consideration and scheduling. b. Supporting documentation related to the request must be provided to the Administrator’s office by noon on the Thursday prior to the meeting. The Chairperson may remove requested agenda topics that are made without supporting documentation. 2. The Select Board encourages public participation as follows: a. Town residents can bring comments before the Select Board that require discussion and are on the agenda, only after being recognized by the Chair. If your issue is not on the agenda, you may bring it up under “Future agenda items”. b. “Topics not anticipated” should be brought to the Chair for possible consideration prior to the meeting. c. Please try to keep your comments short and to the point. d. If it appears that the topic(s) being discussed will consume longer than the time allocated then, at the discretion of the Chair, the matter will be placed on an upcoming Select Board meeting agenda. e. If you believe that your topic will require more time or desire to make a more formal presentation than is allowed under these guidelines, please contact the Town Administrator to ask to be put on a future agenda so that we can properly allocate enough time. f. You are free to ask questions or to make your point for all to consider. However, engaging in active debate with Select Board or audience members will not be allowed. g. All comments and questions must be directed to the Chair of the Select Board per MGL Chapter 30A, Section 20(g). h. Participants are expected to speak from the presenter/guest table. 3. Employees and Board members who have business with the Select Board should be placed on the agenda beforehand (see Item # 1.). 4. Anyone wishing to contact the Select Board in writing may do so at: Town of Erving, Attn: Select Board, 12 East Main Street, Erving, Massachusetts 01344 Alternatively, members of the public can complete a Select Board submission form at the meeting sign in table and office staff member will follow up. The Select Board appreciates your cooperation in honoring these guidelines. From Massachusetts Attorney General Official Website What public participation in meetings must be allowed? Under the Open Meeting Law, the public is permitted to attend meetings of public bodies but is excluded from an executive session that is called for a valid purpose listed in the law. Any member of the public also has a right to make an audio or video recording of an open session of a public meeting. A member of the public who wishes to record a meeting must first notify the Chair and must comply with reasonable requirements regarding audio or video equipment established by the chair so as not to interfere with the meeting. The Chair is required to inform other attendees of such recording at the beginning of the meeting. While the public is permitted to attend an open meeting, an individual may not address the public body without permission of the Chair. An individual is not permitted to disrupt a meeting of a public body, and at the request of the Chair, all members of the public shall be silent. If after clear warning, a person continues to be disruptive, the Chair may order the person to leave the meeting, and if the person does not leave, the Chair may authorize a constable or other officer to remove the person. Subscribe TOWN-CITY-GOVERNMENT Erving, Athol celebrate state, federal funds for housing development by Erin-Leigh Hoffman September 8, 2026 Juana Matias, secretary of the Executive Office of Housing and Livable Communities, announces funding for the Evergreen Circle housing complex on Care Drive in Erving at the Erving Senior & Community Center on Thursday. Credit: PAUL FRANZ / Staff Photo Opt-Out Signal Honored Erving, Athol celebrate state, federal funds for housin 1x About 7 Minutes ERVING — The mood at the Erving Senior & Community Center was jubilant on Thursday afternoon as Juana Matias, secretary of the Executive Office of Housing and Livable Communities, announced that $14.7 million in state and federal funding will go to Rural Development Inc. to support the Evergreen Circle housing development. The gathering in Erving was part of a larger announcement by the Healey-Driscoll administration that nearly $278 million in state and federal financing will support 29 developments in 20 municipalities across Massachusetts. This includes state and federal low-income housing tax credits and subsidy financing from the Executive Office of Housing and Livable Communities. Erving, in partnership with Rural Development Inc. (RDI), Berkshire Design Group and Austin Design Cooperative, will build 18 one-bedroom apartments for seniors ages 62 and older, and eight multigenerational units, each with two or three bedrooms, along an extension of Care Drive. This will bring senior housing to the community 24 years after the town first identified the need for senior housing in its June 2002 Master Plan. Opt-Out Signal Honored Juana Matias, secretary of the Executive Office of Housing and Livable Communities, announces funding for the Evergreen Circle housing project on Care Drive in Erving at the Erving Senior & Community Center on Thursday. Matias said the event in Erving was a “tremendous celebration” of the Healey-Driscoll administration’s commitment to building housing across the state. “Here we are supporting 26 units of intergenerational living that the state has never done before in a community like Erving, and we’re interested in continuing to work with local partners, because it happens locally,” Matias said. “That’s where it first needs to happen.” Gov. Maura Healey was expected to attend the celebration, but a personal matter prevented her from being there, Matias said. In a statement released prior to her scheduled tour in six communities that are benefiting from this funding, including Northampton in Hampshire County, Healey said the money will support the development of new housing, along with the preservation and rehabilitation of existing housing. Opt-Out Signal Honored “This is about making sure that Massachusetts is a state where teachers, nurses, firefighters and young people can actually afford to live,” Healey said. “Communities of every size are stepping up with smart, creative plans to build the homes their residents need,” Lt. Gov. Kim Driscoll said in a statement. “These awards will turn underused properties into housing, modernize housing and preserve homes that residents already depend on.” In Erving, RDI, a nonprofit created by the Franklin County Regional Housing & Redevelopment Authority, received a combined $10.8 million in state and federal low-income housing tax credit allocations, and $3.9 million in subsidy financing from the state Executive Office of Housing and Livable Communities. When coupled with previous grants and loans, the latest awards bring RDI’s project budget to $17.4 million. RDI Executive Director Gina Govoni and Real Estate Project Manager/Housing Development Director Alyssa Larose shared their excitement about the announcement and the visit from state officials. Govoni pointed out how Erving is unique for being a community that earned funding in its first round of applications. Opt-Out Signal Honored “I think this award shows how well prepared and how well developed it is,” Govoni said, giving credit to her colleague Larose, who is the project lead for Evergreen Circle. Govoni noted this funding from the state is exclusively for RDI and its role in constructing the housing, while the town of Erving is supporting the underground infrastructure development needed to support the housing. Larose said there is a funding gap of $650,000, and a Housing Choice Grant is being explored to complete the scope of work. Erving has a $2.4 million grant from the HousingWorks Infrastructure Program for water and sewer infrastructure upgrades, along with an extension of Care Drive that the multigenerational townhouses and senior housing will abut. Town Administrator Bryan Smith, who was hired in 2016, recalled how he was first introduced to the project while interviewing for his job. Ten years later, he said it “feels amazing” to be part of seeing the project get this far. “To know that we are here 10 years later, and we’ve finally got all the pieces,” Smith said, citing the right organizing partners, permitting and funding, “we’re at the precipice of construction. This is amazing. It all feels like it’s all come to fruition.” Before Smith’s tenure, other town officials and residents led the charge for senior housing, and they continue to be involved. Chair of the Senior Housing Committee and Selectboard member William Bembury, who sat on the 2002 Master Planning Committee, said he’s “ecstatic,” but he is also feeling some shock over the realization that, at long last, “this is going to happen.” Opt-Out Signal Honored When asked how momentum for furthering the housing project has been maintained for more than two decades, Bembury credited the continued support of local and state organizations and their knowledge on how to proceed. Admittedly, Bembury said he was sad that some seniors moved out of town because they could no longer afford to live in Erving due to the cost of homeownership. Then there’s those who have died before senior housing could become a reality. However, Bembury is looking to the future for those who can make it back to Erving. “That’s the sad part, but there’s still some folks out there that have an opportunity to come back,” Bembury said about Evergreen Circle. “They’re still with us, and so I hope they take that opportunity on.” Athol among other funding recipients The Pequoig House in Athol is among the projects to receive a portion of this funding. Kevin Connor, spokesman for the Executive Office of Housing and Livable Communities, told the Athol Daily News that Pequoig House will be getting just over $1.8 million. Pequoig owner Kyle Carbone said the award will supplement an $850,000 Affordable Housing Trust grant the former hotel received from the Federal Home Loan Bank of Boston in January to undertake a building-wide renovation. “That $1.8 million is going directly into the rehabilitation project for the property,” said Carbone. “One of the great parts of affordable housing in this regard is that tenants’ rents are not changing at all, at least the tenants’ portions of the rents. The rents they’re paying today are the exact same rents they’ll be paying once the rehab is finished.” Carbone called the overall project at the Pequoig “very creative.” “Beside these funding sources, we also obtained federal and state historic tax credits, LEAN (Low-Income Energy Affordability Network) funding, which is state funding designed for insulation and air sealing,” he added. “So, there are a lot of moving parts here that we now need to piece together and get to the closing table, but we’re extremely excited about this award, which completes our capital stack.” A capital stack is the structured hierarchy of financing sources used to fund a company, real estate project or investment venture. Opt-Out Signal Honored “From here, we’ll be wrapping everything up at the end of November and closing on all of this funding, and our architect will finalize the construction drawings, and we’ll probably be starting the rehab in January of 2027,” Carbone said. Athol Town Manager Shaun Suhoski said that since 1895, “the Pequoig building has stood sentinel as a landmark structure in Athol’s central business district.” First operated as a hotel into the mid-20th century, the building was renovated into affordable, senior housing in 1982. “The property owners will utilize these funds to make needed improvements to the historic building while ensuring the retention of 53-units of needed affordable housing for decades to come,” Suhoski added. “The town appreciates the Healey-Driscoll administration’s emphasis on supporting quality housing options affordable to a range of income.” © 2026 Athol Daily News Opt-Out Signal Honored COMMONWEALTH OF MASSACHUSETTS TOWN OF ERVING OFFICE OF THE BOARD OF WATER COMMISSIONERS Water Commissioners Warrant to the Collector Final Water Use Charges 2nd Commitment, Fiscal Year 2027 To: Michele Turner, Tax/Water Collector for the Town of Erving in the County of Franklin Greetings: IN THE NAME OF THE COMMONWEALTH OF MASSACHUSETTS, you are hereby required to levy on and collect One Hundred Forty-two Dollars and Seventy-seven Cents ($142.77) for final charges at 16 Prospect Street (#190), for total charges of One Hundred Forty-two Dollars and Seventy-seven Cents ($142.77). Said charges are to be paid to Michele Turner, Town of Erving Tax Collector, or to his/her successor in office, at the times and in the manner provided by General Laws, Chapter 60, Section 2. As Collector, you must provide the Treasurer an account of all charges and fees collected by you. In addition, you are to make written return of said water charges and interest with your water charge list and of your doings thereon at such times as the Water Commissioners shall require. You are to complete and make up an account of the collection of the whole sum hereon, committed to you, with interest, on or before December 31 of the current year. The owner of the premises shall be responsible for the payment of all charges for water and service furnished to the property. Under the General Laws of Massachusetts Chapter 40 Section 42A as accepted in Article 7 of the Erving Special Town Meeting June 29, 1992, unpaid water bills become a lien on the property immediately following the due date for such rate or charge and collections will be made by the sale of property. Water bills will be mailed semi-annually. Water bill payment will be due thirty (30) days from the postmarked date of the original bill. Overdue notices will go to property owners and "current occupant" fortyfive (45) days after the postmarked date of the original bill. Shut off notices will go to property owners and “current occupant" sixty (60) days after the postmarked date of the original bill. The shut off notice will specify that shut off will occur on or after Monday. Shut off will not occur sooner than seventy-five (75) days from the postmarked date of the original billing. The shut off notice will clearly state the earliest date that shut off can occur. There will be no further notice. Service will be restored as soon as possible, upon payment in full of all amounts due. The levy and collection of the amounts are hereby committed to you. All interest, charges, and fees as provided by law, also apply. You are to have and to exercise all the powers conferred by the laws of this Commonwealth upon collectors of taxes. Given under our hands this 14th day of September 2026. WATER COMMISSIONERS OF ERVING ___ Jacob A. Smith, Chair ___ William A. Bembury ___ Jacquelyn M. Boyden Select Board Bryan Smith Town Administrator September 4, 2026 To: Select Board From: Bryan Smith, Town Administrator RE: Treasurer After your last meeting our Office had correspondence with the finalist and was able to confirm participation in a finalist interview for Monday, September 14, 2026. Your finalist candidate is Michele Turner. Michele is scheduled to interview you at 7:00PM. A copy of her resume and cover letter is included for your review along with a copy of the interview questions that you worked on at your last meeting. Treasurer Finalist Interview Questions September 14, 2026 1. Tell us about your experience in municipal ﬁnance, treasury operations, and payroll administration. 2. Describe your experience processing payroll from start to ﬁnish. How do you handle payroll corrections when errors are discovered? 3. What steps do you take to protect the conﬁdentiality of employee information? 4. How would you prevent fraud or unauthorized payments and please describe a time when you identiﬁed an error or control weakness in a payroll or ﬁnancial process. 5. Knowing that this is a two-person office, how would you maintain delineation of duties while allowing for cross training and continuation of operations? 6. What experience do you have with municipal investments and investment policies and how would you balance liquidity, safety, and investment earnings? 7. What does good customer service look like in a Treasurer office? Please describe what it looks like to work with employees, members of public and work with department heads. 8. Describe how you would explain a complex ﬁnancial or payroll issue to nonﬁnancial staff. How would you present ﬁnancial matters to the Finance Committee, Select Board members, and to members of the public at Town Meeting? 9. If we were to ask a coworker, what are three positive and three negative things they would say about you? 10. If you were hired, what would be your priorities during your ﬁrst 90 days? 11. Do you have any questions that the Select Board can answer? Invoice Warrant Report

Boyden Select Board Bryan Smith Town Administrator August 28, 2026 To: Select Board From: Bryan Smith, Town Administrator RE: Town Branding As requested by the Select Board, I am including the last draft logo image and color pallet from 2020 that were being considered by the Select Board for the Town Branding project. As we discussed, a great deal of time was spent at Select Board meetings reviewing colors and fonts. It may be possible to identify aspects that the Select Board would like to proceed with, even if the imagery needs to be changed. Also, in 2019 and 2020, the Select Board also worked with UMass Amherst on the Erving Center visioning project and there were example signs that the Board members seemed interested in considering. I have included a rendering from the project for your review. Additionally, there have been some conversations amongst department heads of the last year or so regarding this topic. While no formal logo proposal has been identified, the staff would like to continue build on the slogan “A great place to live” and identified a request to continue efforts such as the banners that were displayed a few years ago that had messages such as: “A great place to work” “A great place to play” “A great place to learn” “A great place to read” “A great place to paddle”, etc. Staff members have also asked that the goal be to develop a style guide and templates for things such as internal building signage, department specific logos, and presentation slide templates. This would include decals for Town-owned trucks and vehicles, exterior building and park signs. Smith Issue Date / Effective Date This manual of policies and procedures is issued and effective on September ___, 2026. Table of Contents Welcome... 2 Article 1: Registration and attendance ... 2 Article 2: Behavioral Expectations ... 2 Confidentiality ... 2 Health & Hygiene ... 2 Independent Function ... 3 Appropriate Attire... 3 Inappropriate Behavior Policy ... 3 Article 3: Exercise Program Participation ... 4 Article 4: Children and Animals ... 4 Children ... 4 Animals ... 4 Article 5: Lost and Found... 4 Article 6: Volunteers ... 4 Article 7: Closings ... 5 Article 8: Donations and Contributions ... 5 Article 9: Emergency Protocols and Evacuation Plan ... 5 Medical Situations ... 6 Fire/Evacuation Situations ... 6 Tips for dealing with dealing with an emergency situation ... 6 Senior & Community Center Policy Mannual 1 Welcome The Town of Erving welcomes you to the Senior & Community Center. We are committed to making everyone feel accepted and part of our community. We welcome all people, whatever their race, religious affiliation, age, socio-economic status, nationality, ethnic background, gender, sexual orientation, veteran status, or mental/physical ability. Article 1: Registration and attendance We expect that all program participants are required to complete a member profile form before participating in any programs or activities. This form is located at the main desk. Members are required to sign in daily to document their program attendance on the touch screen located in the main lobby. If a member forgets their key tag, they can still sign in. Please ask a member of staff for assistance. Members must update their profile as information changes so that we may keep accurate contact information. Especially in the event of am emergency, this information is crucial. Article 2: Behavioral Expectations We expect that all visitors, participants, volunteers and staff will be conscious of the rights of others and will act in a courteous, considerate and socially appropriate manner. We expect all to show respect for others, their possessions, the building and our equipment. Confidentiality The policy of the Senior & Community Center is to maintain confidentiality on all matters concerning visitors, participants, volunteers and staff. 1. All information contained in Senior Center files and records, as well as information obtained while performing Center duties, are CONFIDENTIAL. Information will not be shared, released, or discussed with unauthorized persons. It will only be used by personnel authorized to perform duties relative to the files and records. 2. Individual identities or information concerning specific members, volunteers or staff may not be released without his/her permission. 3. Violations of the Confidentiality Policy are subject to disciplinary action. Health & Hygiene Participants must: 1. Maintain personal hygiene in accordance with health and safety standards. Participants must be able to take responsibility for their own personal care which includes, but is not limited to, toileting, feeding and medication. Senior & Community Center staff are not trained or otherwise qualified to provide assistance with medication and other personal health and medical matters. 2. Refrain from smoking, using tobacco, or electronic smoking devices inside the Center or within 50’ of any entrance. 3. To ensure a healthy and welcoming environment for everyone, the Senior & Community Center respectfully asks that visitors, participants, staff, and volunteers refrain from wearing Senior & Community Center Policy Mannual 2 strongly scented perfumes, colognes, or lotions. Some individuals have sensitivity or allergic reactions to strong scents, which can cause respiratory distress, headaches, or other symptoms. 4. Participants shall not use the bathroom facilities for personal care such as hair washing or sponge bathing. Independent Function Participants must be: 1. Capable of functioning independently and performing basic skills of daily living, including self-toileting, self-feeding; or having a care giver present to assist with personal needs. 2. Capable of self-mobility such as walking safely and independently, or with the use and ability to operate and maintain their own assistive devices. 3. Participants must not present a danger to themselves or others. Appropriate Attire Visitors, participants, volunteers, and staff are expected to wear appropriate attire while at the Senior & Community Center, which includes: 1. Clothing must be free of discriminatory or offensive language, images or logos. 2. Clothing should not be overly tight or revealing. 3. Footwear must be appropriate to allow for safe participation in the activity or program. Inappropriate Behavior Policy This policy and procedures are intended to maintain the integrity of the Senior & Community Center, its mission, the visitors, participants, and volunteers. The following is considered inappropriate behavior as directed towards other visitors, participants, volunteers, staff or the public: 1. Verbal, physical or any other form of harassment or unwanted contact; 2. Disruptive behavior during activities- i.e. yelling, inappropriate comments, vulgar language, or rudeness; 3. Removing items from the Center or from other member’s personal belongings without permission; 4. Mistreating or damaging the facility and/or furnishings; 5. Failure of the aide/companion to abide by center guidelines; 6. Any behavior which is construed as bullying. This includes prohibiting anyone from sitting next to you during an activity (saving seats), coercing others to give money or rides and “picking” on an individual or group. Procedure: 1. A staff member will confidentially discuss any incident with the participant, reminding them of the policies and procedures regarding participation. The staff member may also speak to the family or caregiver regarding the incident. These conversations will be documented in the participant’s file as an Incident Report. 2. If inappropriate behavior continues, a written warning will be issued regarding participant’s behavior and possible consequences. Participant/family/caregiver shall receive a copy, and another will be placed in the participant’s file. 3. Temporary suspension from participation in Center activities, for a time to be determined, will follow if the participant is not able to correct or modify behavior as outlined in the section above. The decision of suspension will be made by the Director. Senior & Community Center Policy Mannual 3 4. In the case of a more serious infraction, such as violence, the Director will immediately suspend the member from the Center, and the Police will be called. Article 3: Exercise Program Participation We expect that all visitors, participants, volunteers, staff have consulted with their personal physician prior to beginning an exercise program. 1. Partcipants are required to complete a registration form. 2. After injury or medical procedure, the participant must have a signed physician’s note to return to the exercise program. 3. The Center reserves the right to deny or suspend participation of any member at any time. 4. All instructors must maintain current liability insurance and appropriate teaching certification(s). 5. In the event of an accident or injury, emergency medical services will be called, and an incident report shall be completed. Article 4: Children and Animals Children Children are permitted to visit the Senior & Community Center for specific intergenerational programs and under controlled conditions, as scheduled and approved by the Director. When children are permitted to participate, the age for participation must be appropriate for the activity; children too young to properly participate will not be allowed. Children must be supervised by a caregiver or guardian at all times. Animals Service animals are permitted to visit the Senior & Community Center, but as a general matter pets are not permitted. At the discretion of the Director, and as scheduled, animals as part of a program may be allowed. Article 5: Lost and Found 1. The Senior & Community Center Lost and Found is located in the Great Room. 2. Items will be stored for one month and donated to the appropriate facility thereafter. 3. Cash, jewelry or any other item believed to be of significant value will immediately be secured and turned over to the Erving Police Department. 4. Please make sure to check with staff as soon as you notice a personal item is missing. 5. The staff will make every effort to locate the appropriate owner of a misplaced item; however, the Center is not responsible for personal belongings. Article 6: Volunteers 1. Unpaid volunteer positions are available on an ongoing or one-time basis. Positions may include instructors, program leaders, kitchen, garden and front desk. Senior & Community Center Policy Mannual 4 2. 3. 4. 5. 6. 7. A written job description will be provided for each volunteer position. Prospective volunteers will receive orientation, training and updates to help them complete their position responsibly. Volunteers will be supervised by a staff member. The Center encourages volunteers to discuss their ideas, concerns and responsibilities with the staff. Both volunteers and staff have the right to request a change in responsibilities. Volunteers must record their hours. Volunteer applications are available at the front desk. Once completed, the application can be returned to a staff member. Volunteers must submit to a CORI/SORI check. After the mandatory background check is returned the volunteer coordinator will schedule the volunteer for training and shifts. The Town of Erving accepts student volunteers who need community service hours. Students are asked to commit to a set schedule and maintain a record of their hours. For the safety of our members, we do not accept court mandated volunteers. Article 7: Closings 1. The Senior and Community Center may remain open regardless of school delays or closures. 2. The Staff will make every attempt to notify individuals in the event of a closure. 3. If the Senior and Community Center is closed for a weather-related event, information will be posted on WWLP.com, the Erving Town website and our Facebook page (Erving Senior Center). 4. The Director or a member of staff will notify class instructors or program facilitators regarding cancellations and closures. 5. If you have a commitment at the Center that you need to cancel or delay, please call the main number at (413)423-3649 and leave a message. 6. Please see our website for more information regarding notification options. Article 8: Donations and Contributions 1. The Senior & Community Center accepts monetary donations. 2. title: Falmouth Rights of Nature Implementation Collaborative
text: Members of the Falmouth Select Board will attend and participate in the following meeting: AGENDA Falmouth Rights of Nature Implementation Collaborative Tuesday, September 15, 2026 Falmouth Public Library Hermann Room 300 Main Street, MA 02540 6:30 P.M. – 8:30 P.M. Hosted by: Falmouth Climate Action Network (FalCAN) Event Details: • Date: Tuesday, September 15 • Networking Period: 6:15 PM • Panel Discussion: 6:30 PM – 8:30 PM • Location: Hermann Room, Falmouth Public Library (Main Branch) • Hospitality: Light refreshments will be provided FALMOUTH RIGHTS OF NATURE IMPLEMENTATION COLLABORATIVE A REGIONAL WORKING GROUP FOR MUNICIPAL INNOVATION AND ENVIRONMENTAL GOVERNANCE OPPORTUNITY Falmouth has the opportunity to become a statewide model for municipal Rights of Nature implementation by demonstrating how RON principles and Article 97 protections can be translated into practical, collaborative action that benefits both communities and the ecosystems upon which they depend. In 2024, the Town of Falmouth Selectboard unanimously adopted the Rights of Nature Resolution, recognizing the rights of ecosystems and directing that these principles guide municipal decisionmaking. Massachusetts also provides constitutional protection for conservation lands and natural resources through Article 97 of the Massachusetts Constitution Together, these legal and policy frameworks present a unique opportunity: to explore how municipalities can translate and innovate rights of nature values into practical governance, planning, conservation, and community decision-making. PURPOSE The Falmouth Rights of Nature Implementation Collaborative is a proposed interdisciplinary working group that will convene legal, environmental, municipal, scientific, Tribal, nonprofit, and community leaders to identify practical strategies for implementing RON principles at the local level. The Collaborative will serve as a forum for shared learning, legal and policy analysis, and the development of implementation tools that municipalities can use to strengthen environmental stewardship while operating within existing legal authority. INITIAL OBJECTIVES Identify opportunities to integrate Rights of Nature and Article 97 principles into Municipal decisionmaking. Develop practical guidance, model policies, and implementation tools for local governments. Identify pilot projects in Falmouth Foster collaboration amoung municipal officials, conservation organizations, legal professionals, scientists, educators, and community stakeholders. Create a scalable model that may inform other Massachusetts communities. POTENTIAL AREAS OF FOCUS Municipal planning, zoning, conservation, land use and natual resource protection. Climate resilience and nature-based solutions, watershed and coastal ecosystem stewardship. Policy, governance, community education and public engagement WHO SHOULD PARTICIPATE? The Collaborative seeks participation from individuals with expertise or interest in: Municipal governance and planning, Environmental/Municipal/Earth Law, Conservation and Land Trusts, Climate reseilience, Scientific research, Wampanoag Tribal Leadership. Initial Convening: The first meeting will bring together intived participants to: Explore shared goals and opportunities and identify priority implementation projects; Establish working groups and develop a roadmap for future collaboration. CONVENED BY: Dr. Elizabeth Gladfelter, Michelle J. Morris, Esq, Geralyn Schad & Mike Fogarty

text: FITCHBURG CITY CLERK Aug 28 2026 3:23 pm WELCOME TO THE FITCHBURG CITY COUNCIL September 2, 2026 Fitchburg Legislative Building 700 Main Street Fitchburg MA 01420 7:00 PM This meeting can also be viewed live on FATV. Go to www.fatv.org/watch-fatv for more information on accessing this meeting. This is intended to help you understand the meeting format and assist you with the rules of the Council as they pertain to your participation. All meetings of the Fitchburg City council are open to the public. This does not mean that the public participates in all aspects of the meeting. It simply means that the meeting itself, including all discussions and votes, is open for public view. Executive Session The only time a Council meeting can be closed to the public is when the Council votes for Executive Session in order to discuss sensitive matters in private, such as pending litigation. Any votes taken however, must be taken in open session. OPPORTUNITIES FOR THE PUBLIC TO SPEAK DURING A COUNCIL MEETING: Public Forum The Public Forum occurs immediately following the Pledge of Allegiance. The President will ask if anyone in the audience wishes to speak on any matter appearing on the Agenda. If you wish to address the Council, you must stand and be recognized and follow these rules before speaking: 1. 2. 3. 4. State your name and city of residence. Approach the center table and either stand or sit. This allows you to be seen and heard clearly by everyone in attendance. You may speak only on items appearing on the agenda for no more than (2) minutes. Copies of the agenda are available on the center table prior to the meeting. Please state the petition, order, ordinance, or resolution number to which you refer. Public Hearings Public hearings are held on various issues such as Special Permits and Zoning changes. The same rules apply with the following exceptions: 1. You must stand and be recognized either “in favor” or “in opposition” when asked by the Council President. 2. You need not refer to the petition number. If you have any questions or comments either before or after the meeting, any Councilor would be happy to assist you. Thank you for your interest! I. Go to www.fatv.org/watch-fatv for more information on accessing this meeting. This is intended to help you understand the meeting format and assist you with the rules of the Council as they pertain to your participation. All meetings of the Fitchburg City council are open to the public. This does not mean that the public participates in all aspects of the meeting. It simply means that the meeting itself, including all discussions and votes, is open for public view. Executive Session The only time a Council meeting can be closed to the public is when the Council votes for Executive Session in order to discuss sensitive matters in private, such as pending litigation. Any votes taken however, must be taken in open session. OPPORTUNITIES FOR THE PUBLIC TO SPEAK DURING A COUNCIL MEETING: Public Forum The Public Forum occurs immediately following the Pledge of Allegiance. The President will ask if anyone in the audience wishes to speak on any matter appearing on the Agenda. If you wish to address the Council, you must stand and be recognized and follow these rules before speaking: 1. 2. 3. 4. State your name and city of residence. Approach the center table and either stand or sit. This allows you to be seen and heard clearly by everyone in attendance. You may speak only on items appearing on the agenda for no more than (2) minutes. Copies of the agenda are available on the center table prior to the meeting. Please state the petition, order, ordinance, or resolution number to which you refer. Public Hearings Public hearings are held on various issues such as Special Permits and Zoning changes. The same rules apply with the following exceptions: 1. You must stand and be recognized either “in favor” or “in opposition” when asked by the Council President. 2. You need not refer to the petition number. If you have any questions or comments either before or after the meeting, any Councilor would be happy to assist you. Thank you for your interest! I.
