Anniversary Committee September 2026 FRANKLIN 250 From Planning to Action A brief look at what we've built, what's coming, and how the Town can help make 2028 a community-wide celebration. A once-in-a-generation civic moment The 250th is an opportunity to create a shared story—not simply a calendar of events. Proud Included Connected Energized Celebrate Franklin's history and what makes this community unique. Create opportunities for residents of every age and background to participate. Bring people, organizations and institutions together around a common story. Build momentum and civic pride that continues beyond 2028. Our goal: not just events, but a shared story and a lasting civic legacy. FRANKLIN 250 WHY IT MATTERS A moment worth remembering. PHOTO Replace with a strong archival, community or event image. 250th Anniversary Celebration Committee following their swearing-in on November 20, 2025. Front row, left to right: Debbie Pellegri, Lyn Pickhover, Julie Cornoni, Swati Rao, Roberta Trahan, and Leone Mulligan. Back row, left to right: Alan Earls, Town Administrator Jamie Hellen, Charleen Belcher, Rob Browne, Town Clerk Nancy Danello, Daniel Brunelli, and Jayson Joyce. Participating remotely: Ali Rheaume. What we've built so far The committee has moved from formation into active planning and execution. Committee 15-member committee with leadership and four working subcommittees. Roadmap 2026–2029 macro timeline developed across events, fundraising, communications and history. FRANKLIN 250 Funding $50,000 FY26 state earmark allocated and deployed toward early infrastructure. Brand Partnerships Early outreach to Town departments, community organizations and peer anniversary committees. Projects Events, oral history, historical materials, website, communications and fundraising moving forward. Franklin 250 visual identity established for consistent public communication. PROGRESS The road to 2028 Four phases of work, with 2028 as the visible peak and 2029 as the legacy. 2026 2027 2028 2029 BUILD ENGAGE CELEBRATE CONTINUE Signature events Parade + show Family programming Closing gala Preserve stories Legacy projects Maintain momentum Infrastructure Brand + website Fundraising Early outreach FRANKLIN 250 Horace Mann Legacy Collaboration Historical programming Community outreach Event production Fundraising ROADMAP The celebration is taking shape A year of signature moments, connected to the community's existing traditions. March 2027 Public Launch Fundraiser and friendraiser at “3” June 2027 Golf Tournament Community launch March 2028 Bell-Ringing Kickoff Announcement/ participation April 2028 Founders' Play / Reenactment Franklin history/the arts July 2028 Family Fun Day/Athletic Contests Beaver Pond/Horace Mann Campus September 16, 2028 Parade + Fireworks / Drone Show Signature public event November 4, 2028 Closing Gala Lake Pearl FRANKLIN 250 EVENTS To realize these ideas, we need two things: VOLUNTEER POWER + FUNDING Other events under consideration The calendar can grow beyond the signature events—but only with community ownership. Community meal on the Common A large, inclusive gathering centered on food and community. Children's book party Celebrate the commemorative book with families and young readers. Taste of Franklin Showcasing local restaurants at event in library reading room. Horace Mann Day A civics education collaboration with Franklin Public Schools. Liberty Tree Planting a tree to honor the occasion on the Common or public park. 250th history walks FPL collaboration; Guided walks connecting residents with Franklin places and stories. Time capsule Capture Franklin in 2028 for future generations. Carnival Fundraiser and celebration– connected with Fiesta. Public art / memorial Visible legacy project that remains after anniversary. Franklin Recipe Book Recipes from past and present community members. FRANKLIN 250 EVENTS UNDER CONSIDERATION Making the 250th belong to the whole Town The committee can coordinate the effort; the community has to make it meaningful. One Celebration. Many Partners. We are beginning to connect the 250th to the institutions, programs, businesses and people that already make Franklin work. City Council Chamber Roll Call Members Present: ● ● ● ● ● ● ● ● ● President George Tyros Councillor Calvin Brooks Councillor Craig Cormier Councillor Alek Dernalowicz Councillor Dana Heath Councillor Brad Heglin Councillor Elizabeth Kazinskas Councillor Judy Mack Councillor David Thibault-Muñoz Members Absent: ● ● Councillor Karen Hardern Councillor Paul Tassone Open Meeting Law Announcement President Tyros announced that any person wishing to make an audio or video recording of the meeting, or transmit the meeting through any medium, was required to notify the Chair pursuant to Massachusetts General Laws Chapter 30A, §20. Reading of Minutes of Prior Meetings August 6, 2026 – Regular Meeting Councillor Mack moved to waive the reading of the minutes and approve them as presented. The motion was seconded by Councillor Kazinskas. Councillor Dernalowicz moved to amend the minutes to add that date to the header of the minutes. The motion was seconded by Councillor Heath and passed. The main motion to approve the minutes as amended then passed unanimously. Page 1 of 6 Page 3 4 City of Gardner City Council - Regular Meeting of September 8, 2026 Item 11922 – A Communication from the Mayor Updating on the Status of City Property Sales Councillor Dernalowicz moved to place the communication on file. The motion was seconded by Councillor Heglin and passed unanimously. Item 11923 – Gardner City Council Investigative Report: Review of Fraudulent Vendor Payment Incident and Opportunities for Process Improvement Councillor Heglin moved to place the report on file. The motion was seconded by Councillor Dernalowicz. Councillor Heglin summarized the findings of the Council-authorized investigation into the fraudulent vendor payment incident. He stated that the City had been the victim of a sophisticated fraud scheme and that the review found no evidence of malicious conduct or negligence by City employees. He noted that the incident exposed vulnerabilities in the relatively new electronic vendor-payment process, particularly regarding independent verification of changes to vendor banking information. Councillor Heglin commended the Auditor’s Office, Treasurer’s Office, Department of Public Works, Police Department, and other City staff for their prompt and professional response, noting that their actions contributed to the recovery of nearly all of the stolen funds. He outlined recommendations arising from the review, including stronger independent verification of vendor banking changes; improved interdepartmental communication; greater use of safeguards available through the City’s financial software; continued cybersecurity training; periodic review of procedures; and appropriate notification to the City Council when significant incidents occur. Councillor Heglin emphasized that the purpose of the report was not to assign blame but to identify opportunities to strengthen City procedures. The motion to place the report on file passed unanimously. Page 2 of 6 Page 4 5 City of Gardner City Council - Regular Meeting of September 8, 2026 Item 11841-A – Ordinance to Amend Attachment F of Chapter 8 to Add the Position of Transfer Station Safety Program Development and Compliance Coordinator Councillor Heglin moved that the ordinance be sent to first printing. The motion was seconded by Councillor Dernalowicz. Councillor Heglin reported that the Finance Committee had reviewed the proposal at multiple meetings. He explained that the position had previously been established and that the ordinance would set the stipend for the additional duties. He stated that the proposal was budget-neutral, with adjustments to staffing hours offsetting the cost without affecting services. The Finance Committee had unanimously recommended the proposal. Councillor Kazinskas noted that the Health Director had also presented the proposal to the Economic and Community Development Committee and thanked the Director for keeping multiple committees informed. The motion to send the ordinance to first printing passed unanimously. Item 11862 – Ordinance to Increase Oversight of Professional Development and Travel Councillor Heglin moved that the ordinance be sent to second and final printing. The motion was seconded by Councillor Dernalowicz. Councillor Heglin explained that the ordinance was intended to establish baseline standards and greater clarity regarding professional development and travel expenditures. He stated that the ordinance would provide consistency, transparency, and equitable access to professional development funds while creating a structure that future administrations and Councils could follow. Councillor Mack thanked Councillor Heglin for proposing the ordinance and Director Morse for developing an electronic professional development form. She stated that the changes would streamline the process and provide greater transparency concerning employee travel, professional development, and associated costs. The motion to send the ordinance to second and final printing passed unanimously. Item 11870 – Ordinance to Increase Financial Transparency, Financial Governance, and Budget Preparedness Councillor Heglin requested additional time, noting the significance of the proposal, the absence of several Councillors, and comments and suggestions made during previous consideration of the ordinance that he wished to review further. Page 3 of 6 Page 5 6 City of Gardner City Council - Regular Meeting of September 8, 2026 There being no objection, more time was granted. Item 11872 – Measure Accepting a Donation of $5,000 from Lynn Barrieau in Memory of Deputy Chief Rock Barrieau for Gardner Police Department Community Policing Programs Councillor Mack reported that Mrs. Barrieau has been a generous supporter of the Police Department’s community policing programs since her husband’s passing in 2013 and that her donations have helped expand those programs. She also noted that the Junior Police Academy had been renamed in honor of Deputy Chief Barrieau during the summer of 2026. Councillor Mack moved the measure. The motion was seconded by Councillor Dernalowicz and passed unanimously. Item 11873 – Measure Accepting a Donation from Keller Partners Co. of an American Flag Flown over the United States Capitol Building to Commemorate the 250th Anniversary of the United States Councillor Mack reported that Keller Partners Co., the City's on-call grant writing firm, had donated an American flag flown over the United States Capitol in recognition of the nation’s 250th anniversary. She stated that the approximate value of the flag was $58 to $60 and that the Finance Committee had recommended acceptance. Councillor Mack moved the measure. The motion was seconded by Councillor Dernalowicz and passed unanimously. Item 11874 – Measure Accepting a Donation of a 2026 Chevrolet Pickup Truck for the Gardner Police Department K9 Program Councillor Mack moved the measure, seconded by Councillor Dernalowicz. Councillor Mack explained that the donation provides a 2026 Chevrolet pickup truck for Officer Willis and K9 Rocky through a three-year lease from Salvadore Chevrolet, with the Police Department intending to purchase the vehicle at fair market value at the conclusion of the lease. She expressed appreciation for the continued support of the Salvadore family and Salvadore Chevrolet. The measure passed unanimously. Page 4 of 6 Page 6 7 City of Gardner City Council - Regular Meeting of September 8, 2026 Item 11885 – Ordinance to Amend Section 22 of Chapter 600, “Parking Meter Fees Waived,” to Add an Exemption for Blue Star Plates Councillor Dernalowicz moved that the ordinance be sent to second and final printing. The motion was seconded by Councillor Heglin and passed unanimously. Item 11919 – Order Transferring $189,009.21 from Various FY2026 Salary Accounts to the City Health Insurance Operating Expense Account Councillor Dernalowicz reported that, following consultation with the Mayor and City Auditor, the recommendation was to remove the item from the calendar. He stated that the funds would fall to Free Cash and could be appropriated at a later date. Councillor Dernalowicz moved to remove the item from the calendar. The motion was seconded by Councillor Heglin and passed unanimously. Item 11920 – Measure Setting the Rate of Compensation for the City Conservation Agent Councillor Dernalowicz reported that the individual for whom the measure had been proposed had accepted another position and that the measure was therefore no longer necessary. Councillor Dernalowicz moved to remove the item from the calendar. The motion was seconded by Councillor Heglin and passed unanimously. Item 11921 – Measure Setting the Rate of Compensation for the Assistant Director of Community Development and Planning Councillor Dernalowicz reported that, following discussions with the Mayor, Mr. Steiner, and Director Stevens, the Finance Committee found Mr. Steiner’s education and professional experience sufficient to warrant an additional year of step credit. Councillor Dernalowicz moved to adopt the measure. The motion was seconded by Councillor Heglin. There being no objection, the rules were suspended and a roll-call vote was taken. Page 5 of 6 Page 7 8 City of Gardner City Council - Regular Meeting of September 8, 2026 Roll Call Vote: Vote: 9–0. Motion passed. Council Comments and Remarks Councillor Brooks commented on the Overdose Awareness Night held at Monument Park on August 31. He commended the organizers, participants, and community for supporting individuals struggling with addiction and those in recovery. He reflected on Gardner’s history of supporting recovery services, including Pathway House and Alyssa’s Place, and praised the community for responding to addiction with support rather than stigma. Councillor Mack recognized Veronica Guay for stepping forward to fill a vacancy on the School Committee. She spoke positively about Ms. Guay’s experience, enthusiasm, and qualifications and emphasized the importance of accountability, fiscal management, and academic standards in School Committee service. Council President Tyros recognized September 10 as World Suicide Prevention Day and encouraged residents to be kind to one another. He also recognized the 25th anniversary of the September 11, 2001 terrorist attacks and noted that several events would be held in the City to commemorate those who lost their lives and those affected by the attacks. President Tyros additionally commended the City Clerk’s Office and election workers for their work during the recent preliminary election, recognizing the long hours, preparation, training, equipment logistics, security, and reporting requirements involved in administering an election. Adjournment Councillor Kazinskas moved to adjourn. The motion was seconded by Councillor Cormier and passed unanimously. The closing prayer was offered, and the meeting adjourned. This memorandum is intended as a summary of the attached requests and their associated fiscal impacts. Request 1: KM-8000TEDD Asphalt Hotbox The first request seeks authorization to purchase a KM-8000TEDD 4-Ton Trailer-Mounted Asphalt Hotbox and associated accessories through Sourcewell Contract #050625-CFC at a total cost of $43,565.00. The equipment would improve the Highway Department's ability to perform durable pothole and pavement repairs throughout the year, increase operational efficiency, and support winter recovery efforts. Request 2: Advance Purchase of Road Salt The second request seeks authorization to purchase eight loads of road salt before the current FY26 contract price expires on October 1, 2026. The estimated cost is $19,632.00 to $22,904.00, providing approximately 240 to 280 tons of additional inventory. The purchase would help ensure adequate winter preparedness while securing current pricing. Combined Fiscal Impact Item Cost Asphalt Hotbox Purchase $43,565.00 Road Salt Purchase $19,632.00 - $22,904.00 Total Funding Requested $63,197.00 - $66,469.00 Approval of both requests would leave approximately $24,782.10 to $28,054.10 remaining from the Town's WRAP allocation for future eligible projects. Respectfully submitted, John Miner Highway Superintendent Town of Gill 196C Main Road, Gill, MA 01354 Telephone 413-863-2324 This institution is an equal opportunity provider and employer. www.gillmass.org highway@gillmass.org To: Gill Selectboard From: John Miner, Highway Superintendent Date: September 9, 2026 Subject: KM-8000T Hotbox Trailer Purchase Request Dear Members of the Selectboard, I respectfully request the Selectboard’s authorization to purchase a KM-8000TEDD 4-Ton Trailer-Mounted Asphalt Hotbox, together with the essential options listed below, using a portion of the Town’s Winter Recovery Assistance Program (WRAP) funds. Gill’s total WRAP allocation is $91,251.10, and the proposed purchase would represent a practical, cost-effective investment in winter recovery, roadway maintenance, and long-term municipal resilience. The KM-8000T would substantially improve the Highway Department’s ability to complete durable pavement repairs year-round, with particular value during the winter and early spring when cold temperatures make conventional repair methods less effective. According to the equipment documentation, the unit can maintain hot mix asphalt for up to 48 hours or reclaim bulk stored virgin HMA, allowing the Department to complete longer-lasting repairs in adverse conditions and during routine roadway maintenance needs throughout the year. Its triple-wall insulated construction and thermostatically controlled heating system also support reliable heat retention and improved fuel efficiency. Pr opa neCy l i nder si nc l udedwi t hPr opa neuni t s ) 52˚Dumpf ea t ur e( a ddi t i ona l opt i on) www. k mi nt er na t i ona l . c om | ( 800) 4921757 4 of 4 www.gillmass.org highway@gillmass.org September 9, 2026 Gill Selectboard Town of Gill 325 Main Road Gill, MA 01354 Re: Request to Use WRAP Funds for Advance Purchase of Road Salt Dear Selectboard Members, I am requesting the Selectboard’s approval to use a portion of the Town’s Winter Recovery Assistance Program (WRAP) funding to purchase eight loads of road salt before the current FY26 price expires on October 1, 2026. Each load of salt is typically between 30 and 35 tons, so eight loads would provide approximately 240 to 280 tons. At the current FY26 rate of $81.80 per ton, the estimated total cost would range from approximately $19,632.00 to $22,904.00. Based on Gill’s total WRAP allocation of $91,251.10, this purchase would leave an estimated WRAP balance of approximately $68,347.10 to $71,619.10, depending on the final tonnage delivered. For additional context, the Town purchased roughly 750 tons of road salt during the winter of FY26, despite beginning the fiscal year with a meaningful amount of salt already in the shed. I make an effort to end each winter season with the salt shed reasonably full to help prepare for the following year and reduce the risk of starting the next season with insufficient inventory. However, I was unable to do so this past spring because the Snow and Ice budget had been depleted. Although the WRAP funds have not yet been added to the Town’s account and payments cannot currently be issued due to the Capital Budget fiscal-year close-out and rollover, MassDOT has advised that the Town may incur eligible expenses now and seek reimbursement once funds are available. A project has been created for Gill under project number 1A-8049. 196C Main Road, Gill, MA 01354 Telephone 413-863-2324 This institution is an equal opportunity provider and employer. MassDOT has further advised that reimbursement requests may be submitted at any time. The requests will be reviewed and prepared so they are ready for payment once the Capital Budget Division authorizes payments to resume. Authorization to process prior-year funds is typically received between late August and October, and FY27 Chapter 90 funds between late August and November, though no specific date has been provided. For these reasons, I respectfully request that the Selectboard authorize the use of WRAP funds for the advance purchase of eight loads of road salt at the current FY26 price. Thank you for your consideration. John Miner Highway Superintendent Town of Gill

title: Great Barrington Selectboard Policy Sub-Committee Agenda (PDF) DRAFT 189
text: Chapter 189. Policies and Procedures [HISTORY: Adopted by the Board of Selectmen of the Town of Great Barrington 6-5-1995, as amended through 4-28-2025. Subsequent amendments noted where applicable.] § 189-1. Selectboard roles. Leadership, governance and oversight responsibilities: promote the Town, serve as advisor to Town Manager, oversight of Town operations, management and strategic planning, set outcomes, evaluate impacts, measure performance, review agendas for meetings. A. Formal/legal responsibilities include: (1) Chief Executive Officer of Town government. (2) Coordinates with other Town elected committees. (3) Appointments and assignments to boards, committees other than those appointed by the Town Manager (4) Local licensing authority unless specified in MGL.. (5) Local permitting authority. (6) A special permit granting authority (besides the Planning Board)). (7) Set policy and propose articles for Town Meeting warrant. (8) Oversee preparationdevelopment and review of budget with Finance Committee and Town Manager for Town Meeting. (9) Call for Town Meetings and approve place all articles for Town Meeting warrants. (10) Set fees, except those determined or granted by a separate authority as outlined in MGL. (11) Review and approve Create general rules and regulations for Town operations as proposed by the Town Manager. (12) Appoint Town Counsel and approve legal strategy. (13) Sign warrants to pay all Town bills. (14) Serve as Road Commissioners. (15) Serve as Sewer Commissioners. (16) Appoint Town Manager. (17) Conduct annual review of Town Manager. (18) Communications to public on Town issues and respond to citizen concerns. (19) Accept donations, gifts, grants, and contributions made to the Town, its departments, boards, committees, programs, or activities, in accordance with applicable law and the Town’s established donation acceptance procedures. B. Annual tasks include: (1) Administrative. (a) Annual board organization: elect Chair, Vice Chair, assign member roles and responsibilities, and assign liaisons to boards/committees and departments as necessary. (b) Issue Town annual report. (c) Resolve government administration issues that have not been settled at lower levels. (d) Set risk management policy. (2) Strategic planning. (a) Set strategic direction of the Board. (b) Hold public "goal setting" meetings at least twice annually. (c) Coordinate with the activities of other boards. (d) Assist in identifying Town projects for Community Preservation Act[1] funding. [1] Editor's Note: See MGL c. 44B, § 5. (3) Financial oversight and budgeting. (a) Tax classification hearing — August. (b) Annual financial policy and budget plan. (c) Participate in the annual Town budget development process. (d) Provide leadership in the development of the capital improvement program. (e) Monitor financial performance of the Town. (f) Sign payment warrants/approve invoices. (g) Review budget policy establishing goals/targets for free cash. (h) Establish stabilization funds policy. (i) Review monthly and quarterly financial reports. (j) Receive and discuss annual Town audit. § 189-2. Selectboard responsibilities. A. Liaison with Town boards and committees. Individual members may be assigned to one or more of the Town Boards and/or Committees on which a Selectboard members is not already a member, to attend the board's/committee's meetings and activities when considered appropriate and maintain current information to be passed on to the Selectboard upon request or as per regular agenda item. B. Liaison with Town departments. With consent of the Town Manager, individual members may be assigned to one or more of the Town departments to serve as a policy liaison, to maintain overall information on the department status and operations and objectives, to assist the Town Manager with resolution of issues and to advise the Town Manager on overall policy and strategy. Provide expertise or information to Selectboard on department subject matters to guide general oversight, and provide regular public updates to the Board when appropriate. C. Liaison with outside groups. Individual members may be assigned to serve as liaison or member of outside committees, to represent the Selectboard and exchange information, and provide regular public updates to the Board when appropriate. D. Selectboard subcommittees. Formed by the Board to address specific issues, strategies or projects. E. Responsibilities to the community. The primary responsibility of a Board member is to all citizens of Great Barrington. Therefore, each member should: recognize that the Board's function is policymaking and not administrative or operational; be mindful that he/she is one of a team and must abide by, and carry out, all Selectboard decisions once they are made; be well informed concerning the responsibilities of a Selectboard member and on issues affecting the Town, whether at a local, regional, or statewide level; remember that he/she represents the entire community at all times; treat the office of Selectboard member as one of public service and not as a means to derive personal benefit or conduct political activities. F. Responsibilities to fellow Board members and others. In relations with fellow Selectboard members and other persons, a Board member shall: acknowledge differences of opinion as part of the democratic process; treat others with respect and act in a civil manner; refrain from personal criticism; respect that Board action at official meetings is binding and that he/she alone cannot bind the Selectboard outside such meetings; refrain from making promises regarding how he/she will vote on applications that will come before the Selectboard; not withhold relevant information on Town matters either from other Selectboard members or from members of other Town bodies or departments whose duties relate to that information; make decisions only after all facts on an issue have been presented to and discussed by the Selectboard; cooperate with the Chair in the conduct of meetings. § 189-3. Officers of the Board. A. The Chair. The Chair is chosen by fellow Selectboard members to serve a term of one year. The responsibilities of the Chair include: preparation of the agenda for all Selectboard meetings in coordination with the Town Manager, calling meetings of the Board, coordinating an annual evaluation of the Town Manager, presiding over all meetings and public hearings (per Robert's Rules of Order and/or applicable legal requirements), recognizing others to speak during each meeting and encouraging complete discussion of all relevant issues before the Board. Being Chair does not mean the Chair forfeits the right to vote on any matter, the right to make a motion or the right to express himself/herself as a Board member. The Chair of the Board shall sign all documents as required by law. B. Vice-Chair/Clerk. The Vice-Chair/Clerk is responsible for serving as Chair in the Chair's absence or recusal. Should the Chair resign, the Vice-Chair automatically succeeds him/her. The Vice-Chair/Clerk of the Board shall sign all documents as required by law. C. Designated alternate. If both the Chair and Vice Chair are unable to perform their duties, the senior member of the Board present at the time shall be designated to perform the applicable duties. § 189-4. Meeting schedule. A. Regular meetings. Regular meetings of the Selectboard generally shall be the second and fourth Mondays of the month. The Board shall not meet on days designated as legal holidays. When a meeting date is to be rescheduled because of a legal holiday, the Board shall agree on a date to reschedule. B. Notice of meetings. All meetings of the Selectboard shall be duly posted in compliance with Massachusetts General Laws (MGL) Open Meeting Law[1] requirements. The Town Manager, on behalf of the Chair, is responsible for providing the agenda to the Town Clerk in accordance with the Open Meeting Law for posting on the Town's website, notice board inside and outside of the Town Hall, and for notifying the media and those persons with business listed on the agenda. [1]Editor's Note: See MGL c 39, § 23B. C. Meeting procedures. (1) Meetings are to be conducted in accordance with generally accepted rules of parliamentary procedure. Robert's Rules of Order is used as a guide in matters requiring clarification or definition. Motions to reconsider must be made no later than the next regularly scheduled business meeting following the meeting at which the original vote was taken. (2) A quorum of the Board is required to hold a meeting and take action. A quorum is defined as a majority of the members of the Board. At times when only three members are present, all three members must vote similarly for a majority vote. Approvals of special permits shall require a concurring vote of at least four members of the Board as per Chapter 40A of the MGL. (3) Any rules or procedures as to functioning of the Board may be amended, repealed or otherwise acted upon by a majority vote, at a duly posted meeting of the Selectboard. (4) In accordance with the Town bylaws, the Chair is encouraged to take public comment when appropriate. The press and the public have the right to be present at any open meeting, however they have no right to participate except during public hearings, citizen speak, or media time unless and until they are recognized by the Chair. All inquiries shall be addressed to and through the Chair. (5) Meeting participants shall conduct themselves in a professional manner. No demonstrations or signs will be allowed in the meeting room. Individuals shall refrain from verbal outbursts. Cell phones and pagers shall be silenced at all times during the meeting. (6) Anyone addressing the Board during the meeting, including citizen speak time, shall proceed to the lectern after being recognized by the Chair, and adhere to the citizen speak procedures. Before speaking, they shall state their name and address. There shall be a time limit of three minutes per speaker, unless extended by the Chair. § 189-5. Preparing the agenda. A. The responsibility for preparing the agenda for the Selectboard meetings shall be with the Chair and the Town Manager. The goal is for finalized agendas, along with supporting background information, to be available no later than the close of business on the Friday of the week prior to the next scheduled meeting. Any Board member wishing to add an agenda item shall make the request in writing to the Chair. The deadline for having requested items on the agenda is 12:00 p.m. noon the Wednesday of the week prior to the next scheduled meeting. All information relevant to the agenda topic shall also be provided by this time. All information shall be provided to the office of the Town Manager to be included in the agenda packets. B. Any items requested by members of the Board shall be placed on the agenda, however, the Chair and Town Manager will use discretion and may need to defer a topic to the next available meeting. Agenda items will ordinarily be deferred to the next meeting if supporting documentation is received after the 12:00 noon deadline. C. Agenda items should include background information to be included with the agenda packets so that Board members can review and prepare for discussion prior to the meeting. This procedure does not limit an individual member of the Selectboard from raising a concern about an issue under "Selectboard Time." at a meeting. However, no formal action shall be taken by the Board until a future meeting. D. Before raising issues publicly at a meeting, Board members should first advise the Town Manager prior to the meeting of issues, concerns, or complaints so that an appropriate response or update can be provided. § 189-6. Public hearing procedures. State laws and various Town bylaws require the Selectboard to hold public hearings on certain issues before any action can be taken. For certain matters, like special permits, the Board may ask the Town Manager to develop a draft findings of fact for consideration. A. The Board will schedule the dates for the hearings. B. The Chair will open the hearing by identifying the purpose of the hearing and the rules to be followed during the hearing. The Chair will ask for a motion to open the public hearing to be voted on by members of the Board. C. The Selectboard has the authority to subpoena a person or relevant information. (Refer to MGL c. 233, § 8.). D. The basic format of the hearing will be: (1) Chair shall open the public hearing. (2) Applicant explanation of request/project. (3) Persons invited to speak in favor/opposition/questions. The Chair shall also note if there are any letters submitted and if they were in favor or opposition. (4) Answers or clarifying comments from the applicant. (5) Motion to close public hearing. (6) Motion re: findings of fact (if applicable). (7) Motion re: approval or denial, continuance, or other procedural action. § 189-7. Approval of licenses. A. The applicant is strongly urged to appear at the Selectboard meeting when the license application will be discussed. If no representative is present, the Board reserves its right to postpone the issue to the next business meeting of the Board or disapprove the application. B. If a license application is filed between Selectboard meetings, and the Chair determines that failure to obtain the license before the next Selectboard meeting would cause the applicant irreparable harm, the Chair will have authority to call a special Selectboard meeting. § 189-8. Board and committee speak procedures. All Town boards and committees have the right to request agenda time to address the Board on matters related to the particular board or committee. Prior to the meeting, the chair of the board or committee shall provide background material on the matter(s) to be discussed along with the results of any board or committee vote(s) on the matter(s) being presented. All members of the board or committee shall be informed by its chair that the matter will be presented to the Selectboard and communication to the Selectboard shall be the responsibility of the chair. When a board or committee addresses the Selectboard, the chair of said board or committee should be in attendance. If the chair cannot attend, the chair shall include with the background material a statement as to who will be speaking on behalf of the board or committee. § 189-9. Citizen speak procedures. A. All Town residents, and owners of property or businesses in Town shall have the right to speak at a Selectboard meeting for a period not to exceed three minutes after being recognized by the Chair unless a longer period of time is granted by the Chair. B. Those who choose to speak during citizen speak time shall have the opportunity to address the Selectboard once during citizen speak time. C. Speakers are encouraged to be courteous and respectful. D. Speakers shall speak for themselves and not speak on behalf of others who are not present unless specific permission is granted by the Chair. E. The Chair may rule the speaker out of order and the speaker will lose the right to speak, if the speaker acts in a non-peaceable or disorderly manner. F. The Chair may respond to a speaker and put an item on a future agenda but the Selectboard and Chair are unable to problem solve or enter debate during citizen speak. G. Citizen speak time shall not be used for comments or questions regarding a matter which is pending before or will be scheduled to come before the Selectboard as part of a public hearing. Comments and questions on such a matter may be presented during the hearing process. § 189-10. Minutes. A. Regular meeting. Minutes will be available to the public after review and approval by the Board. (1) Draft meeting minutes, when available, will be included in agenda packets. (2) Meeting minutes should be on the agenda of the next regularly scheduled meeting or by 30 days after the meeting at the latest. B. Executive session meeting minutes. Minutes of executive sessions should be reviewed at reasonable intervals to determine if the subject matter warrants continued non-disclosure under the Open Meeting Law. (1) Minutes shall be released once they have been approved for release, in executive session, by the Board. (2) Upon a request for minutes of an executive session, the law requires a two-stage review of minutes. First, to determine whether the executive session purpose continues to warrant confidentiality and second, to determine whether the attorney-client privilege or one or more of the exemptions under the Public Records Law[1] apply to withhold the minutes, or a portion thereof, from disclosure. After review, the Selectboard must respond to the requester and either make the minutes available or provide an explanation of what is being withheld and why. Please refer to MGL c. 30A, § 22(f), (g)(2). [1] Editor's Note: See MGL c. 66, § 1 et seq. C. All approved minutes are considered public record and will be made available upon request. They will also be posted on the Town's website within 48 hours of approval. § 189-11. Town Manager evaluations. The Selectboard is responsible for an annual evaluation of the Town Manager in accordance with the Town Charter. A. The evaluation shall begin around April 1 and be completed no later than May 1. B. Bi-annually (every other year) in lieu of a Selectboard evaluation, a comprehensive community evaluation will be conducted by a third party. Staff, press, elected officials, business owners, and residents will be selected at random to participate in the community evaluation. C. Copies of all Town Manager evaluations are public records. § 189-12. Communication with legal counsel. When access to legal counsel is necessary, the Chair or Board members shall communicate through the Town Manager. In the event that the required legal advice is related to contract negotiations with, or the performance of, the Town Manager, all communication shall be through the Chair. § 189-13. Selectboard response to received communication and member communications. A. The Selectboard welcomes communication through whatever vehicle is chosen by its constituents, i.e., email, written letters, phone calls, personal contact. It is the intent of the Board to handle inquiries on a timely basis (within 24 business hours) when possible. When communication is addressed to the entire Selectboard, the Town Manager will, within one business day, confirm receipt of the communication to the individual and inform (CC) the rest of the Board when a response has been sent. B. The Chair and Town Manager shall review the matter as follows: (1) Routine matters. If the matter can be routinely handled by staff, the Town Manager shall, within one business day from receipt of the communication, contact the individual providing adequate information on said matter. Appropriate staff should always be included in communication from the Town Manager, where applicable. (2) Non-Routine matters. Should the matter not be a routine administrative matter, the Chair and Town Manager shall arrange for the matter to be included on the agenda of the earliest occurring/most convenient Selectboard meeting. The Town Manager shall notify the individual when the item will be on the Selectboard agenda. The Selectboard shall discuss the matter publicly and may refer the matter to the Town Manager and/or an appropriate board/commission/committee for further investigation. Should the matter be acted upon by the Selectboard, the Town Manager shall so inform the individual. Alternatively, a meeting may be scheduled among the Chair, Town Manager and appropriate staff when appropriate. (3) Should the matter be referred to another board or to a staff person, the Selectboard may request a report from the referral entity to be reviewed at a regular meeting of the Selectboard at a time the Selectboard designates. Bannon, Chair Eric Gabriel Garfield Reed Benjamin Elliott Philip Orenstein Great Barrington Selectboard Cc: Rep Leigh Davis Dear Chair Bannon and Members of the Great Barrington Selectboard, On behalf of BRIDGE, I am submitting for your consideration a proposed Resolution Supporting Temporary Protected Status (TPS) for Haitian Residents and Families, together with the draft Haitian Community Engagement Report prepared by BRIDGE’s Public Health Team. We bring this request forward because the national uncertainty and precarity surrounding Haitian TPS has very real local implications. Our Public Health Team’s data documents the participation, contributions, leadership, and needs of Haitian families connected to BRIDGE and the broader Berkshire community. BRIDGE is currently connected with approximately 66 Haitian community members. Our data demonstrates that this is not simply a community receiving services—it is a community actively contributing to the infrastructure that supports our region. Many of them work, live, study and contribute to a higher quality of life for our Great Barrington and southern Berkshire 6d. Proposed Resolution Page 2 of 6 community. Among the community documented so far by our Public Health Team: At least 10 Haitian community members work in community-serving roles in Great Barrington, including as drivers, translators, agronomists, growers, Mutual Aid workers, stewards, and other community supports. 18 participate in BRIDGE’s Farm Program, contributing to agriculture, food sovereignty, environmental stewardship, and workforce development. Haitian community stewards have increased from 7 to 10 in 2026 demonstrating growing leadership and responsibility. In 2024&205, we have had as many as 15 stewards in workforce development training. 3 Haitian staff members work within BRIDGE, providing multilingual and culturally grounded support and leadership. 20 Haitian families receive Mutual Aid food support, while Haitian community members also work and volunteer within Mutual Aid. 11 of 32 Haitian children participated in BRIDGE’s 2026 summer programming, and Haitian youth have volunteered at community events and one served as a paid youth corps leader. Haitian families participate in our schools and access BRIDGE, People’s Pantry, the Family Resource Center, wellness programs, and other community resources while also contributing labor, knowledge, language skills, agricultural expertise, volunteer service, and leadership. This is a story of reciprocity, contribution, and belonging. Our Haitian neighbors grow food, drive, translate, volunteer, work Mutual Aid, raise children in our schools, and strengthen community-based organizations. They contribute directly to agriculture and food security, workforce development, community health, language access, and the social fabric of the Berkshires. For this reason, uncertainty surrounding Haitian TPS is not an abstract federal policy matter for our community. Destabilization of these families can affect local workers and employers, farms and food systems, schools, transportation, community organizations, public health, and the networks of care upon which our residents depend. We believe supporting continued and restored TPS protections is aligned with the principles of Great Barrington’s Trust Policy and Trust Policy 2.0 and with Massachusetts’ PROTECT Act. It also complements the federal leadership of Congresswoman Ayanna Pressley, Co-Chair of the Congressional Haiti Caucus, and other Massachusetts leaders advocating for Haitian TPS protections. We respectfully ask the Selectboard to review the accompanying BRIDGE Public Health Team's interim report data cited here, consider adoptint a proposed resolution supporting Haitian TPS ( draft below), and place the matter on an upcoming Selectboard agenda for public consideration. 6d. Proposed Resolution Page 3 of 6 BRIDGE and members of our Public Health Team would be available to present the more complete local data and context, answer questions, and support opportunities for Haitian community voices to be heard directly. Our Haitian neighbors are not simply beneficiaries of our community infrastructure. They help build, operate, strengthen, and sustain it. Standing with these families at this moment is an expression of the trust, reciprocity, and belonging that our community has worked to establish together with Trust Policy locally and Protect Act statewide. Thank you for your consideration and your continued service to Great Barrington. Warmly, Gwendolyn VanSant Founding Director & CEO BRIDGE Suggested draft of….. RESOLUTION SUPPORTING TEMPORARY PROTECTED STATUS FOR HAITIAN RESIDENTS AND FAMILIES WHEREAS, the Town of Great Barrington adopted its Trust Policy in 2017 and approved Trust Policy 2.0 in 2026, reaffirming the Town’s commitment to civil rights, lawful governance, public safety, transparency, accountability, equitable access to services, and community trust; and WHEREAS, Trust Policy 2.0 recognizes the importance of community care coordination and collaboration among municipal government, community-based organizations, service providers, schools, public-health partners, and residents, particularly in supporting protected and vulnerable populations; and WHEREAS, on August 5, 2026, the Commonwealth of Massachusetts enacted the PROTECT Act — An Act Promoting Rule of Law, Oversight, Trust and Equal Constitutional Treatment, establishing additional protections related to civil immigration enforcement and access to courthouses, schools, hospitals, health-care facilities, and other essential institutions; and WHEREAS, Haitian residents and families are an integral part of the social, economic, educational, agricultural, cultural, and civic fabric of Berkshire County and the Commonwealth of Massachusetts; and WHEREAS, local data collected by BRIDGE demonstrates this contribution directly: BRIDGE currently engages 66 Haitian community members, including at least 10 people working in community-serving roles, 18 Farm Program participants, 10 community stewards, and 3 Haitian staff members; and WHEREAS, Haitian community members contribute as drivers, translators, agronomists, growers, agricultural workers, Mutual Aid workers, volunteers, stewards, cultural 6d. Proposed Resolution Page 4 of 6 navigators, and community leaders, supporting BRIDGE and other community-based organizations throughout the region; and WHEREAS, Haitian families participate in a reciprocal network of community care: 20 Haitian community members receive Mutual Aid food support, while Haitian residents themselves help grow, transport, distribute, and provide food and other resources to their neighbors; and WHEREAS, Haitian families also participate in People's Pantry, Family Resource Center, BRIDGE, schools, wellness programs, and other community institutions while simultaneously contributing their labor, expertise, language skills, cultural knowledge, volunteer service, and leadership to those institutions and to the broader community; and WHEREAS, Haitian children attend our schools and participate in local educational and youth programs, including 11 Haitian children participating in BRIDGE's 2026 summer camp, creating relationships and a sense of belonging that extend across families, schools, workplaces, and communities; and WHEREAS, the loss of Temporary Protected Status and associated work authorization threatens not only individual TPS holders, but also family stability, employers, schools, agricultural and food systems, community-based organizations, public health, and the local and regional workforce; and WHEREAS, Congresswoman Ayanna Pressley, Co-Chair of the Congressional Haiti Caucus, has led federal efforts to preserve and extend Temporary Protected Status for Haitian nationals, and the United States House of Representatives passed legislation in April 2026 to extend Haiti TPS for three years, with companion legislation subsequently introduced in the United States Senate; and WHEREAS, these federal efforts recognize that Haitian TPS holders are workers, parents, caregivers, business owners, community members, and contributors whose continued presence strengthens communities and the economy; and WHEREAS, Great Barrington's experience reflects this national reality at the local level: Haitian residents are not simply recipients of community services but are essential contributors to agriculture, food security, workforce development, Mutual Aid, community health, transportation, language access, education, and community life; and WHEREAS, immigration instability can undermine the trust necessary for residents to access schools, health care, public services, public safety, food assistance, community organizations, and other institutions, directly affecting the goals and principles embodied in Great Barrington's Trust Policy; NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED, that the Great Barrington Selectboard: 1. AFFIRMS that Haitian residents and families are valued and integral members of Great Barrington, Berkshire County, and the Commonwealth of Massachusetts; 2. RECOGNIZES the substantial contributions Haitian residents make to our agricultural 6d. Proposed Resolution Page 5 of 6 economy, workforce, schools, food systems, community-based organizations, Mutual Aid networks, public health, cultural life, and overall community wellbeing; 3. SUPPORTS the restoration, continuation, and extension of Temporary Protected Status for Haitian nationals, including federal legislative action necessary to provide meaningful and durable TPS protection; 4. SUPPORTS the federal efforts led by Congresswoman Ayanna Pressley and Massachusetts congressional leaders to protect Haitian TPS holders and preserve their ability to live and work lawfully in the United States; 5. RECOGNIZES that maintaining family and workforce stability for Haitian residents is consistent with Great Barrington's interests in public health, public safety, food security, workforce development, education, economic stability, and community wellbeing; 6. AFFIRMS that this resolution is consistent with the principles of the Town's 2017 Trust Policy and Trust Policy 2.0, including community trust, lawful governance, equitable access, transparency, community care, and collaboration with community-based organizations; 7. RECOGNIZES the complementary protections established by the Commonwealth of Massachusetts through the PROTECT Act and affirms the Town's commitment to ensuring that residents can safely access schools, health care, municipal services, community organizations, and other essential institutions consistent with applicable law; and 8. CALLS UPON the United States Senate, the United States Congress, and appropriate federal authorities to take all lawful action necessary to restore and preserve Temporary Protected Status for Haitian nationals and prevent the unnecessary destabilization of families and communities. BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED that the Great Barrington Selectboard recognizes a fundamental principle demonstrated by our own community: Haitian residents are not simply beneficiaries of our community infrastructure. They help build, operate, strengthen, and sustain it. Protecting the stability of Haitian families protects our workforce, our farms and food systems, our schools, our community organizations, our public health, and the relationships of trust upon which a strong community depends. Adopted this ___ day of ___, 2026, by the Great Barrington Selectboard. SELECTBOARD MEMBERS Chair Selectboard Member

text: Posted 9.10.26 @ 5:00pm by JAD SELECT BOARD AGENDA Tuesday, September 15, 2026 7:00pm SusanMary Redinger, Ahmet Corapcioglu, Kara McGuire Minar, Eve Wittenberg, Eric Ward The Select Board Regular Meeting will be held virtually in accordance with Chapter 2 of the Acts of 2025, An Act extending certain COVID-19 measures adopted during the state of emergency and signed into law on March 28, 2025. To attend and have the ability to participate in meeting use the Zoom link below. Display full name when entering Zoom. UpperTH ProWebinar is inviting you to a scheduled Zoom meeting. Topic: Select Board Time: Sep 15, 2026 07:00 PM Eastern Time (US and Canada) Join Zoom Meeting https://us02web.zoom.us/j/87143911544?pwd=Exuq8rXmLKaokvXCaX7cHsuCUxDaNE.1 Meeting ID: 871 4391 1544 Passcode: 665436 One tap mobile +16469313860,,87143911544# US +19294362866,,87143911544# US (New York) AGENDA ITEMS 1) Call meeting to order – Chair, SusanMary Redinger (7:00) 2) Public communication (7:00) 3) Introduction of Executive Assistant Michelle Stockman (7:05) 4) Meet with Addiction Abatement Fund Working Group to vote on recommendation for a mini grant from the Addiction Referral Center (ARC) (7:10) 5) Appointments: (7:20) a) Addiction Abatement Fund Working Group - Superintendent Dana Labb as the school rep. b) Community Media Committee - Robert Blanck & Andrew Gavin from alternate to full member c) Open Space Committee – Jim Lee 6) Review and finalize budget memo/process (7:30) 7) DPW/Transfer Station update (7:40) 8) Review draft Special Town Meeting Warrant (7:50) 9) Town Administrator Report (8:05) 10) Select Board Reports (8:15) 11) Public communication (8:30) Next Regular Select Board Meeting Tuesday, September 29, 2026 From: Aaron Farber-Chen <afarberchen01434@gmail.com> Date: September 9, 2026 at 8:42:43 AM EDT To: SusanMary Redinger <smredinger@gmail.com> Subject: Fwd: Town of Harvard Addiction Abatement Fund Working Group – Mini Grant Application Update Hi SusanMary, Would it be possible to request to add an agenda item to the September 15th Select Board meeting to review the latest recommendation from the Addiction Abatement Fund Working Group, please? At our September 4th meeting, the committee voted to recommend approval for the funding proposal from the Addiction Referral Center (ARC). Please see the note below to Tracey Gustafson for further details. I am also happy to share any additional information as needed. Many thanks, Aaron --- Forwarded message ---From: Aaron Farber-Chen < Date: Tue, Sep 8, 2026 at 4:51 PM Subject: Town of Harvard Addiction Abatement Fund Working Group – Mini Grant Application Update Dear Ms. Gustafson, Thank you for submitting your mini-grant application to the Town of Harvard Addiction Abatement Fund Working Group on behalf of the Addiction Referral Center. The Working Group sincerely appreciates the care and thoroughness with which you and your colleagues prepared the Emergency Sober Housing Rental Assistance proposal, and we are grateful for the Addiction Referral Center's continued commitment to supporting individuals in recovery throughout Middlesex and Worcester Counties. After careful review of your application, the Working Group is pleased to inform you that it has voted to recommend your proposal to the Town of Harvard Select Board for approval of a mini-grant award in the amount of $9,999.99 in support of the Emergency Sober Housing Rental Assistance program. This recommendation reflects the Working Group's determination that the proposed project is well-aligned with the fund's goals of supporting addiction and/or substance use disorder treatment and recovery, specifically through the provision of first month's rent assistance to individuals transitioning from substance use disorder treatment into Massachusetts Association of Sober Housing (MASH)-certified sober living environments within the Middlesex and Worcester County region. The Select Board will now review the Working Group's recommendation and take a vote on final approval. Following that review, the Working Group will be in touch with next steps and further information regarding the status of your award. We are grateful for the Addiction Referral Center's partnership in addressing the opioid crisis in our region and look forward to the outcome of the Select Board's review. Please do not hesitate to reach out to the Working Group with any questions in the meantime. Respectfully, Aaron Farber-Chen, Chair On Behalf of the Town of Harvard Addiction Abatement Fund Working Group September 8, 2026 ADDICTION ABATEMENT FUND MINI GRANT APPLICATION FORM Instructions This application is for individuals, organizations, and municipalities seeking funding for addiction abatement initiatives up to a maximum of $10,000. Applications will be evaluated based on alignment with program goals, feasibility, measurable outcomes, collaboration, and costeffectiveness. Please complete all sections thoroughly. SECTION 1: APPLICANT INFORMATION 1. Representative (point of contact) Tracey Gustafson 2. Organization/Other Parties (if applicable): Addiction Referral Center 3. Mailing Address: P.O. Box 225, Marlborough, MA 01752 (physical address is 33 Main Street, Marlborough) 4. Email Address: office@theaddictionreferralcenter.org 5. Phone Number: 978-257-6959 (Tracey Gustafson cell) 6. Website (if applicable): https://theaddictionreferralcenter.org/ 7. Type of Applicant (Check one): ○ ☐ Individual ○ X Nonprofit Organization ○ ☐ Business Entity ○ ☐ Government Agency ○ ☐ Coalition or Collaborative Group SECTION 2: PROJECT OVERVIEW 1. Project Title: Emergency Sober Housing Rental Assistance 2. Total Amount of Funding Requested: $_10,000___ 3. Brief Summary of the Project (100-250 words): The Addiction Referral Center will use $10,000 to provide emergency sober housing rental assistance to individuals in Middlesex County, enabling them to enter a safe, sober living environment following treatment for substance use disorder, avoiding potential homelessness or housing instability. The individuals served do not have the financial means to pay for their first month's rent in sober housing. This expense is not covered by private insurance or MassHealth. Sober housing vacancies are very limited, and if a person does not move quickly when they find a vacancy, they will lose the opportunity. We pay the sober house directly so the individual can focus on their recovery journey, knowing they will have a safe place to stay. The ARC Recovery Coach meets with the individual to assess their needs and provide a recovery plan as they enter sober housing. The Recovery Coach continues to follow up and meet with the individuals throughout their time at the Sober House and beyond, according to their needs. SECTION 3: PROJECT GOALS & ALIGNMENT 1. Describe the primary goals of the project. What addiction-related problem does this project aim to address? Following treatment for substance use disorder, individuals are often encouraged to transition to sober housing, which provides a supportive and structured environment to continue their recovery. Sober housing, which is not covered by insurance, requires the first month’s rent to be paid up front. Often at this stage, a person is experiencing financial insecurity. The ARC provides the first month’s rent to enable them to begin living in this drug-free setting. This overcomes a hurdle that prevents a person from finding a safe place to live as they begin their recovery journey. Helping those in early recovery find safe housing avoids potential homelessness or housing instability. This service was conceived because ARC staff observed this gap in assistance and its impact on those seeking sober housing. Once they are living in the sober house, the person will work with the sober house Director on financing their ongoing rent through employment and service programs. 2. What strategies will be used to achieve these goals? In order to provide emergency sober housing rental assistance, the ARC staff works directly with Case Managers at treatment facilities and Sober Housing Directors. Clients with financial need are connected to the ARC through a Case Manager, Sober House Director, or by calling the ARC directly. The ARC staff first verifies that the sober house is Massachusetts Association of Sober Housing (MASH) Certified and that the client is within the Middlesex County/Worcester County region and in need of emergency assistance. The ARC Recovery Coach then meets one-on-one with the client for an intake appointment. This meeting contains several parts. It provides the information we need for proper reporting on the funds used. It helps the Recovery Coach assess the client’s needs, coach them on strategies for early recovery, and connect them with other resources to begin this recovery journey. The ARC Recovery Coach is available, at no cost to the client, to meet for ongoing coaching. Separately, the ARC Executive Director works directly with the Sober House Director to process an agreement document and provide payment of the first month’s rent on the client’s behalf. 3. How does this proposal specifically support addiction prevention, treatment, or recovery efforts? Helping individuals find safe, stable, sober housing addresses treatment and recovery efforts. To begin recovery from substance use disorder, an individual starts at a detoxification facility, then transitions to in-patient treatment for 7 to 30 days. Following treatment, individuals are often encouraged to transition to sober housing, which provides a supportive and structured environment to continue their recovery. These homes offer structured routines, peer support, and accountability, helping individuals rebuild their lives, find employment, and develop healthy coping mechanisms. Stable, safe, sober housing avoids potential homelessness or housing insecurity, which is essential for recovery. SECTION 4: PROJECT ACTIVITIES & FEASIBILITY 1. List and describe the key activities that will be undertaken as part of this project. 2. What is the expected timeline for project implementation? ○ Estimated Start Date: _1/1/2026___ ○ Estimated End Date: __12/31/2026___ 3. Describe any potential barriers or risks to project success and how they will be addressed. The demand for Emergency Sober Housing Rental Assistance continues to grow and exceed the funding we have budgeted. We have relationships with substance use disorder treatment centers, and the professionals at these centers reach out for our help to place their patients into a sober home when leaving treatment. Our program is well regarded and urgently needed. Sober housing rent ranges from $800 to $1200 per month. We can only provide emergency rental assistance as long as we have available funds. As a nonprofit, our funding comes from individuals, local businesses, fundraising events, and grant applications. We hold two annual fundraisers, a Comedy Show in the spring and a Golf Tournament in the summer, which cover over half of our general operating costs. We rely on donations to support our programs. Due to the small staff, all fundraising and grant applications are completed by ARC volunteers. We seek multi-year grant funding to optimize our volunteer efforts. 4. What resources (staff, facilities, equipment, etc.) are required for this project? Are they already secured or do they need to be acquired? All necessary resources, including the ARC Executive Director and Recovery Coach, are in place. In the first 6 months of 2026, we have placed 59 people in sober housing, 80% of whom identify as addicts (the other 20% identify as alcoholics). Our cost in the first 6 months has been $49,360. We are seeking funding so that we can continue the program this year without having to turn away those in need. The Executive Director reviews requests, approves/disapproves based on criteria, secures the contract with the Sober House, and processes payment. The Recovery Coach handles the intake appointment prior to final approval and follows up on the placement and recovery plan for the client. The staff uses two donated laptops. We utilize Google Docs at no cost. The banking and accounting systems are already in place. SECTION 5: MEASURABLE OUTCOMES & EVALUATION 1. What specific outcomes will this project achieve? How will success be measured? This project will help remove barriers to improved mental health for our region’s most vulnerable individuals and ensure that those who face monetary insecurity issues still have access to proper substance use treatment. Emergency sober housing rental assistance was created when we saw clients who had completed treatment for substance use disorder facing potential homelessness or housing instability. Our goal is to provide this safety net and help them take the next step of their recovery journey. By also offering free Recovery Coach services and daily peer-support meetings at the ARC, we help individuals create a relapse prevention plan for long-term sobriety. 2. What data or indicators will be used to track progress? We track all requests and client placements. Information about individuals is gathered during the intake appointment with the ARC Recovery Coach. We ask clients for feedback on the Sober House and request feedback and evaluations from the Sober Homes. The ARC Recovery Coach adheres to a follow-up schedule to reconnect with each client after the initial placement. In these meetings, the Recovery Coach works with the individual to create a relapse prevention plan and set goals for short- and longterm outcomes. Ongoing meetings build trust and accountability, track goals, provide encouragement, and continue to connect the client with resources as needed. 3. Will you conduct formal evaluations (e.g., surveys, interviews, data tracking)? If so, describe how. The Recovery Coach collects information from the client during an intake appointment. This also includes initial coaching to identify other areas of need. We have this data, including demographics and substance use. We also request informal feedback from clients and from the sober houses after placement. 4. How will the community benefit from this project in measurable ways? Helping individuals with substance use disorder find long-term recovery rebuilds families. Children are provided a more stable, nurturing environment. Individuals rejoin the workforce, boosting the economy. Potential healthcare and criminal justice costs can be eliminated. People in recovery often give back to the community by providing support to others struggling, creating a supportive peer network, building compassion, and reducing stigma. 5. Estimate the volume of individuals expected to be affected by this project: a. Total estimated individuals impacted: 10-15 individuals will receive rental assistance b. Breakdown (if applicable, e.g., by age group, geographic area, or other relevant categories): ■ Youth (18 & under): ___ ■ Adults (19-64): __90%_(estimate)___ ■ Seniors (65+): ___10%___(estimate)___ ■ Other specific groups (e.g., individuals in recovery, families, healthcare providers, etc.): _100% people with SUD, 80% identify as addicts___ 6. Commitment to Reporting: ● If awarded funding, the applicant agrees to provide regular impact reports (e.g., quarterly) detailing: ○ Project status and progress toward stated outcomes, including any adjustments made ○ Evaluation metrics and measurable impact ○ Financial updates on fund expenditures SECTION 6: COMMUNITY COLLABORATION, REGIONAL PARTNERSHIPS & SURVEY ALIGNMENT 1. Describe any partnerships with local organizations, government agencies, or community groups that will support this project. 2. What roles will each partner play in project implementation? 3. Does this project involve collaboration with surrounding municipalities? If so, describe how the project will have a regional impact. The ARC Executive Director and Recovery Coach work with individuals struggling with substance use disorder by providing referrals to detoxification facilities and in-patient and out-patient addiction treatment centers. The ARC also provides transportation to treatment when needed. The ARC staff meets with representatives from these treatment centers to understand their services, requirements for admission (especially insurance options), and specialty areas. By creating these relationships and understanding the available services in our region, the ARC staff can provide individualized referrals to help clients begin their recovery journey from substance use disorder. Just a few examples of the many treatment centers we partner with are Aware Recovery, Mayflower Recovery, Paramount Recovery Centers, Rockland Recovery, Charles River Recovery, Recovery Centers of America, and Kiwi Recovery (specializing in adolescent care). In addition, we work directly with state agencies such as Advocates, South Middlesex Opportunity Council (SMOC), Adcare Hospital, and Spectrum Health Services to provide clients without private insurance with a safe and reliable detoxification and treatment option. In order to provide emergency sober housing assistance, the ARC staff works directly with Case Managers at treatment facilities and Sober Housing Directors. Clients with financial need are connected to the ARC through a Case Manager or Sober House Director. The ARC staff first verifies that the sober house is Massachusetts Association of Sober Housing (MASH) Certified and that the client is within the Middlesex County/Worcester County region and in need of emergency assistance. The ARC Recovery Coach then meets one-on-one for an intake with the client. The Executive Director works directly with the Sober House Director to procure an agreement and make the payment of the first month’s rent on the client’s behalf. The ARC staff and Board of Directors members regularly engage with community organizations to promote the ARC’s services and support regional events. Local partners include the Marlborough Alliance for Prevention, Hudson Youth Substance Abuse Prevention organization, Nashoba Valley Opioid Abatement Collaborative, Great Meadows Public Health Collaborative and Health Department Directors in the region. 4. How does this project align with the results of the 2024 Harvard Opioid Settlement Survey? Harvard is a community where people recognize the impact of the opioid crisis and believe that help should be extended beyond the boundaries of one specific municipality. It’s a national crisis that we can help fight locally by supporting the organizations that help people in our region struggling with substance use disorder. The Emergency Sober Housing Rental Assistance program fits into the Treatment & Recovery strategies category supported by Harvard residents. Also, although it does not directly provide help for youth, the positive impact on families is strong. This program was conceived by the ARC staff who work directly with those struggling with SUD. The ARC staff leverage their own sobriety journeys to identify with and understand the needs of those they serve. Seven of the nine members of the ARC Board of Directors are in recovery from SUD. All decisions made at the ARC are representative of the voice of those with lived experience. SECTION 7: BUDGET & COST-EFFECTIVENESS 1. Provide a detailed budget breakdown (attach a separate document if necessary). ○ Personnel: $__0___ ○ Supplies & Materials: $___0___ ○ Equipment (if greater than $1,000, then attach itemized inventory): $__0___ ○ Outreach & Marketing: $___0___ ○ Other (describe): $ Sober Housing Rental assistance__ $10,000___ ○ TOTAL BUDGET REQUESTED: $_10,000___ 2. Is this project leveraging other sources of funding? (if applicable) ○ X☐ Yes (Describe funding sources): ___ The full rental assistance budget is $71,000. Funding has been secured from Agnes M. Lindsay Trust, Avidia Bank, City of Marlborough, and Town of Hudson. Also in progress are requests to Reliant Foundation, Brigham Family Trust, … MGL Chapter 40A 7 Reorganization of Use Regulations 8 9 Amend Large-Scale Ground Mounted Solar Photovoltaic Facilities Overlay District Reorganization of Dimensional Regulations 10 Amend MBTA Communities Multi-Family Overlay District … to (i) enter into net metering credit purchase agreements with the owner of a solar photovoltaic facility for a period of up to 20 years, and (ii) take any actions and execute any other documents and ancillary agreements necessary … into a 30-year lease for a net metering credit purchase agreement with the owner of a solar facility. Any agreements over three (3) years require a vote of the Town Meeting. Select Board Recommendations: Finance Committee Recommendations … file with the Town Clerk, incorporating standards for Solar Photovoltaic Installations, Battery Energy Storage Systems, and Consolidated Local Permitting consistent with 225 CMR 29.00 and Chapter 239 of the Acts of 2024; or take any other … The proposed bylaw establishes local siting standards and a consolidated permitting process for solar energy systems, and for the first time, includes standards for battery energy storage systems (BESS).
