HARVARD PLANNING BOARD MEETING MINUTES SEPTEMBER 14, 2026 Chair John McCormack called the meeting to order at 7:00pm virtually, pursuant to Chapter 107 of the Acts of 2022, An Act Relative to Extending Certain COVID-19 Measures Adopted during the State of Emergency, and signed into law on July 16, 2022, and under M.G.L. Chapter 40A and Code of the Town of Harvard Chapter 125 Members Present: John McCormack, Doug Thornton, Irene Battaglia and Paul Robertson Richard Abt (absent) Others Present: Jenny Gingras (Community and Economic Development Director) Public Comment: Public Hearing: 7:30pm – Continued discussion regarding the proposed amendment to Chapter 125 of the Code of the Town of Harvard, the Protective Bylaw, to be considered at the 2026 Fall Special Town Meeting, which will be held on October 20, 2026, are summarized as follows: • Amend §§125-3 (Non-conforming Structures and Uses), 125-4 (Existing Lots), 125-45 (Board of Appeals), 125-46 (Special Permits), and 125-49 (Enforcement) to conform to recent amendments to the Zoning Act, MGL Chapter 40A, enacted by the FY2027 state budget (House Bill 5555, effective July 1, 2026), • Amend Article IV, Permitted Uses by District (§§125-19 through 125-24) by replacing §§125-19 through 125-24 with a new §125-19. • Replace §125-29 (Lot Size Standards) and §125-30 (Land-Structure Relations) in their entirety with a new §125-29 • Amend §125-53 by replacing the Large-Scale Ground-Mounted Solar Photovoltaic Facilities Overlay District in its entirety with a new Clean Energy Facilities Bylaw • Amend §125-60, MBTA Communities Multi-Family Overlay District • *Details on page 4 and 5 Standard Business: Approve Minutes: Doug Thornton made a motion to waive the reading of the August 17th, 2026 minutes. Irene Battaglia seconded the motion. All in favor: Doug – aye, Irene – aye, Paul - aye and John – aye. Doug Thornton moved to approve the amended August 17th minutes. Irene Battaglia seconded the motion. All in favor: Doug – aye, Irene – aye, Paul - aye and John – aye. Approve Invoices: Worcester Telegram and Gazette invoice for legal notice - $816.84 Irene Battaglia moved to approve the invoice for a legal notice from the Worcester Telegram and Gazette for $816.84. Doug seconded the motion. All in favor: Doug Thornton – aye, Irene Battaglia – aye, Paul Robertson – aye and John McCormack – aye. Old Business: Metrics: no comments Community Development Director Report: Jenny Gingras reported met with the Climate Initiative Committee regarding the MVP 2.0 process. The grant application is coming up in the fall and Jenny wanted to talk to them about moving forward and submitting a grant application. The MVP 2.0 is something that all towns will have to eventually go to, to be able to continue to get action grants. MVP stands for Municipal Vulnerability Program. Jenny is also working with the Affordable Housing Trust regarding an RFP to hire a consultant to do a strategic plan. They're meeting on Thursdays, September 17th this week at 6pm to discuss that in more detail, and hopefully vote to approve the RFP to go out to bid. She attended the Community Connections event on September 3rd which the Girl Scouts hosted. She thought it was a really good event where she handed out information on the zoning articles. Jenny will be on the Common at an event which is hosted by the General Store and the Harvard Family Association. She will have information about the zoning articles there, and also general information about what her office does. Finally, Jenny mentioned that on September 29th she will be hosting a Zoning 101 and then a Town Meeting preview of the zoning articles at the Council on Aging. It will start at 6 PM. Board Member Reports MRPC Updates: No update Historic Commission: Richard reported to John that the Historical Commission did meet last week to hear the request by Five Sparks for mounting two outdoor sculptures. The historical commission voted four to one to not permit Five Sparks to display those sculptures. It seems, from Richard's report, that there was an overwhelming verbal opposition. CPC: Paul reported the deadline for applications is the end of October. About one million dollars is in the kitty to distribute again this year. One of the ideas the CPC discussed is to have the people from previous years come back and report on what the status is, show some photos for half an hour or so to get an update / status on grants. DRB: No update Bare Hill Pond Watershed Committee:. Harvard Devens Jurisdiction Committee: John spoke about how he and Jenny both went on a tour of Vicksburg Square. Senator Eldridge and Representative Sena were also there looking at the decrepit buildings. John said that it looks like Mass Development is going to get more engaged with the jurisdiction conversations. They plan to start re-attending the meetings. He was not sure if they were going to reclaim their voting position on the committee or just be observers. Either way he felt it was a good sign that they were participating again. HDJC is surveying all the town departments, boards and other entities and plans on putting together a summary for the town by Spring. 2026 Master Planning: no updates Climate Initiative Committee: no updates Rural Life Preservation Bylaw: no updates Clean Energy Facilities bylaw: to be discussed in public hearing New Business a) Discussion on Erosion Control Permit Procedures b) Designation of Director of Community and Economic Development as Planning Board Designee for Minor Permits Jenny led a discussion about whether the Planning Board's designee could issue minor erosion control permits, presenting research on how other towns handle similar processes. The board discussed Section 133-38 of the bylaw, with subsection A2 requiring full board approval while subsection C7 allows designee issuance. The group agreed that while the Conservation Agent should continue reviewing applications, Jenny could potentially serve as the designee if the board chooses to proceed with this approach. The board decided to verify the Conservation Agent's role in the current process before making any final decisions about changing the permit approval process. The planning board discussed the interpretation and procedures for minor permits, particularly regarding Erosion Control permits and the role of the planning board versus its designee. They reviewed potential conflicts in the language regarding permit issuance and decided to maintain current practices while planning to review regulations in more detail after town meeting. The board then designated Jenny as the planning board's designee for Erosion Control permits Doug Thornton made the motion that the Planning Board designate the Director of Community and Economic Development as the Planning Board's designee under 133-38 for the purposes of Erosion Control By-law. Paul Robertson seconded the motion. All in favor: Doug Thornton – aye, Irene Battaglia – aye, Paul Robertson – aye and John McCormack – aye. Adjournment Paul Robertson made a motion to adjourn the meeting at 9:26 pm. Irene Battaglia seconded the motion. The vote was unanimously in favor of the motion by roll call: Doug Thornton – aye, Irene Battaglia, aye, Paul Robertson – aye and John McCormack, aye Page 3 Public Hearing: Harvard Planning Board Meeting September 14, 2026 Chair John McCormack called the meeting to order at 7:30pm virtually, pursuant to Chapter 107 of the Acts of 2022, An Act Relative to Extending Certain COVID-19 Measures Adopted during the State of Emergency, and signed into law on July 16, 2022, and under M.G.L. Chapter 40A and Code of the Town of Harvard Chapter 125 Members Present: John McCormack, Irene Battaglia, Doug Thornton and Paul Robertson Richard Abt (Absent) Others Present: Jenny Gingras (Community Economic Development Director) 7:30pm Continued discussion regarding the proposed amendment to Chapter 125 of the Code of the Town of Harvard, the Protective Bylaw, to be considered at the 2026 Fall Special Town Meeting, which will be held on October 20, 2026, are summarized as follows: • Amend §§125-3 (Non-conforming Structures and Uses), 125-4 (Existing Lots), 125-45 (Board of Appeals), 125-46 (Special Permits), and 125-49 (Enforcement) to conform to recent amendments to the Zoning Act, MGL Chapter 40A, enacted by the FY2027 state budget (House Bill 5555, effective July 1, 2026), including revised variance standards, durations, and extension periods; protections for pre-existing nonconforming uses and structures; abandonment determination timelines; zoning freeze periods; and lot merger protections. • Amend Article IV, Permitted Uses by District (§§125-19 through 125-24) by replacing §§125-19 through 125-24 with a new §125-19, Use Regulations, consolidating general use provisions, use standards, prohibited uses, and district use allowances into a single section, with permitted uses and required permits consolidated into Table 1, Use Regulations. • Replace §125-29 (Lot Size Standards) and §125-30 (Land-Structure Relations) in their entirety with a new §125-29, Dimensional Regulations, establishing a consolidated table of dimensional standards by zoning district (Table 2, Dimensional Standards) along with standards for types of lots. • Amend §125-53 by replacing the Large-Scale Ground-Mounted Solar Photovoltaic Facilities Overlay District in its entirety with a new Clean Energy Facilities Bylaw, establishing local siting standards and permitting procedures for solar energy systems and battery energy storage systems (BESS), providing for the consolidated local permit process and standards for Small Clean Energy Infrastructure Facilities established by the Department of Energy Resources at 225 CMR 29.00. • Amend §125-60, MBTA Communities Multi-Family Overlay District, to clarify the applicability of the inclusionary zoning requirement within the overlay district and to make other clarifying and corrective revisions to the provisions of that section. Jenny presented five zoning articles proposed for the Fall Town Meeting, covering Chapter 40A updates, use regulation updates, dimensional regulations, MBTA community updates, and clean energy updates. Chapter 40A updates - align local bylaws with state law changes, particularly regarding non-conforming structure expansions. The PB discussed updates to article 40A, focusing on feedback from ZBA and Town Counsel. They decided to leave the text as written to minimize changes, with John suggesting they should cite specific sections if Town Counsel approves. Jenny agreed to find the correct section reference and ask Town Counsel about wording for section references if the changes fail. The group also noted that the order of articles at Town Meeting would be decided the next day, and they needed to weigh in on the organization. Page 4 The use regulation updates and dimensional regulations article Jenny presented updates to the bylaw document, including added definitions and use tables. John provided feedback on ensuring consistency across bylaws and requested that uses in the B district match those in the AR district. Jenny agreed to make the necessary changes and investigate missing footnotes in the document. The MBTA Community By-law The meeting focused on reviewing updates to the MBTA Community Multifamily Overlay District bylaw. The board decided to remove maximum setback requirements from the current table, keeping only minimum requirements. They also agreed to add language clarifying that frontage and setback standards apply only to buildings fronting the street on lots with multiple principal buildings. The PB approved moving waiver language to its own section to give the planning board discretion to waive dimensional standards, parking requirements, and general design standards in the interest of design flexibility. The Clean Energy Facilities By-law The board discussed regulations for solar panel installations, specifically focusing on canopy-mounted systems. They agreed to revise the definition of canopy-mounted systems to clarify that they are accessory uses, which would allow for site plan review rather than special permits. The team aligned on maintaining consistent standards between ground-mounted and canopy-mounted systems, with both requiring site plan review for smaller sizes and special permits for larger installations. John confirmed that building-mounted systems up to 250 kilowatts are by right, while larger systems require state approval through EFSB. The board discussed how they felt the order of the articles should go into the Warrant for Town Meeting. Jenny recommended that the order should be first MBTA, then Use Regulations, Dimensional Regulations, 40A updates and then Clean Energy. John voiced an opinion about having the Clean Energy bylaw go early before they discuss the energy contract. They cannot build a facility without having the zoning in place. Doug Thornton made motion to continue this public hearing on September 28, 2026 at 7:30pm. Paul Robertson seconded the motion. All in favor: Doug Thornton – aye, Irene Battaglia – aye, Paul Robertson – aye and John McCormack – aye. text: Posted 09.24.2026 at 4:00pm by MMS SELECT BOARD AGENDA Tuesday, September 29, 2026 7:00pm SusanMary Redinger, Ahmet Corapcioglu, Kara McGuire Minar, Eve Wittenberg, Eric Ward The meeting of the Select Board will be held virtually in accordance with Chapter 2 of the Acts of 2025, An Act extending certain COVID-19 measures adopted during the state of emergency and signed into law on March 28, 2025. To attend and have the ability to participate in meeting, use the Zoom link below. Display full name when entering Zoom. Join Zoom Meeting: https://us02web.zoom.us/j/86055008003?pwd=marHQUstczblvfDUMCF71WQiPbXjI0.1 Meeting ID: 860 5500 8003 / Passcode: 605294 One Tap Mobile: +13052241968,,86055008003# US // +13092053325,,86055008003# US AGENDA ITEMS 1) 2) 3) 4) 5) Call Meeting to Order – SusanMary Redinger, Chair (7:00) Public Communication (7:00) Approve Prior Meeting Minutes of 9/1/2026 and 9/15/2026 (7:05) Energy Manager Report – Andres Correa (7:10) Appointments & Resignations (7:20) a. Agricultural Advisory Commission: Resignation of Christiane Turnheim (as of 9/18/2026) b. Bare Hill Pond Watershed Management Committee: Resignation of Rainer Park (as of 9/8/2026); Vote to Appoint JoAnne Crystoff as Regular Member (Previous Alternate)* c. Open Space Committee: Vote to Re-Appoint Jim Lee as HCT Representative* d. Warner Free Lecture Trustees: Resignation of Seth Trotz (as of 9/19/2026) 6) Local Action Unit Application for Emerson Green Project* (7:30) 7) Consider and Vote to Amend One-Day License for Harvard Alpaca Ranch (Dirigible Brewing Company) Due to Inclement Weather: From 9/26/2026 to 10/11/2026* (7:35) 8) Finalize and Vote to Approve Special Town Meeting Warrant* (7:40) 9) Review and Vote to Approve Budget Guidance* (8:00) 10) Review and Vote to Approve Position Letter re: MA House Bill 5175 and MA Senate Bill 3166* (8:15) 11) Consider Date for All Boards Meeting (8:25) 12) Town Administrator’s Report (8:30) 13) Select Board Reports (8:40) 14) Public Communication (8:55) 15) Adjournment (9:00) Next Regular Select Board Meeting Tuesday, October 6, 2026 *Denotes Select Board Vote Select Board Minutes Tuesday, September 1, 2026 7:00pm The Select Board Regular Meeting was held virtually in accordance with Chapter 2 of the Acts of 2025, An Act extending certain COVID-19 measures adopted during the state of emergency and signed into law on March 28, 2025. Select Board participants: SusanMary Redinger, Ahmet Corapcioglu, Eric Ward, Eve Wittenberg, Kara McGuire Minar Town Department participants: Town Administrator Dawn Dunbar, Assistant Town Administrator Julie Doucet and DPW Director Eric Ryder Additional participants: Public communication Tom Aciukewicz, 61 Depot Road, asked the Select Board for a clearly itemized cost breakdown separating landfill, transfer station, and DPW expenses. He raised concerns about potential property value impacts from the proposed DPW siting and asked whether the Town would compensate affected abutters. He also urged shifting from a competing constituency framing to a collaborative approach, and requested an update on whether redesigning within the current footprint has been fully explored. Minutes SusanMary declared the minutes of 8/4 & 8/18, approved as amended. Initial FY28 budget discussion Town Administrator Dawn Dunbar presented initial FY28 budget projections from Finance Director Jared Mullane, showing an estimated $829,000 deficit based on 3.2% cost-of-living increases and a 10% health insurance increase. The board will review in more detail at their Strategic Planning Session on September 10, and after the tri-board representative meeting on September 14, the Select Board will finalize the budget process and memo. DPW/Transfer Station updates SusanMary announced a public meeting will be scheduled between September 29 and early October to gather input from residents. Dawn outlined five potential siting options, with Option D keeping the facility within its current footprint emerging as the most feasible option as it maintains transfer station operations during capping and preserves three playing fields while allowing improved parking. DPW Director Eric Ryder confirmed MassDEP’s assurance that the town can operate a temporary landfill and transfer station throughout construction. Dawn detailed technical requirements such as test pits, grading, and possible capping needs. They continue researching costs for curbside pickup, transfer station relocation, equipment modernization, and potential regional partnerships. Open Space Committee Composition Eve Wittenberg provided an overview of the Open Space Committee’s mission, its current composition, and recent work, emphasizing the committee’s role in protecting open space and its past efforts to identify land for athletic fields, including contributing to the Old Mill Road acquisition. She explained that the committee has since focused on inventorying unprotected land and updating the Open Space and Recreation Plan, and is Select Board Minutes prepared by Julie Doucet 1 September 1, 2026 now seeking Select Board input to clarify its future mission. The Select Board agreed to schedule a joint meeting with the Open Space Committee to discuss priorities, potential adjustments to the committee’s scope, and possible changes in composition. Town Administrator Report (Attachment A) Select Board Reports Ahmet reported that HCTV videos are now available and that podcast technology is being explored for both the Select Board and School Committee. He also shared updates on the CPA site selection process HEAC is working on and announced they will have upcoming information sessions. He noted the Stow Road appraisal came in at $940,000. Eric discussed an informative water and sewer meeting focused on upcoming changes related to the connection with Devens. He noted the school department is making progress on the HVAC project. He also mentioned that the CPC has set its schedule. Eve shared that the Conservation Commission is handling permitting for the Eldridge Road culvert and that Municipal Affordable Housing Trust (MAHT) is continuing work on its strategic plan through an RFP process. She noted the Agricultural Committee needs new members and will post an advertisement. Kara reported she is following up with Senator Jamie Eldridge on lighting bids and the related earmark for Fivesparks. SusanMary provided an update on the Addiction Abatement Fund Working Group balance and noted membership changes. She reported that CPIC is down one member and a memo has gone out. She confirmed the police cruiser article will be on the October Fall Town Meeting warrant and that the Devens questionnaire has five responses so far, including comments on Vicksburg Square. She added that the Framework Committee is revisiting its process and reminded everyone to read the COA’s September newsletter. Public Communication Tom Aciukewicz, 61 Depot Road, asked for a meeting in person regarding the DPW/Transfer Station. He was pleased with the presentation tonight. Executive Session per MGL Ch. 30A, s. 21(a) 6 By a roll call vote, Corapcioglu – aye, Wittenberg – aye, Ward – aye, Minar – aye, Redinger – aye, the board voted unanimously to enter executive session at 8:30pm as per MGL 30A Sec. 21.3 6 to consider the purchase, exchange, lease of value of real property if the chair declares that an open meeting may have a detrimental effect on the negotiating position of the public body. session. The public portion of the meeting was adjourned at 8:30pm. Documents referenced: General Fund - Budgeted Revenue / Expense Projection General Fund - 5 Year Budgeted Revenue Projection DPW/Transfer Station siting options – dated 9.1.2026 Harvard CHAPTER 61 Lands Policy & Process – dated Sept 2026 Select Board Minutes prepared by Julie Doucet 2 September 1, 2026 Select Board Minutes Tuesday, September 15, 2026 7:00pm A regular meeting of the Select Board (the “Board”) was held virtually on Tuesday, September 15, 2026 in accordance with Chapter 2 of the Acts of 2025, An Act extending certain Covid-19 measures adopted during the state of emergency and signed into law on March 28, 2025. Select Board Participants: SusanMary Redinger, Chair; Ahmet Corapcioglu, Vice-Chair; Eve Wittenberg; Eric Ward. Absent: Kara McGuire Minar. Town Department Participants: Dawn Dunbar, Town Administrator; Julie Doucet, Assistant Town Administrator; Michelle Stockman, Executive Assistant to the Town Administrator. Additional Participants: Aaron Farber-Chen, Addiction Abatement Fund Working Group Chair; Patrick Vallaeys, Community Media Access Committee Chair; Robert Blanck, Community Media Access Committee Nominee. A quorum was declared and the meeting was called to order by Chair SusanMary Redinger at 7:00pm. Michelle Stockman kept the minutes of the meeting. The Chair opened the meeting to public communication, and there being no questions, comments, or concerns, proceeded to business matters. Introduction of Michelle Stockman: The Select Board welcomed Michelle Stockman, the new Executive Assistant to the Town Administrator, who started on September 14, 2026. Appointments: Following the departure of former Superintendent Linda Dwight, a motion was made by Eve Wittenberg and seconded by Eric Ward to appoint Superintendent Dana Labb as School Representative to the Addiction Abatement Fund Working Group. By a roll call vote, Corapcioglu – aye, Wittenberg – aye, Ward – aye, Redinger – aye, the motion carried unanimously, 4-0. Robert Blanck introduced himself to the Board, and described his background and experience in relation to his nomination to the Community Media Access Committee. It was clarified that Mr. Blanck was nominated as a new member. 1 A motion was made by Ahmet Corapcioglu and seconded by Ms. Select Board Meeting Minutes – September 15, 2026 1 Wittenberg to appoint Mr. Blanck as a new member of the Community Media Access Committee. By roll call vote, Corapcioglu – aye, Ward – aye, Wittenberg – aye, Redinger – aye, the motion carried unanimously, 4-0. Next, Mr. Corapcioglu explained that Andrew Gavin, an alternate on the Community Media Access Committee, was nominated for regular membership. Committee Chair Patrick Vallaeys joined the meeting and offered remarks. A motion was made by Mr. Corapcioglu and seconded by Ms. Wittenberg to appoint Mr. Gavin as a regular member of the Community Media Access Committee. By roll call vote, Corapcioglu – aye, Ward – aye, Wittenberg – aye, Redinger – aye, the motion carried unanimously, 4-0. The appointment of Jim Lee to the Open Space Committee was postponed until the next regularly scheduled meeting as it was necessary for the Harvard Conservation Trust to appoint him first. Review and Finalize Fiscal Year 2028 Budget Memorandum and Process Mr. Ward led the Board in a review of the draft budget memorandum regarding the process timeline for fiscal year 2028.2 The Board agreed to schedule a special meeting on Tuesday, September 22 at 2:00pm to discuss and vote upon the budget guidance. Town Administrator Dawn Dunbar confirmed that she would distribute the draft timeline to department heads, and provide guidance separately when ready. A motion was made by Mr. Corapcioglu and seconded by Ms. Wittenberg to approve the fiscal year 2028 budget process timeline as submitted. By roll call vote, Corapcioglu – aye, Ward – aye, Wittenberg – aye, Redinger – aye, the motion carried unanimously, 4-0. Addiction Abatement Fund Working Group Recommendation re: ARC Mini Grant The Board was joined by Aaron Farber-Chen, Chair of the Addiction Abatement Fund Working Group, who presented a proposal from the Addiction Referral Center (“ARC”) requesting $9,999.99 to provide first-month rent for individuals transitioning out of detox or treatment into sober housing. 3 The working group reviewed the proposal and unanimously recommended it for approval. Mr. Farber-Chen confirmed the project start date of January 1, 2026 and project end date of December 31, 2026. A motion was made by Ms. Wittenberg and seconded by Mr. Ward to approve the grant application as recommended. By roll call vote, Corapcioglu – aye, Ward – aye, Wittenberg – aye, Redinger – aye, the motion carried unanimously, 4-0. DPW/Transfer Station Update Ms. Dunbar reviewed the five previously presented siting options for the Department of Public Works (“DPW”) facility, highlighting the pros and cons of each. At the conclusion of the presentation, the Board determined that no vote was required, but agreed to eliminate options A, B, and E and narrow its focus on options C and D. Ms. Dunbar noted that option D showed promise as it would place the DPW building over its existing footprint and not result in the loss of playing fields. However, she indicated that option D would require a temporary relocation of offices and facilities during construction, unlike option C. The next steps in the procurement process were outlined, including engaging the Permanent Building Committee, which had three vacancies. Ms. Dunbar presented a plan to utilize $10M in funds leftover from a previous DPW building approval to hire an Owner’s Project Manager (“OPM”) for this construction in accordance with M.G.L. c. 149, §44A½. A discussion ensued regarding the need for more detailed cost analysis of transfer station services versus alternative options, such as curbside pickup. It was noted that two public meetings had been scheduled to gather community input: a virtual Select Board Meeting Minutes – September 15, 2026 2 offering on October 5 at 1:00pm and an in-person offering on October 8 at 7:00pm. A vote was not necessary, but the Board approved the hire of an OPM and directed Ms. Dunbar to issue a request for proposal. The Permanent Building Committee, DPW Director Eric Ryder, Ms. Dunbar, and Ms. Redinger as liaison would be responsible for the selection process. The estimated length of the process from bid through selection was at least a month. Review Draft Special Town Meeting Warrant Ms. Dunbar reviewed each of the draft Special Town Meeting warrant articles and presented changes intended to make the information more accessible, including the addition of a cover page, table of contents, and article summaries.4 Postcards will be mailed to all households instead of the full warrant to save on printing cost. Ms. Dunbar proposed making the full 50-page document and attachments available digitally via QR code, while providing the summaries in the warrant. The Board agreed with this approach, while acknowledging that some hard copies would need to be printed. It was noted that Jenny Gingras would present the Planning Board warrant articles at the Special Town Meeting, and would host a zoning informational session for the community in advance on September 29, 2026 at 6:00pm. Finalization of the warrant would take place at the September 29 Select Board meeting. Town Moderator Bill Barton was invited to join the Board at its October 6 meeting to introduce changes being implemented at the Special Town Meeting. Town Administrator Report At the invitation of the Board, Ms. Dunbar delivered a Town Administrator Report. Project updates included: potentially going live the following Monday at the Harvard/Devens Water System Interconnection Pump Station; renovation progress at McCurdy Track and Field; and the prospective completion of the building management system at the library the following week. With respect to personnel, Ms. Dunbar shared that a DPW truck driver recently resigned and there was eagerness to fill that position in anticipation of the winter months. Operations updates included: entering a one-year contract with a cleaning company to replace the current custodian following their retirement on September 30; no longer pursuing a purchase of property on Old Mill Road in connection with DPW facility siting; and a recent site walk of Vicksburg Square that took place on September 2. Ms. Dunbar closed her presentation by highlighting upcoming events and correspondence received. Select Board Reports Ms. Wittenberg provided updates on behalf of the Tree Warden, Municipal Affordable Housing Trust, and Conservation Commission. The Tree Warden was working on a memorandum of understanding with the schools to ensure that trees are properly maintained in light of recent droughts. There would be an upcoming lottery for the affordable housing unit at The Village at Robin Lane. The Conservation Commission was planning for its discussion on September 24 with the Bear Hill Pond Watershed Management Committee regarding the annual report. Mr. Corapcioglu presented on behalf of the Climate Initiative Committee, Community Media Access Committee, Zoning Board of Appeals, and Bear Hill Pond Watershed Management Committee. Mr. Corapcioglu reported on pending state legislation that may affect MassSave funding. He also informed the Board of the need to complete an inspection of the new Harvard Media Cooperative production studio located at the school, which would be coordinated with Superintendent Labb. Mr. Ward had no updates to report. Select Board Meeting Minutes – September 15, 2026 3 Chair Redinger provided a report on behalf of the Harvard-Devens Jurisdiction Committee and Devens Framework Committee. Chair Victor Normand of the Harvard-Devens Jurisdiction Committee recommended postponing a vote at the Special Town Meeting, and offering a presentation instead. Following some concern, it was confirmed that the cameras in town were not Flock cameras, rather were specific to monitoring weather and precipitation. Public Communication The meeting was opened to public communication. Lisa Aciukewicz of 61 Depot Road inquired about the Massachusetts Department of Environmental Protection approval process regarding the DPW project. title: MONTACHUSETT REGIONAL PLANNING COMMISSION(MRPC) Meeting
text: MONTACHUSETT REGIONAL PLANNING COMMISSION (MRPC) 464 Abbott Ave. Leominster, MA 01453 REMOTE MEETING ONLY THURSDAY, SEPTEMBER 17, 7:00 PM MRPC MEETING MATERIALS: September 17, 2026 MRPC Commission Meeting Materials MINUTES 1. Open Meeting, Introductions and Announcements This meeting will be recorded to ensure we have an accurate record of our discussion. If anyone has any concerns about being recorded, please let us know. This meeting is held under An Act Extending Certain COVID-19 Measures Adopted During the State of Emergency signed by Governor Healey on March 28, 2025, allowing local and regional governments to hold public meetings remotely or in a hybrid fashion through June 30, 2027. All votes will be taken by roll call. Vice Chair, G. Corbosiero opened the meeting at 7:01 pm. Roll Call Followed: G. Corbosiero – present R. Swartz – present T. Russo – present L. Shifrin – present P. Cunningham – present D. Thornton – present A. Pease – present A. Reid – present P. Fontaine, Jr. - present 2. MRPC Minutes – August 6, 2026 – Approval of Commissioners Requested Having no objections or corrections, P. Cunningham moved to accept the August 6, 2026 minutes as presented. The motion was seconded. Roll Call Vote Followed: G. Corbosiero – yes R. Swartz – yes T. Russo – yes L. Shifrin – yes P. Cunningham – abstain D. Thornton – yes A. Pease – yes A. Reid - abstain P. Fontaine Jr. - abstain 3. Cash Schedule – August 2026 – Acceptance of Commissioners Requested R. Swatz presented the August 2026 cash schedule. The opening balance for August 1, 2026 was $705,916.83, total receipts $107,522.49, total cash on hand before this warrant $813,439.32, less amount of this warrant $213,582.24, left a balance after the warrant of $599,857.08. Having no objections, R. Swartz moved to accept the cash schedule as presented, subject to audit. The motion was seconded. Roll Call Vote Followed: G. Corbosiero – yes R. Swartz – yes T. Russo – yes L. Shifrin – yes P. Cunningham – yes D. Thornton – yes A. Pease – yes A. Reid - yes P. Fontaine Jr. - yes 4. Guest Announcements and Questions No announcements or questions were presented. 5. Administrative Matters 5.1 Report of the Executive Committee Meeting of 6:00 p.m., Thursday, September 17, 2026, Concerning Executive Director Transition – Information or Action Item Chair, K. Munroe was scheduled to lead this discussion, however, he was unable to attend the meeting. The Executive Committee met very briefly from about 6:00 pm – 6:15 pm. Members requested all copies of the Executive Directors job description that we had so they can be reviewed prior to the next meeting scheduled for October 8th. H. Ford, Administrative and Human Resource Director will send an email which will contain all copies on file. 5.2 FY25 Audit Presentation: Information or Action Item In August, management continued a FY25 Audit completion date from Grassi Advisors. On September 2nd, Grassi emailed management, informing us that our final draft audit is undergoing a final review. Management was only informed of this additional review task on September 2nd. We were informed to contact Grassi’s Chelmsford office to determine when their review would be completed. We reached out to the Chelmsford office on September 2nd and 14th. As of September 15th, a response from Grassi had not yet been received. Concerning audits, please be advised that Tracy Warrington, Fiscal Director, completed a request for proposals (RFP) for the hiring of an independent auditor for the completion of the FY26 audit. The RFP has been advertised. (Ms. Warrington recently completed the Massachusetts Certified Public Procurement Officials [MCPPO] Program which aided her and the MRPC in the development of this RFP and other RFPs in the future.) T. Warrington is hoping to have some assessments, evaluations and interviews completed in hopes of bringing forth a candidate(s) at the next meeting. 5.3 Personnel Updates: Hiring of a Replacement Planner and New Support Staff Hired – Information Only Please be advised that Mackenzie Miller has been hired as a part-time Administrative Support Intern to assist the Fiscal Director with some audit preparation tasks. MRPC has advertised for a part-time Administrative and Fiscal Assistant. Lastly, an advertisement was posted for one or more planners for the Comprehensive Planning Department. At least one is needed to replace an employee who resigned in June, and a second planner may need to be hired due to the receipt of new grant awards and an increase in workload in the Comprehensive Planning Department. Management has completed four interviews for the planner position(s) and additional interviews will be held during the week of September 14 (after the Executive Director returns from vacation during the week of September 7th). Commissioners will be updated throughout the hiring process. 5.4 CEDS Adoption Update – Information Only Please be advised that The Federal Economic Development Administration (EDA). EDA’s approval occurred after two final edits, required by EDA, were made. MRPC was told to replace the word “race” with ethnicities” and delete the word “electric” from “electric vehicles.” 5.5 Next Combined Meeting of the Montachusett Economic Development District, CEDS Group and the Brownfields Group Meeting – Information Only The next MEDD/MRCEDS/Brownfields Group meeting concerning zoning and related matters for tiny homes, data centers, or both will be held at 3:00 p.m. on Thursday, September 24th. The registration link can be found below and on the MRPC’s website. https://forms.cloud.microsoft/g/2iFZkeSz4m Through June 2027, these meetings will be held on the fourth Thursday of each month at 3:00 p.m., as follows. • October 22, 2026 • November 19, 2026 (This meeting will be held on the third Thursday of the month due to the Thanksgiving Holiday to be held in the following, 4th, week of the month) • December 17, 2026 • January 28, 2027 • February 25, 2027 • March 25, 2027 • April 22, 2027 • May 27, 2027 • June 24, 2027 It is possible that some meetings may be held in person at MRPC’s office, 464 Abbott Avenue, Leominster. Meeting agendas, registrations instructions, and locations will be issued each month. 5.6 MRPC Lunch-and-Learn Meetings, FY27 - Information Only – Tiny Homes, Data Centers The next Lunch and Learn meeting concerning zoning and related matters for tiny homes, data centers, or both will be held at Noon, on September 30, 2026. The registration link for the September 30th meeting can be found below and on the MRPC’s website. https://forms.cloud.microsoft/g/XhbRWgS3M2 Lunch and Learn meetings will be held online, at Noon, on the last Wednesday of each month, as follows (some meetings will be held on the third Wednesday of the month, as indicated below). • • • • • • • • • October 28, 2026 November 18, 2026 (This meeting will be held on the third Wednesday of the month due to the Thanksgiving Holiday to be held in the following, 4th, week of the month) December 30, 2026 January 27, 2027 February 24, 2027 March 31, 2027 April 28, 2027 May 26, 2027 June 23, 2027 It is possible that some meetings may be held in person at MRPC’s office, 464 Abbott Avenue, Leominster. Meeting agendas, registrations instructions, and locations will be issued each month. P. Cunningham addressed that the PFAS dynamic is emerging rapidly and questioned if there may be any grants to assist with remediation. L. Shifrin stated Townend is dealing with the bylaw for battery storage and if that would be discussed on the 30th as well. G. Eaton asked that questions be sent to Bernie (bcahill@mrpc.org) and or Glenn (geaton@mrpc.org) and they will see if they can start a dialogue to ee what can be done. P. Fontaine Jr. added that the City of Fitchburg has a moratorium for both data centers and battery storage. L. Shifrin stated she may go to one of the meetings to learn more. 5.7 Other Administrative Matters 6. Department Updates Status of all ongoing projects can be found by clicking on the link, below: https://mrmapper.mrpc.org/webapps/v2.27/CurrentProjects/ MRPC staff are prepared to answer questions about any contract with any local, state, and federal entity. Commissioners are welcome to ask questions about projects in their respective communities 6.1 Geographic Information Systems (GIS) No new updates at this time. 6.2 Planning & Development In addition to the other 12 RPAs in the state, we are in receipt of a two-year grant project. It will be about $200,000 each fiscal year. There will be three aspects to the program. The first is that RPAs are going to be required to work with their communities to come up with a regional resiliency portfolio. The next step will be working with our 22 communities to develop five different feasible projects that are reviewed and approved by EEA. Once this step is complete, two will be chosen to be worked on. We will update you as this progresses. 6.3 Transit & Transportation B. Doherty shared his department is finishing up their fiscal year by the end of this month. There are a number of projects that we’ll be posting on our website in October. As a reminder, the MPO and MJTC will be meeting every other month through the end of the calendar year. The next MJTC meeting will be October 14th and the MPO meeting will be held on October 21st. 7. New Business Open session - This time is reserved for topics that the chair did not reasonably anticipate would be discussed. 8. Adjournment - The date of the next MRPC meeting – Thursday, October 8, 2026, 7:00 p.m. Having no additional comments or objections, R. Swartz move to adjourn the meeting. Motion was seconded. Meeting was adjourned at 7:42 pm. This meeting will be recorded by the Zoom app and will be made available for viewing at https://www.youtube.com/user/MontachusettRegion/videos. Meeting ID: 818 3127 9424 Passcode: 754763 PROPOSED ZONING BYLAW AND ZONING MAP AMENDMENT Pursuant to M.G.L. c. 40A, § 5 and the Town of Lancaster Zoning Bylaw, notice is hereby given that the Lancaster Planning Board will hold a public hearing on Monday, September 28, 2026, at 7:00 PM to receive public comments and discuss proposed amendments to the Town of Lancaster Zoning Bylaw and Official Zoning Map via zoom and in the Nashaway Meeting Room, the Prescott Building 2nd floor, 701 Main Street, Lancaster, MA, on Monday September 28, 2026 at 7:00 PM to hear and act upon the following: To consider an amendment to the Lancaster Zoning Bylaw to create and adopt a new zoning district for the stateowned site on 220 Old Common Road commonly known as the Lancaster Industrial School for Girls. The proposed redevelopment of the site for mixed use and single and multifamily housing is through the Commonwealth’s State Land for Homes Initiative that is part of Chapter 156 of The Acts of 2024/the Affordable Homes Act. The proposed zoning amendment will create a new zoning district within the Lancaster Zoning Bylaw that will establish allowed uses, dimensional requirements, density controls, design guidelines, and open space preservation and other permitting criteria specific to the proposed district. The Official Zoning Map will also be amended to identify the proposed zoning district. A complete copy of the proposed text of the zoning amendment, legal descriptions, and associated maps are on file and available for public viewing at the Department of Community Development and Planning, 701 Main Street, Lancaster, MA, 978-368-3326 x1081. All interested parties are invited to attend the hearing and provide written or verbal comments. Written comments may be submitted ahead of time via email at bkeating@lancasterma.gov or by mail to the Planning Board c/o of the Department of Planning & Community Development 701 Main Street, Suite 4, Lancaster MA 01523 Frank Streeter, Chairman Lancaster Planning Board For publication in The Worcester Telegram: Monday, September 14, 2026 Monday, September 21, 2026

ADJOURNMENT Rules of Procedure for Board Meetings of Lanesborough Select Board Meetings IL AGENDA The Town Administrative Assistant, in consultation with the Town Administrator and Chairman of the Select Board shall prepare an Agenda for the Select Board meetings. Any requests for matters to be placed on the agenda shall be submitted in writing to the Town Administrative Assistant by noon three business days prior to regularly scheduled meetings. Anyone requesting items be placed on the agenda shall provide the topic of the item and sufficient information and detail so as to provide a reasonable notice of the nature and purpose of the agenda item. Agendas will be posted a minimum of 48 hours in advance of any meeting on our Town website and Town bulletin board. Those wishing to speak in the public comment portion of the agenda shall provide their name and the topic of their comment, Topics shall be limited to matters of concern, official action or deliberation which are or may be before the Select Board. MEETINGS Public Notice of the meetings shall be advertised and posted by the Administrative Assistant as required by law. It. on The Chairman of the Select Board shall direct the meeting. In the absence of the Chairman, the senior member of the Select Board shall direct the meeting and shall have all powers and duties of the Chairman. The Modern Rules of Order shall be used to conduct the meeting unless otherwise modified by these Rules or altered by the Select Board. The Lanesborough Select Board shall be addressed by their respective titles. Residents and/or taxpayers may use audio or stenographic recorders to record all or any portion of the meeting. Said recorders shall be operated from the area set aside for the general public seating and may not be placed on the Select Board’s table without prior consent of the Chairman. Video recorders may be used to record all or any portion of a public meeting. The operator of the recorder shall remain seated in the area set aside for the general public or stand in the rear or to the side of the general public seating area so as to not interfere in any way with the activities of the Select Board or the ability of the general public to observe the Board. PUBLIC COMMENT Residents and taxpayers of Lanesborough shall have the right to speak in the meetings during the Public Comment portion of the agenda. In order to conduct meetings in an orderly and productive manner the following rules and regulations shall govern such speakers: Comment from residents/taxpayers shall be received only after the speaker is recognized by the Chairman. The speaker shall announce his or her name and address prior to addressing the Select Board. The Chairman may rule out-of-order scandalous, impertinent, irrelevant, and redundant comments, or comments that attempt to disrupt or needlessly protract the proceedings of the meeting. The Chairman may request any individual to leave the meeting and may contact security to that end when that individual does not observe reasonable decorum. Further, the Chairman may request the assistance of law enforcement officers to remove a disorderly person when his/her conduct interferes with the orderly progress of the meeting. The Chairman may call a recess or adjournment to another time when the lack of public decorum interferes with the orderly conduct of the meeting. The Chairman may allocate available time among individuals wishing to comment. Time allocated for the public comment period at each meeting shall not exceed thirty (30) minutes and limited to citizens of Lanesborough unless prior approval is granted by the Lanesborough Select Board. Each speaker will be allotted three (3) minutes to present his or her topic. Said time limitations may be altered or waived at the Chairman’s direction. At the discretion of the Chairman conducting the meeting, a group of citizens registered to address the Select Board on the same issue may be required to designate a spokesperson.

title: Planning Board Public Hearing on Zoning Bylaw Amendments
text: Notice of Town of Lenox Planning Board Public Hearing In accordance with the provisions of MGL Chapter40A, Section 5, the Town of Lenox Planning Board will hold a Public Hearing on Tuesday, September 22" at 6:00pm at the Lenox Town Hall (6 Walker Street, Lenox MA 01240} to present and receive comments on proposed Zoning Bylaw amendments to be included in the Warrant at the Special Town Meeting on November 5, 2026. The proposed amendments are as follows: e Amending Section 4 “Definitions,” to revise the definitions for “Frontage Lot Line”, “Lot Width”, “Setback”, “Building Setback”, and “Street Setback”, “Lot Line Setback”, “Parking Area Setback”, and “Sign Setback”; remove the definitions for “Street Setback” and “Street Line”; add a new definition for “District Boundary Line Setback.” These definition amendments then necessitate changes in other various bylaw sections for overall bylaw consistency and clarity: ° oO oOo 0 0 O° Amending Section 2.2 “Zoning Map”, to revise 2.2.2 “Interpretation” Amending Section 5 “Use Regulations,” specifically H-8 under Table 5.2 “Schedule of Uses” Amending Section 6 “Dimensional Requirements” to revise and clarify 6.1, 6.1.2, 6.1.6, 6.1.7, 6.1.11, 6.2.3, 6.3 and 6.3.1 Amending 6.1.1 “Table of Dimensional Requirements” Amending Section 7 “General Regulations” to revise and clarify 7.1.8 and 7.1.10 Amending Section 8 “Special Regulations” to revise and clarify 8.1, 8.5, 8.15, and 8.18 Amending Section 9 “Special Residential Regulations” to revise and clarify 9.1, 9.1.3, 9.2, 9.3.2, 9.4 and 9.8 Amending Section 10 “Special District Regulations” to revise and clarify 10.2.13 e Amending Section 8.8 “Educational and Religious Uses” to strike the existing section in its entirety and replace with new Section 8.8 “Limited Site Plan Review for Certain Institutional and Exempt Uses.” ie) Oo Amending Section 4 “Definitions,” to revise the definition for “Educational Use, Non- Exempt” and change definition of “Child Care Facility” to “Child Care Center”; remove the definition for “Family day care home, large or small”; add new definitions for “Family Child Care Home”, “Large Family Child Care Home”, and “Religious Use, Exempt” based on new Section 8.8 “Limited Site Plan Review for Certain Institutional and Exempt Uses.” Amending Section 5.2 “Use Regulations,” specifically A-8, B-1, B-2, B-3, B-7, B-8, B-9, B- 10, F-21, F-23 and F-24 under Table 5.2 “Schedule of Uses” on new Section 8.8 “Limited Site Plan Review for Certain institutional and Exempt Uses.” Amending Section 7.1 “Off-Street Parking and Loading Requirements” by revising the Parking Space Quantity Requirements Table from “Office” to “Offices & Institutional Uses” based on new Section 8.8 “Limited Site Plan Review for Certain Institutional and Exempt Uses.” Amending Section 7.2 “Signs” by removing Section 7.2.4.4 related to signage for Institutional Uses based on new Section 8.8 “Limited Site Plan Review for Certain Institutional and Exempt Uses.” e Amending Section 5.2, “Schedule of Uses”: o F-14 “Gas Station, which may include a convenience store”: amend table to allow the use by ZBA Special Permit in the C-1A zoning districts; o F-15 “Motor Vehicle Light Service”: amend table to allow the use by ZBA Special Permit in the C-1A and C zoning districts, and as a “by right” use in the industrial “I” zoning district. Copies of the proposed zoning amendments are available from the Town Clerk during regular business hours and on the Town of Lenox website www.townoflenox.com. Comments may be sent to landuse@townoflenox.com or mailed to the Land Use Department at Lenox Town Hail. Information for Zoom access to the Public Hearing will be posted on an agenda no less than 48 hours in advance of the Public Hearing on the Town of Lenox Website.

Since we are meeting in person, we will not be responsible for any technical difficulties, so if you would like to be sure of participating, please attend in person. Join Zoom Meeting https://zoom.us/j/94460276391?pwd=N294R3hyQzlyMUtsZ1ZkMTBjL3BPdz09 Meeting ID: 944 6027 6391; Passcode: 650146 Protocols for Public Address to the Board: During meetings, the Selectboard will attempt to find a balance between hearing from members of the community and conducting required business. All public address is at the discretion of the Chair. When speaking, please identify yourself by name or the company/institution you represent. Please make your comments are concise (less than 2 minutes); avoid repeat statements made by others; address your comments to the Board Chair. Audience members may not interrupt a recognized speaker nor the discussion of the Board. Please be cordial and respectful of others. The Selectboard will generally listen to comments rather than respond immediately. If a topic comes up that is not on the agenda yet further action is required by the Board, the Chair will add the matter, as appropriate, to a forthcoming agenda. Depending on the comment, the Board may, if they are able within the confines of the Open Meeting Law, respond with information as opposed to needing to deliberate on the matter. This meeting agenda is being posted in compliance with Massachusetts’ Open Meeting Law. The agenda may change to reflect unforeseen business. Article 2: Town Charter Select Board [text needed] Article 3: Adoption of the Provisions of Chapter 40U Select Board § [INSERT NO.] Noncriminal disposition of violations. Adoption of the provisions of Chapter 40U of the General Laws; noncriminal disposition is hereby authorized for the violation of any rule, regulation, order, ordinance or bylaw regulating the housing, sanitary, or snow and ice removal requirement. § [INSERT NO.] Municipal fine procedures. A. Definitions. MUNICIPAL HEARING OFFICER — A person appointed by the Town Administrator to conduct hearings of alleged Code violations pursuant to this chapter. UNPAID CHARGE — An unpaid fine incurred as a result of a violation of a rule, regulation, order, ordinance or bylaw regulating the housing, sanitary or municipal snow and ice removal requirement. B. Effective date. This chapter shall take effect in Littleton upon its acceptance. C. Procedures for payment of municipal fines; power to revoke or rescind. By adopting Chapter 40U §§1-18, the Town of Littleton has adopted procedures for the payment of the municipal fines provided in this Chapter 40U and may revoke or rescind any such acceptance. D. Municipal Hearing Officer. The Officer shall hear appeals of violation notices issued within the municipality. The Municipal Hearing Officer may be the same person appointed as a Municipal Hearing Officer pursuant to Chapter 148A of the General Laws. E. Inclusive Adoption of the Provisions of M.G.L. c. 40U §§1-18. These provisions set forth in M.G.L. c. 40U, et seq., establish the processes for determinations and issuances of Violation Notices, delivery of Violations, appeals, notices, payments and enforcement. 1 F. Schedule of fines for violation. The Town of Littleton has, within this bylaw, established a schedule of fines for violations subject to this chapter committed within the municipality; provided, however, that all such fines shall be uniform for the same offense committed in the same zone or district, if any. A first fine under this chapter shall be $300.00. Any additional fines issued shall not exceed the maximum allowable amount under the relevant sections of the sanitary code, excluding late fees. G. Unpaid M.G.L. c. 40U Violations to Become Real Estate Liens and Added to Property Tax Bill. If the fine remains unpaid at the conclusion of the appeal process and all required notices have been sent, additional penalties and interest may be attached, and such amount shall become an additional assessment on the property owner’s tax bill, and shall also be a lien upon such real estate as provided in M.G.L. c. 40 § 42B. This action, without more, will constitute a lien on the property. H. Revolving Fund. Funds received from M.G.L. c. 40U Violations shall be paid into a revolving fund and utilized for the purpose of administering the Town’s code enforcement program. Such revolving fund shall be subject to annual review and re-authorization pursuant to the Massachusetts General Laws. I. Local ordinances superseded. By accepting Chapter 40U of the General Laws, this chapter shall supersede any local ordinances or bylaws to the contrary including but not limited to §1-2, §1-4, §202-10, §38-6, and §38-21. Enforcing officers shall include all those authorized pursuant to the state sanitary code, building code, and fire code. Town Code §41-3 provides that: For every annual and special town meeting, the Select Board shall mail to each occupied dwelling at least fourteen (14) days prior to said meeting a Town Meeting Report containing the full text of the articles as posted in the Warrant; proposed motions and town board recommendations, if any; and concise explanations of each article, including the fiscal impact of any financial articles. The Town Meeting Report for the annual town meeting shall include the Finance Committee's report to the voters. Here is the format in which information is presented for each article in this Report: ARTICLE # Title of the Article Article Sponsor/Inserter [If needed, any special voting requirements] Full text of the Warrant article as printed in the Town Meeting Warrant, as posted. [Brief explanation of the article.] Motion proposed by the sponsor, as reviewed by Town Counsel. Recommendations of Town Boards. The Select Board welcomes your feedback. Littleton Select Board Gary Wilson, Chair Charles DeCoste, Vice-Chair Mark Rambacher, Clerk Karen Morrison Kyle Bubp Town Moderator: Town Meeting Procedures “A Call of the Articles” In our continuing effort to streamline and improve the efficiency of Town Meeting, and after having discussed ways to improve the process with the Select Board, the Town Clerk and Town Counsel I am proposing to continue the following procedures: We will continue with “A Call of the Articles” which was successfully introduced several years ago, to speed up the passage of Warrant articles which should generate no controversy and can be properly voted without debate allowing additional time to debate more significant articles. Specifically, as one of the first orders of business at Town Meeting, the Moderator will call out the numbers/titles of the articles, one by one. Any voter who has doubts about passing any motion, or wishes an explanation of any article, should say the word “hold” in a loud voice when the article number is called by the Moderator. The Moderator will inquire as to whether the request is for a question or for debate. If the purpose of the request is merely a question, then an attempt will be made to obtain a satisfactory answer. If the purpose is to hold the article for debate, the article will be removed from the list of articles included in the “Call” and restored to its original place in the Warrant to be brought up, debated and voted in the usual manner. It is hoped that voters will remove articles from the “Call” only in cases of legitimate concern. After calling each article on the Warrant, the Moderator will ask that all remaining articles in the “Call” be passed as a unit by unanimous vote. There will be a motion to take all the articles identified in the “Call” and act upon them by means of a single, brief affirmative main motion which will be inclusive of the separate and specific motions as printed in this Report. The use of “A Call of the Articles” is intended to speed up passage of Warrant articles which each Town Meeting voter believes should generate no controversy and can be properly voted without debate and give Town Meeting additional time to thoughtfully consider the rest of the Warrant articles. General Town Meeting Guidelines • Presentations - The individual, board or committee responsible for placing an article on the Warrant will be permitted ten (10) minutes to make a presentation once the main motion is properly placed before Town Meeting. A single presenter is preferred and in the event of multiple presenters no additional time shall be granted. Presentations in opposition will likewise be limited to 10 minutes and must be approved in advance of Town Meeting by the Moderator. The Moderator reserves the right to grant additional time, within reason, to presentations that the Moderator believes Town Meeting would benefit from hearing in their entirety. In the interest of fairness, the Moderator will extend the offer of additional time to both sides. • Limits on length/number of speeches - Speakers shall be limited to no more than three (3) minutes and no one shall speak more than once per article except for the following situations: responses to questions posed by and through the Moderator, brief clarification of a previous statement with the permission of the Moderator, or by majority vote of Town Meeting. • Time limit for consideration of Warrant articles (evening meetings) –Town Meeting shall not begin consideration of any new Warrant article after 10:30p.m., unless the Moderator determines that there is a reasonable likelihood of concluding action on that article prior to 11:00p.m. and a majority of Town Meeting votes to continue its business past 10:30pm. Accessibility/Requesting Reasonable Accommodations Additionally, towns have an obligation under the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) to: 1. Make their Town Meetings accessible to people with disabilities; and, to 2. Respond to requests for reasonable accommodations at Town Meetings. The Town of Littleton does not discriminate based on disability and is committed to hosting accessible meetings. To request a reasonable accommodation to attend Town Meeting, please contact the municipal ADA Coordinator at 978-540-2433. More information about Town Meeting is available online at https://www.littletonma.org/townmeetings. Thank you for your cooperation in implementing these procedures and allowing me the privilege of serving as your Moderator. ARTICLE 2 Adoption of a Special Act Establishing a Town Charter Select Board [Majority Vote Required] To see if the Town will vote to authorize and direct the Select Board to petition the General Court for the enactment of a special act establishing a Town Charter for the Town of Littleton substantially in the form attached to this Warrant as Exhibit A. The Legislature may make clerical or editorial changes in form only to the bill, unless the Select Board approves amendments to the bill before enactment by the Legislature. The Select Board is hereby authorized to approve amendments that shall be within the scope of the general public objectives of this petition; or take any other action related thereto. [Article 2 asks Town Meeting to authorize the Select Board to petition the Massachusetts General Court for a special act establishing a Home Rule Charter for Littleton. The proposed Charter would retain Littleton’s Open Town Meeting as the legislative body and the Select Board as the Town’s chief policymaking executive board, while creating a Town Manager position to serve as the Town’s chief administrative officer. The Town Manager would be appointed by and accountable to the Select Board, oversee day-to-day administration of Town affairs, supervise departments and department heads within the Charter’s scope, administer personnel matters, serve as chief procurement officer, and participate in the annual budget process, including submission of a proposed balanced budget and ten-year capital plan. The Charter preserves the statutory operation of the Fire Department and Police Department, exempts the School Department from Town Manager authority, and excludes facilities under the control of the School Committee, Board of Light Commissioners, Board of Water Commissioners, Board of Library Trustees, and Park and Recreation Commission from the Town Manager’s facilities jurisdiction. It also continues existing elected and appointed officials through transition provisions unless and until changed in accordance with the Charter.] Motion: Moved and seconded that the Town vote to approve a petition to the General Court for the enactment of a special act establishing a Town Charter for the Town of Littleton substantially in the form attached to this Warrant as Exhibit A, and to authorize the Select Board to submit said petition and to approve revisions and amendments requested by the General Court, Legislative Counsel, or other legislative officials, provided that such revisions do not materially alter the intent and purpose of the Charter approved by this vote, and further to take all actions necessary to carry this vote into effect. Recommendation: ARTICLE 3 Adoption of the Provisions of G.L. Chapter 40U Select Board [Majority vote required] To see if the Town will vote to adopt the provisions of .G.L. c. 40U and amend the Town's bylaws by inserting the following: § [INSERT NO.] Noncriminal disposition of violations. Adoption of the provisions of Chapter 40U of the General Laws; noncriminal disposition is hereby authorized for the violation of any rule, regulation, order, ordinance or bylaw regulating the housing, sanitary, or snow and ice removal requirement. § [INSERT NO.] Municipal fine procedures. A. Definitions. MUNICIPAL HEARING OFFICER — A person appointed by the Town Administrator to conduct hearings of alleged Code violations pursuant to this chapter. UNPAID CHARGE — An unpaid fine incurred as a result of a violation of a rule, regulation, order, ordinance or bylaw regulating the housing, sanitary or municipal snow and ice removal requirement. B. Effective date. This chapter shall take effect in Littleton upon its acceptance. C. Procedures for payment of municipal fines; power to revoke or rescind. By adopting Chapter 40U §§1-18, the Town of Littleton has adopted procedures for the payment of the municipal fines provided in this Chapter 40U and may revoke or rescind any such acceptance. D. Municipal Hearing Officer. The Officer shall hear appeals of violation notices issued within the municipality. The Municipal Hearing Officer may be the same person appointed as a Municipal Hearing Officer pursuant to Chapter 148A of the General Laws. E. Inclusive Adoption of the Provisions of M.G.L. c. 40U §§1-18. These provisions set forth in M.G.L. c. 40U, et seq., establish the processes for determinations and issuances of Violation Notices, delivery of Violations, appeals, notices, payments and enforcement. F. Schedule of fines for violation. The Town of Littleton has, within this bylaw, established a schedule of fines for violations subject to this chapter committed within the municipality; provided, however, that all such fines shall be uniform for the same offense committed in the same zone or district, if any. A first fine under this chapter shall be $300.00. Any additional fines issued shall not exceed the maximum allowable amount under the relevant sections of the sanitary code, excluding late fees. G. Unpaid M.G.L. c. 40U Violations to Become Real Estate Liens and Added to Property Tax Bill. If the fine remains unpaid at the conclusion of the appeal process and all required notices have been sent, additional penalties and interest may be attached, and such amount shall become an additional assessment on the property owner’s tax bill, and shall also be a lien upon such real estate as provided in M.G.L. c. 40 § 42B. This action, without more, will constitute a lien on the property. H. Revolving Fund. Funds received from M.G.L. c. 40U Violations shall be paid into a revolving fund and utilized for the purpose of administering the Town’s code enforcement program. Such revolving fund shall be subject to annual review and re-authorization pursuant to the Massachusetts General Laws. I. Local ordinances superseded. By accepting Chapter 40U of the General Laws, this chapter shall supersede any local ordinances or bylaws to the contrary including but not limited to §1-2, §14, §202-10, §38-6, and §38-21. Enforcing officers shall include all those authorized pursuant to the state sanitary code, building code, and fire code. and to take any other action related thereto. That local board is how the departments keep rates competitive, reliability high, and community investment intentional. • The five members of the Board are Dick Taylor (Chair), Melissa Hebert (Vice Chair), Joe Knox (Secretary), Ivan Pagacik, and Scott Larsen. Officers rotate by Board vote after each annual reorganization (most recently June 24, 2026). All five have served through the sewer build, Boxborough water extension, Devens contract, fiber and tree-wire programs, and the Volt Typhoon response. • The Board’s record since 2021 is one of decisive, documented votes: multi-year electric, water, and sewer budgets; Town Meeting articles; the $45 million Common sewer and certified betterments; the Boxborough IMA and easements; the Devens O&M bid; the formation of GML Utility Services; depreciation fund transfers; and more than thirty community grants paid from earned surplus, not the tax levy. • They have also done the quieter work of good government: timely posted minutes (the Town Clerk has called this Board among the best at getting minutes in), Open Meeting Law review when a complaint was filed, betterment hearings with Town Counsel, and a three-year GM evaluation that has locked in goals and compensation tied to department performance and securing the Department’s leadership team for the near future. • Commissioners show up where the work is. They tour the WRRF, attend NEPPA and APPA conferences, sit with FinCom and the Select Board, are present throughout department jobs, and take public comment without losing sight of equitable treatment across the community that LELWD serves. • That combination of fiduciary discipline, infrastructure courage, and community presence is why LELWD can take on generation-scale projects and still plant trees, fund helmets and STEM, and keep the lights on and water flowing. The successes that follow are staff-executed; they are Board-authorized. General Manager Leadership — NEPPA & APPA • The Board appointed Nick Lawler, P.E., General Manager in August 2018, succeeding Scott Edwards (26 years at LELWD, last four as GM). Lawler is just the 10th General Manager in the 114-year history of LELWD. He has been with LELWD since 2001, when he was hired as an Electrical Engineer. He holds a B.S. in electrical engineering from Villanova University, an M.B.A. from Bentley University, and a Massachusetts P.E. license. • Lawler served (2021–2024) as the longest-serving President of the Northeast Public Power Association (NEPPA), the regional association of community-owned utilities headquartered in Littleton. At the 2024 Annual Meeting (Omni Mount Washington), he passed the gavel to John Tzimorangas of Energy New England and served as NEPPA President Emeritus / Past President from 2024–2026. He has chaired the NEPPA Mutual Aid Committee since 2016. Page 1 LITTLETON ELECTRIC LIGHT AND WATER DEPARTMENTS | Select Board Joint Meeting • September 28, 2026 • In June 2024, at APPA’s National Conference in San Diego, Lawler was installed as Chair of the American Public Power Association (APPA) Board of Directors, the national voice of more than 2,000 public power utilities. He had served as ChairElect in 2023–2024. He handed the gavel to John Haarlow of Snohomish County PUD in June 2025 and served as Immediate Past Chair through June 2026. He has served on many national committees, most notably the APPA Executive Committee, Mutual Aid Committee, and as current Chair of the APPA National Cyber Committee. He was the first APPA Board Chairman from Massachusetts since 1998. NEPPA leadership called the chairmanship “a big deal for us to be represented at this level.” • That national platform amplified LELWD’s work: after Volt Typhoon, Lawler and staff briefed peers and federal partners and presented the topic at conferences throughout the country. At an APPA event in 2025, Gen. Paul Nakasone (former NSA Director) sought Lawler out to thank the Board for combatting a foreign adversary and for going public. • Lawler received the 2018 NEPPA Distinguished Service Award for contributions to Florida and St. Thomas after Hurricanes Irma and Maria, and the 2026 APPA Distinguished Service Award for seven years of service to APPA and the APPA Board of Directors. National Recognition & Reliability • LELWD received the APPA Sue Kelly Community Service Award at the 2025 National Conference in New Orleans (prior award in 1992), recognizing work beyond keeping the lights on: senior luncheon, Thanksgiving baskets, Toys for Tots, free shade trees, school technology grants, dual enrollment, and the Pagacik scholarship. • LELWD was awarded the APPA Safety Award of Excellence, Diamond level, two consecutive years (2024: 89,470 workerhours; 2025: 64,159 worker-hours) in the 60,000–109,999 hour class. An internal, cross-department safety committee drives the culture of safety at the department. • Nine consecutive years of APPA Excellence in Reliability (certificates in 2015 and every year from 2017 through 2025). In 2025 customers were out 8.2 minutes on average versus 169 minutes nationwide (2024: 30 minutes vs. 149). SAIDI 8.2 minutes; SAIFI 0.11. Hardening includes tree wire and squirrel guards. Commissioner Scott Larsen and AGM Dave Ketchen presented “Storm Hardening with Spacer Cable” at APPA’s 2026 Boston conference recapping lessons learned from the 2008 Ice Storm that impacted our region and department. • Smart Energy Provider designation renewed (among fewer than 100 of 2,000+ public power utilities). • 2026 E-ISAC Electricity Security Service Award (Michael J. Assante honor) and Dragos Community Impact Award (February 2026) for sharing Volt Typhoon lessons; 60 Minutes case-study coverage. Dave Ketchen earned a Commonwealth cybersecurity award and E-ISAC recognition for a substation security analysis. LELWD hosted an E-ISAC / NEPPA physicalsecurity workshop at a Littleton substation; LPD joined on response times. • Mutual aid: Navajo Nation (19 poles, 12,000 ft of wire to three homes); Hurricane Helene; Mississippi water-works (MWWA Pride Awards for Paul Denaro and Alan Woitowicz). In May 2026 AGM Dave Ketchen flew 7,834 miles to the Northern Mariana Islands after a typhoon left 52,000 Commonwealth Utilities Corporation customers dark, which is the farthest LELWD mutual-aid trip on record. In 12 days he helped restore about half of Saipan, completed a full Tinian damage assessment, designed temporary generation, and left CUC three close-out reports with FEMA, DOE, Guam Power Authority, and the Army Corps. Financial Stewardship • In 2025 LELD continued to offer among the lowest residential electric rates in Massachusetts on a 12-month comparison with other utilities. • On the official 2024 Massachusetts rates dashboard, a typical Littleton water bill is $36.55 a month, about $6 or %14 below the statewide median, with rates that still cover operations and depreciation and send a conservation signal at high use. Page 2 LITTLETON ELECTRIC LIGHT AND WATER DEPARTMENTS | Select Board Joint Meeting • September 28, 2026 • Consistently positive rate of return; strong cash position (electric operating cash near $9–11 million at mid-year 2026). Fund balances rose 5–8% in multiple reporting periods. • Energy-efficiency spending far above mandate: 2024 required $79,212 / spent $207,102; 2025 spending was 281% of the required amount. • Transfers into the Depreciation Fund ($1,000,000 in 2025; additional transfers completed and planned). • PFAS class-action settlement payments received: $1.458 million to date. A second federal lawsuit filed in June 2026 continues to pursue recovery of PFAS monitoring and treatment costs. • $1.1 million in federal funding confirmed for sewer expansion. • FY26–FY27 Water and Sewer enterprise budgets adopted on schedule; 2026 Electric Budget approved at $36,217,466. Water 5-year plan projects ~$5 million year-end cash while funding critical infrastructure upgrades. Electric System — Large Projects Completed or Underway • Foster Street rebuild completed (under budget on the water side by $53,000); Mass Ave bridge overhead removed; pole and tree-wire upgrades across Bulkley, Grimes, Mill, Harwood, Moore, Coughlin, Blood Road, Long Lake, and Fort Pond Hill. • Blood Road underground conversion advanced; additional underground reliability work at Nelson Lane, Beaver Brook Road, and Sara Indian Way. • Two Massachusetts Community Compact fiber grants (including a new $250,000 award through 2027) to expand the municipal fiber ring; original ring approaching capacity. • MassCEC grid-resilience grant of $285,522 plus federal DOE support to replace six reclosers (on order for 2027; close-out November 2027). • Won MassDevelopment’s competitive bid to operate and maintain the Devens electric system under an eight-year contract (~$1 million per year plus capital funding) serving ~850 meters on the 4,400-acre campus. • Parlee Garage rehabilitation nearing completion; new bucket trucks, squirt boom, chipper, and fork truck on order or delivered. • Non-carbon power supply reached 55–60% in 2026 reporting months; 3.9 MW of Maine wind and hydro added. EV charging program generating revenue; Common EV charger ribbon-cutting hosted. • Stony Brook Intermediate share authorized for sale, relieving LELWD from an ancient fossil fuel facility. Water — Treatment Plants, Mains, Wells & Boxborough • LWD maintains three well sites, three storage tanks, two treatment plants, and more than 100 miles of water main. The 2025 Consumer Confidence Report documented major completed work and zero sanitary-survey violations in the prior cycle. • Whitcomb Avenue Water Treatment Plant: 1.8 million gallons per day. Biological filtration removes iron and manganese (the main cause of discoloration after main breaks) and granular activated carbon removes PFAS. The plant treats Whitcomb wells (about 45% of town supply) plus Spectacle Pond via a new 3.5-mile raw-water transmission main. Finished water at Whitcomb has no detectable PFAS. • Boxborough Water Main Extension: about 4.5 miles of finished main from Nancy’s Way / Whitcomb Avenue through Littleton County Road into Beaver Brook, Swanson, and Codman Hill Roads. Serves about 1,100 Boxborough residents whose small public wells tested above Massachusetts standards for PFAS and road salt. Intermunicipal agreement is for 65,000 gallons per day. Project financed with a zero-interest state SRF loan because it addresses PFAS; MassDOT saltremediation funds and new Boxborough customers cover the share that benefits them. Littleton Town Meeting approved Page 3 LITTLETON ELECTRIC LIGHT AND WATER DEPARTMENTS | Select Board Joint Meeting • September 28, 2026 the project May 1, 2023. Main installation is complete; paving finished; LELWD is readying customer connections ahead of the new well coming online at no capital cost to Littleton ratepayers for the Boxborough portion. • Trumbull Well (Taylor Street): newest supply well. Late-2025 drill-and-test work initially produced about 250,000 gallons per day; about 27% of that yield is allocated to the new Boxborough customers. Building foundation and well construction continue; Route 2 raw/finished main work is soon to be completed. • Distribution replacements in 2025: more than 5,800 feet of old main. Foster Street, over 3,800 feet from Taylor Street to Balsam Lane, asbestos-cement replaced with cement-lined ductile iron, completed ~$53,000 under budget. Taylor Street, about 2,000 feet of 110- to 113-year-old 6-inch cast iron (1912) replaced with 8-inch ductile iron between Whitcomb Avenue and Porter Road, now live. Sheridan Lane: LWD crews installed 550 feet of DI main, one hydrant, and seven services ahead of Highway paving. White Street connector installed by Water Foreman Greg Leger and crew. • Cedar Hill tank closed out with a neighborhood block party which consisted of pizza, a tour, hats, and coloring books held September 14, 2024 one year … AGENDA ACTION REQUEST September 28, 2026 Select Board Discussions Establishment of a Data Center Working Group Requested by: Kyle Bubp Action Sought: Discussion/Approval Proposed Motion(s) MOVE that the Select Board vote to establish Data … with the insurer, though the final rate will not be known until January or February. - Solar grant funds of approximately $94,021 received in July have been applied to reduce the Senior Center debt payment. - Out-year projections assume
