The premises are to be used for affordable housing purposes in perpetuity. Grantee shall sell the premises with the dwelling unit(s) thereon to an Eligible Purchaser (defined below) by the date set forth in the LDA at a price and on such terms as set forth in the LDA and/or the Regulatory Agreement to be entered into by and among the Town, Grantee, and the Executive Office of Housing and Livable Communities (“EOHLC”) under the Local Initiative Program (either or both, the “Regulatory Agreement”). Grantee shall comply with the Regulatory Agreement and all other criteria, procedures, guidelines and/or policies necessary to include the dwelling unit(s) in the Subsidized Housing Inventory (“SHI”) maintained by EOHLC. An “Eligible Purchaser” shall have an income no greater than 60% of the median income for the area in which the premises are located, satisfy such asset qualifications and other criteria required under the Local Initiative Program (“LIP”), and be selected in accordance with affirmative fair housing Page 1 of 3 marketing and lottery plan or procedures approved by EOHLC so as to include the premises in the SHI. The unit(s) shall be conveyed to an Eligible Purchaser subject to the “Universal Deed Rider”, which deed rider shall survive foreclosure, be enforceable by the Town in perpetuity, meet the requirements of G.L. c. 184, §§31 and 32, and be in form and substance acceptable to the Town and EOHLC under the LIP for inclusion of the premises in the SHI (the “Deed Rider”). The Town shall provide sixty (60) days’ written notice to Grantee of its intent to exercise its Right of Entry if Grantee fails to comply with the conditions set forth in the LDA. If, at the end of such notice period, Grantee has not cured the applicable defect in the Town’s reasonable discretion, the Town may record the Reversionary Deed and take title to the premises and ownership of all improvements thereon without claim or lien of the Grantee and the improvements shall vest in the Town without any necessity for suit. The Town shall reimburse Grantee for improvements made by Grantee to the premises in compliance with the LDA from the proceeds of the sale of the unit(s) to an Eligible Purchaser(s) or from any other sale of the premises, less amounts required to release the premises of any and all liens, subject to Town Meeting appropriation of funds for such purpose. Box 1327 Oak Bluffs, MA 02557 508-693-3554 Ext. 154 Mark Crossland Erik Albert Chris Chambers Bill Davies Scott Slarsky Edwina Hawes, Associate Member PLANNING BOARD MEETING - AGENDA Thursday, September 24, 2026 – 5:00 PM In accordance with Governor Healey’s emergency modification of the Open Meeting Law, this meeting will be held virtually. Join Zoom Meeting https://oakbluffs.zoom.us/j/84788876176?pwd=4pPHJTi0pDKCDTUf2ebv7SiXnlCfXf.1 Meeting ID: 847 8887 6176 Passcode: 306964 One tap mobile +13092053325,,84788876176# US +13126266799,,84788876176# US (Chicago) ___ Approval of Minutes - September 10, 2026 (Attendees: Crossland, Chambers, Slarsky, Albert) Proposed Amendments to Town of Oak Bluffs Zoning By-laws Pursuant to the provisions of MGL ch. 40A §5, the Oak Bluffs Planning Board will open a virtual public hearing at 5:00 p.m. on Thursday, September 24, 2026, for the purpose of accepting public comments on the following proposed additions and amendments to the Town of Oak Bluffs Zoning By-laws: Item 1: To see if the Town will vote to amend Section 11 of the Zoning By-laws governing Definitions concerning the word “structure”. Item 2: To see if the Town will vote to amend Section 11 of the Zoning By-laws governing Definitions by adding the word “Equipment”. Item 3: To see if the Town will vote to amend Section 11 of the Zoning By-laws governing Definitions by adding the word “Footprint”. Item 4: To see if the Town will vote to amend Section 11 of the Zoning By-laws governing Definitions concerning the term “Building Height”. Item 5: To see if the Town will vote to amend Section 5.0 GENERAL REGULATIONS of the Zoning By-laws governing “noise from mechanical equipment in residential zones”. Item 6: To see if the Town will vote to amend Section 3.2.3.6 of the Zoning By-laws governing overnight commercial vehicle parking regulations to include regulations for high-density, multi-unit housing within the Oak Bluffs Zoning Bylaws. Item 7: To see if the Town will vote to amend the Zoning By-laws by: a.) adding Section 3.2.3.5 governing boat storage, repair, maintenance and/or construction; b.) adopting a revised definition of “boat yard or boat service”; and c.) changing the table of uses for boats and boat service. Item 8: To see if the Town will vote to amend Appendix A of the Zoning By-Laws to provide for by-right short term rental. Relevant documents are available online. See: https://www.oakbluffsma.gov/594/Proposed-ZoningBy-Law-Changes---STM-202 . Public Hearings, Public Meetings & Appointments - PUBLIC WELCOME A. 6:05 PM - Appointment - Al Patenaude, Planning Board Chairman - Request To Discuss Proposed Zoning Articles For Fall Town Meeting B. 6:15 PM - Public Hearing Re: The Commission Will Consider A Notice Of Intent Filed By Fuss & O’Neill For Applicant Andrew MacLean (Town Administrator) With The Town Of Pepperell To Remediate Polyfluoroalkyl Substances (PFAS) At 41A Lowell Road, Parcel 31-18-0, Owned By Mass Ave Rentals, LLC, Which Was Originally Released From The Abutting Town-Owned Properties At 45 Lowell Road, Parcel 31-17-0, And 47 Lowell Road, Parcel 31-16-0. Excavated PFAS-Impacted Soils Will Be Transported To A Designated Temporary Stockpile Area On The Abutting Town Of Pepperell Parcels At 45 Lowell Road, Parcel 31-17-0, And 47 Lowell Road, Parcel 31-16-0. The Project May Have Potential Impacts To The Buffer Zone Of BVW. C. 6:25 PM - Continuation Of Public Hearing Re: Burkes Pond Dam Parcel 31-18-0, Owned By Mass Ave Rentals, LLC, Which Was Originally Released From The Abutting Town-Owned Properties At 45 Lowell Road, Parcel 31-17-0, And 47 Lowell Road, Parcel 31-16-0. Excavated PFAS-Impacted Soils Will Be Transported To A Designated Temporary Stockpile Area On The Abutting Town Of Pepperell Parcels At 45 Lowell Road, Parcel 31-17-0, And 47 Lowell Road, Parcel 31-16-0. The Project May Have Potential Impacts To The Buffer Zone Of BVW. C. 6:25 PM - Continuation Of Public Hearing Re: Burkes Pond Dam The Commission will consider a Notice of Intent filed by the Applicant, the Town of Pepperell Department of Public Works, and the Owner Brian McPhail regarding the recently completed Burke's Pond Emergency Dam Removal Project at 2 Blood Street in Pepperell. Project design was underway to remove the dam for the purposes of ecological restoration. However, accelerated rates of deterioration warranted the emergency action taken to remove it, for which an Emergency Certificate was issued by the Pepperell Conservation Commission on December 16, 2025. Burke's Pond Dam was located on Sucker Brook, approximately 2 miles upstream of the confluence of Sucker Brook with the federally designated Wild and Scenic Nissitissit River. Following the 2021 removal of the Keyes-Parker Conservation Area Dam, the Burke's Pond Dam was the only remaining dam along Sucker Brook. Approximately 1.1 miles of the stream upstream of the dam were disconnected from the downstream reaches, limiting habitat access for target species such as eastern brook trout. The majority of the Project area is within Riverfront area (7,050 sf), including 2,900 of overlapping Bordering Land Subject to Flooding. The Project has restored approximately 950 sq ft of Land Under Waterbodies and Waterways (LUWW). Additionally, approximately 60 lf of Bank were restored following removal of the obsolete structure. A communication from Mayor Marchetti reappointing James Conant, Franz Forster and Stephanie Storie to the Conservation Commission. Councilor Cunningham made a motion to approve carried by a unanimous vote of the ten members present. COMMUNICATIONS FROM HIS HONOR THE MAYOR A communication from Mayor Marchetti on an Order to accept a grant of funds in the amount of $79,978.00 from the Feigenbaum Foundation, Inc, Williams Elementary School PTO, Greylock Federal Credit Union, Pittsfield Rotary Foundation, and Lee Bank. Councilor Cunningham made a motion to approve carried by a unanimous vote of the ten members present. A communication from Mayor Marchetti on an Order to accept a grant of funds in the amount of $20,100.00 from the Massachusetts Department of Transportation, Aeronautics Division. Councilor Cunningham made a motion to approve carried by a unanimous vote of the ten members present. A communication from Mayor Marchetti on an Order to accept a grant of funds in the amount of $243,281.00 from the United States Department of Transportation. Councilor Cunningham made a motion to approve carried by a unanimous vote of the ten members present. A communication from Mayor Marchetti on an Order amending Order No. 83 of the series of 2024 to increase the amount to be borrowed for the permitting of Taxiway A at the Pittsfield Municipal Airport not to exceed $400,100.00. Councilor Cunningham made a motion to approve carried by a unanimous vote of the ten members present. A communication from Mayor Marchetti on an Order amending Order No. 69 of the series of 2026 raising and appropriating $232,777,720.00 for the Fiscal year 2027 Municipal Budget, including an additional $458,660.00 to be appropriated to the School Departments Fiscal Year 2027 Budget. Councilor Cunningham made a motion to suspend Rule 27 carried by a unanimous vote of the ten members present. Councilor Cunningham made a motion to approve. Councilor Moody asked the mayor what these funds will be used for and can the council get a report from the school committee on what the funds will be used for. The mayor stated the school committee can provide that information. The motion to approve carried by a unanimous vote of the ten members present. A communication from Mayor Marchetti on an Order authorizing to borrow a sum not exceeding $180,000.00 under Sewer Enterprise Fund for the purchase of sludge treatment equipment. Councilor Cunningham made a motion to approve. Councilor Moody asked the Commissioner is this was included in his budget. Mr. Morales said this is part of the Capital Improvement plan that the council approves but the authorization to borrow comes afterwards. The motion to approve carried by a unanimous vote of the ten members present. A communication from Mayor Marchetti on an Order authorizing to borrow a sum not exceeding $6,900,000.00 for general fund capital expenditures. Councilor Cunningham made a motion to suspend Rule 27 carried by a unanimous vote of the ten members present. Councilor Cunningham made a motion to approve. Councilor Amuso asked the Director Kerwood about the 4 million in roof repairs. Mr. Kerwood stated the council previously approved 3 million for roofs which is slated for Herberg. Part of this 4 million will cover Herberg and for the next school that is slated. Councilor Kavey asked the director what our free cash is at. Director Kerwood stated free cash closed at 5. 7 and will not be available until certified by the state. Councilor Kavey asked what we would do if we had to borrow in an emergency. Mr. Kerwood said he would most likely come forward with an appropriation from the stabilization account which has 6 million in it. Councilor Kavey asked Chief Maddalena what $200,000.00 was going to be used for. The Chief stated that they are transitioning their radios because they have lifed out. Similarly to updating to a newer cell phone so they do not have issues with dead spots throughout the city. The mayor stated that the cost of this borrowing would not impact the fiscal year 27 budget. Councilor Warren said there is no sense in sending this to a committee and it makes sense to approve tonight to get the road work started. Councilor White said it is time that the project in the fire department moved forward and thanked the mayor. The motion to approve carried by a unanimous vote of the eight members present with Councilor Lampiasi out of the room. A communication from Mayor Marchetti on an Order transferring and appropriating $137,244.64 from Unclassified to various departments to fund retroactive compensation by the settled collective bargaining agreement with the Teamsters Union. Councilor Cunningham made a motion to approve. Councilor Kavey asked what the fund will cover. The mayor stated this is the retro amount needed to complete the fiscal year 2026 contracts. When free cash is certified they will be back with an appropriation to cover the salaries for fiscal year 2027 for Teamsters, Library, and the Supervisor and Professional unions. The motion to approve carried by a unanimous vote of the ten members present. A communication from Mayor Marchetti on an Order authorizing the renewal of the ground lease between Leonard F. Gigliotti and the City of Pittsfield. Councilor Cunningham made a motion to approve. Councilor Warren asked the solicitor what businesses are on the property. The Solicitor did not have this information. Director Kerwood stated that Westwood is an industrial park that happens to be on the airport property and managed by the Community Development Office. It does not have anything to do with the airport operations. Councilor Kavey stated there are several businesses in the park, Cresent Creamery, two electrical companies and a manufacturer. Councilor Warren asked the solicitor about the lease and if there were any concessions for the new 40-year lease. The solicitor said he was unsure what happened with the Airport Commission and if concessions were considered. Councilor Warren asked Airport Manager Akor why this was not terminated and asked for new conditions. Ms. Akor stated that the Airport Commission approved the lease as it was written. The motion to approve carried by a unanimous vote of the ten members present. A communication from Mayor Marchetti on an Ordinance amending City Code, Chapter 2. Councilor Cunningham made a motion to suspend Rule 34. Councilor White stated he is in opposition of waving rule 34 as there is a longer conversation that we need to have. Councilor Lampiasi agreed with Councilor White and stated that HR and the department head here. She is not comfortable voting on such major changes without those them here. Councilor Wrinn asked why they are not here. The mayor stated that he spoke with both of the departments and they had not been contacted by any city councilor so he instructed them to stay home and the conversation could be had at Ordinances and Rules as the normal practice. Councilor Cunningham stated that the council waved this rule at the last meeting for the building commissioner. Councilor Cunninham questioned why the department heads were not there. The mayor said this is a bigger issue than let's surprise attack and do something at a meeting. A longer explanation is necessary as some may want to merge this into HR and some who may want to eliminate it altogether. When he looks at the problems with the city, poverty is the number on piece. Where someone's social economic status is what we do for DEi. This is a cycle and we need to put something in place to stop this. Councilor Cunningham continued to ask why the department heads were not present. The mayor's intent isn't to delete a department and ask the council permission to create a new one. 1t is to transition one into another as we did with Personnel and Human Resources. ln normal procedures this would have been sent to O & R. No one reached out to his office and asked to have the full-blown conversation tonight rather than follow normal procedures. He would have obliged and agreed to have the department heads there, but no one reached out. Councilor Amuso asked the president if an ordinance comes forward in the future if it could be directly referred to O&R. President Persip stated that has not been the procedure in the past, but he will if that is what the council wants him to do. Councilor Amuso said we need to be respectful here, we may have differences of opinions, but we don't need to raise our voices and being disrespectful. There are significant changes that need to be made and this needs to go to O&R. Councilor Warren does not think Councilor Cunningham was trying to be helpful. The reason we rushed the building inspector ordinance change was because we needed a building commissioner. Councilor White stated that the council is required to give seven days' notice to appear before the council. Councilor Warren stated this is in the charter. The motion to Wave Rule 34 failed by a unanimous vote of the ten members present. Councilor Cunningham made a motion to refer to the Ordinances and Rules Committee carried by a unanimous vote of the ten members present. COMMUNICATIONS AND REPORTS FROM CITY OFFICES AND BOARDS A communication from Commissioner Morales on a petition from Councilor Lampiasi regarding street sweeping. Councilor Lampiasi made a motion to accept the communication from Commissioner Morales. She asked the commissioner about the new tool he is working on and thanked the him for the report. Mr. Morales stated that the map is currently on the website for public viewing, by navigating through the stormwater section under DPW and it just needs some minor tweaks. Councilor Kavey asked when the map will be fixed on the website so they can use it. He hopes it will be completed by next week. The motion to accept carried by a unanimous vote of the ten members present. REPORTS FROM COMMITTEES Reports from the Audit Services Evaluation Committee A report from the Audit Services Evaluation Committee on a petition from Councilor Warren on procedures to obtain an independent audit, recommending to approve Scanlon & Associates proposal, 4/2. Councilor Cunningham made a motion to accept the report carried by a unanimous vote of the ten members present. Councilor Cunningham made a motion to approve Scanlon & Associates. Councilor Warren stated this was not an easy thing to accomplish. They did not get as much engagement as they hoped. They only had two companies who bid, and they checked references which were both very qualified. The next thing the committee did was to compare pricing. Scanlon's quote was $360,000 for the three years and CLA quoted $492,000 for the three years. Councilor Cunningham said he is not opposed to choosing Scanlon, but we need some due diligence considering if it is worth getting different eyes while still maintaining the price. He suggested having a junior partner do the audit this year or another way to shake it up a bit. He said they could also look at negotiating price if they left it open in their proposal for CLA. Councilor Cunningham will support CLA. The motion carried by an 8/2 vote with Councilors Wrinn and Cunningham in opposition. MATTERS TENTATIVELY REFERRED BY THE PRESIDENT UNDER RULE 27 These items do not require a vote for referral but may be raised for a vote by any Councilor. Referred to the Commissioner of Public Works A petition from Councilor Lampiasi requesting an update on the Berkshire Gas compliance project affecting Roselyn Drive, Loumar Drive, Leroi Drive, Trova Terrace and portions of Jason Street Referred to Ordinance and Rules Committee A proposal from the Community Development Board to reclassify a parcel of land located at 1 Federico Drive, Assessor Map 11, Block 7, Lot 101 At 6:57 p.m., Councilor Cunningham moved to adjourn, carried by a unanimous vote of the ten members present. It’s that time of year again, Suicide Prevention Month is September with International Suicide Prevention Day on Sunday, September 10th. We are reaching out to our towns within Plymouth County to see if each Town will proclaim, Thursday, September 10th and the entire Month of September as Suicide Prevention Month in their respected Town. We would appreciate your help in getting this request to the appropriate department if possible. If you could return the enclosed proclamation to Jennie Babcock at plymouthcountypreventssuicide@gmail.com that would great! Thank you in advance. Terri Kourtz, tkourtz@ocesma.org in care of Jennie M Babcock, Co-Chair Plymouth County Suicide Prevention Coalition 508-254-9320 Reaching Out. Saving Lives. Touching Hearts Proclamation Whereas, suicide is the 10th leading cause of all deaths in the U.S. and the second leading cause of death among individuals between the ages of 15 to 24; and Whereas, in the U.S., one person dies by suicide every 14 minutes; and Whereas, it is estimated that five million people in the U.S. are survivors of suicide loss; and Whereas, the overall suicide rate in our country in 2024 estimates almost 49,000 people dying by suicide; and Whereas, suicide is a public health concern and affects many in our community; and Whereas, The American Foundation for Suicide Prevention and The Plymouth County Suicide Prevention Coalition, promote suicide prevention and awareness in our communities, both urge that we as a community align with the National Strategy for Suicide Prevention at a local level including community-based efforts that support: 1. Effective, broad-based, collaborative, and sustainable suicide prevention partnerships. 2. Invest in upstream comprehensive community-based suicide prevention. 3. Reducing access to lethal means among people at risk of suicide. 4. Integrating suicide prevention into the culture of the workplace and into other community settings. 5. Build and sustain suicide prevention infrastructure at the local, town, and state level. Whereas, a great many suicides are preventable; Therefore, we, the Select Board of the Town of Plymouth, do hereby recognize September as suicide prevention month and designate September 10th, 2026, as Suicide Prevention Day in the town of Plymouth. Chair Iaquinto called the meeting to order at 6:00 p.m. and read the following statements, Per M.G.L. Chapter 30A, Section 20, any person may make a video or audio recording of an open session of a meeting of the Select Board after notifying the chair, subject to reasonable requirements of the chair so as not to interfere with the conduct of the meeting. Members of the public who wish to PARTICIPATE in the meeting may do so in the following manner: In-Person: Cold Spring Elementary School, Gymnasium | 25 Alden St, Plymouth, MA 02360 Remote: Click the following Zoom link to participate in the meeting remotely: https://pactv.zoom.us/j/91695140644?pwd=UGhFZVJmaHVwQmIxa0pVYjRDMlozZz09 • Webinar ID: 916-9514-0644 • Passcode: 121500 • Chair Iaquinto confirmed the meeting's recording status and led the Pledge of Allegiance. 6:05 p.m. Administrative Notes The Board reviewed three administrative notes. Selectman Canty initially moved to approve notes #1-3, but Selectman Keohan and Vice Chair Quintal requested to separate note #1 for discussion. Selectman Canty amended his motion to approve only notes #2-3. On a motion by Selectman Canty, seconded by Selectman Golden, the Board voted to approve administrative notes 2 and 3. 2. The Board will vote to approve and execute the State Primary Election Warrant for the election to be held on September 1, 2026. Page 1 of 3 3. The Board will vote to decline to exercise its right of first refusal to purchase a portion of property totaling 31.75 acres more or less, recorded with the Plymouth County Registry of Deeds in Book 2080, Page 84; Book 15867, Page 20; and Book 33354, Page 194, as recommended by the Land Use & Acquisition Committee (LUAC). Roll Call Vote 5/0: Iaquinto-Yes, Quintal-Yes, Canty-Yes, Golden-Yes, Keohan-Yes Regarding administrative note #1, which involved amendments to the personnel code including reclassifying the Community Preservation Committee coordinator and moving seasonal treasurer/collector workers to non-union status, Selectman Keohan requested deferring the vote until staff could present the ongoing compensation study. Vice Chair Quintal asked about several obsolete positions listed in the packet, such as civilian traffic control officer and police matron. Town Manager Derek Brindisi explained that those positions are no longer active and agreed to have Human Resources strike them from the code. The Board agreed to defer voting on note #1, noting that any pay increases could be made retroactive. Vice Chair Quintal requested a moment of silence for retired Department of Public Works custodian Tom McNal, who passed away on July 19 after a brief illness. Chair Iaquinto introduced Kenzy Philabaum as the new Executive Assistant and Taylor O'Neil as the new Communications Coordinator, welcoming them to the town and noting their previous municipal experience. 6:25 p.m. Town Manager’s Report Mr. Brindisi provided updates on several North Plymouth issues raised by residents and precinct chairs. He noted that infrastructure improvements for the PY Project, including the Prince Street turnaround, looped water main, emergency beacon at Hedge and Court Streets, and rail trail connection, are on hold pending a Zoning Board of Appeals appeal. The Cherry Street water main replacement contract is executed and will take a year, pausing for winter, while Eversource will also replace a gas main. Intersection improvements adding turning lanes at Cherry, Court, and Prince Streets are expected to begin next fall using $2.5 million in appropriated funds. Mr. Brindisi reported that the Massachusetts School Building Authority accepted Hedge Elementary into the feasibility stage to consider consolidation with Cold Spring. He also provided updates on seeking state funding for a Phase 2 hazardous materials site assessment at the North Plymouth Fire Station, recent pedestrian safety improvements on Court Street, the purchase of an additional sidewalk tractor for winter clearing, and a planned consultant to design Veterans Field Park playground improvements with public input. Regarding Hamilton Street truck traffic, police logged twenty-five incidents, none related to large trucks, and residents were urged to report issues to the police. Selectman Keohan requested that the Veterans Park scope of work include improvements to the 366 Court Street entrance. 6:36 p.m. Public Comment The Board opened the floor for a Town Hall question and answer session. Residents raised various concerns, primarily focusing on infrastructure, traffic, and the PY development project. Mr. Brindisi and Board members responded to questions regarding project delays, water main replacements, pedestrian safety, and the town's strategy regarding Chapter 40B developments. Mr. Canty noted the Board's proactive steps to achieve safe harbor to prevent hostile 40B developments, and Mr. Golden expressed that there is near universal agreement across the Commonwealth that 40B needs to change. - Carol Jankowski of Prince Street questioned the long delay in funding and executing the Prince, Court, and Cherry intersection improvements. She requested flashing lights for crosswalks on Court Street, noted the difficulty of engaging English-as-a-second-language families in the Hedge School study process, and asked about replacing the Prince Street water main. Page 2 of 3 - - - - Alex Cook of Prince Street questioned the safety of the intersection during PY construction if improvements are delayed and noted that PY appeared to have pulled the bike path connection from their final ZBA decision to avoid triggering a Massachusetts Environmental Policy Act review over tree removal. Matt Tavares questioned the specific reasons for the six-year delay on the intersection project, noting Eversource and PY were not factors at that time. Everett Malaguti asked about contingency plans for water main breaks during the Cherry Street construction. He also raised sightline issues at the Hamilton and Standish intersection and the Savory Lane and Court Street exit and asked about selling the town's easement at 308 Court Street to fund Veterans Field improvements. Christine Pratt requested an update on speed limit signs for Court Street that were requested a year ago to deter late-night speeding. Meg Sheehan raised concerns about stormwater runoff pollution flowing from Route 3A down Hedge Road directly into Cape Cod Bay due to clogged storm drains, urging the Conservation Commission to review the issue during PY's Notice of Intent hearing. Mike Angerame of Atlantic Avenue urged the town to work with state legislators to change 40B laws and build a coalition with other towns. He also supported implementing speed zones on Route 3A. 7:01 p.m. Select Board Discussion – New Business / Letters / Old Business New Business Under new business, Vice Chair Quintal suggested drafting a letter to neighboring towns to build a coalition to pressure state legislators on 40B reform. Selectman Keohan agreed to work with him on an internal working group for the effort. Selectman Keohan also suggested revisiting the naming of McAuliffe Way in the industrial park to return it to "Christa McAuliffe Way," and mentioned a letter received from a Plymouth South High School student regarding Flock cameras in the Home Depot parking lot. Mike D'Angerami of Atlantic Avenue provided an additional public comment supporting Mr. Quintal's idea of building a coalition across towns to address 40B. 7:25 p.m. Adjournment On a motion by Selectman Golden, seconded by Selectman Canty, the Board voted to adjourn at 7:25 p.m. Roll Call 5/0: Iaquinto-Yes, Quintal-Yes, Canty-Yes, Golden-Yes, Keohan-Yes Recorded by: Kenzy Philabaum, Executive Assistant Page 3 of 3 PLYMOUTH SELECT BOARD Wednesday, July 22, 2026 | 5:30 p.m. MEETING MINUTES 5:30 p.m. Call to Order Present: Deb Iaquinto (Chair) — Present Richard Quintal Jr. (Vice Chair) — Absent Bill Keohan (Member) — Present David Golden Jr. (Member) — Present Kevin Canty (Member) — Present Derek Brindisi, Town Manager Lauren Lind, Assistant Town Manager 5:30 p.m. Call to Order The meeting was held as a Select Board Economic Development Workshop at Plymouth Town Hall in the Ropewalk room. Chair Iaquinto called the meeting to order at 5:30 p.m. and read the following statements, Per M.G.L. Chapter 30A, Section 20, any person may make a video or audio recording of an open session of a meeting of the Select Board after notifying the chair, subject to reasonable requirements of the chair so as not to interfere with the conduct of the meeting. Members of the public who wish to PARTICIPATE in the meeting may do so in the following manner: In-Person: Cold Spring Elementary School, Gymnasium | 25 Alden St, Plymouth, MA 02360 Remote: Click the following Zoom link to participate in the meeting remotely: https://pactv.zoom.us/j/91695140644?pwd=UGhFZVJmaHVwQmIxa0pVYjRDMlozZz09 • Webinar ID: 916-9514-0644 • Passcode: 121500 • Chair Iaquinto confirmed the meeting's recording status and led the Pledge of Allegiance. 5:30 p.m. Select Board Economic Development Workshop Assistant Town Manager Lauren Lind led the second part of the economic development workshop, noting she planned to conclude the meeting by 7:00 p.m. due to a subsequent Planning Board meeting. She reviewed the takeaways from the SWOT (Strengths, Weaknesses, Opportunities, and Threats) analysis conducted during the June 24 workshop. Strengths identified included Plymouth's strong regional identity and natural resources, while weaknesses included infrastructure capacity and housing affordability. Opportunities focused on modernizing zoning and building on the blue economy, and threats included rising housing costs and macroeconomic uncertainty. Chair Iaquinto confirmed with Selectman Golden, who had missed the first session, that the summary resonated with him. Page 1 of 2 Ms. Lind explained that the comprehensive plan's goal for the economy is to support the current business base and increase living wage jobs while advancing long-term fiscal sustainability. Chair Iaquinto asked if anything discussed conflicted with the comprehensive plan; Ms. Lind said no, but noted some new sectors, like data centers and AI, were not fully discussed in the plan. Selectman Canty expressed caution about large data centers, stating that Plymouth has a history of relying on single large industries which is not ideal for a diverse economic base. He supported local data centers for business operations but opposed mid-rise dedicated server farms, and Chair Iaquinto agreed that diversification is key. Ms. Lind outlined seven priority initiatives, noting many are multi-year efforts, beginning with zoning updates to preserve commercial and industrial land. Town Manager Derek Brindisi and Selectman Canty discussed perfecting mixed-use zoning to preserve commercial areas while allowing residential components where appropriate. Chair Iaquinto strongly supported the business recruitment, retention, and marketing strategy, suggesting collaboration with the Plymouth Foundation. Selectman Canty suggested elevating housing and infrastructure priorities over zoning, arguing that infrastructure is necessary for businesses to operate. Selectman Golden emphasized the need to protect industrial lands from hostile residential approaches and stressed that the town must actively welcome and work with businesses to expand the commercial tax base. Ms. Lind listed potential external partners for economic development, prompting suggestions from the board. Selectman Canty suggested adding specific higher education institutions and exploring community college partnerships for vocational programs, Mr. Brindisi suggested adding Manomet Conservation Sciences, and Chair Iaquinto suggested including the state delegation, the airport, and the Old Colony Planning Council. The board also discussed the MBTA station; Selectman Canty suggested advocating for its reopening, but Ms. Lind and Mr. Golden noted that reopening the station would change Plymouth's MBTA Communities law classification, requiring double the zoned units within a half-mile radius and potentially leading to high-density development over existing neighborhoods. Mr. Brindisi noted parking would be a major challenge if the station reopened. For internal resources, Selectman Keohan suggested including organizational charts to clarify divisions within town departments. Ms. Lind offered to attend the upcoming Select Board goal-setting workshop. The Board agreed to ratify the strategy document as an administrative note at their next Tuesday meeting before the goal-setting workshop, and planned to schedule a future joint meeting with the Planning Board and the Plymouth Foundation to align priorities and present the strategy to the community. Chair Iaquinto then asked for a motion to adjourn. 6:45 p.m. Adjournment On a motion by Selectman Golden, seconded by Selectman Canty, the Board voted to adjourn at 6:45 p.m. Roll Call 5/0: Iaquinto-Yes, Quintal-Yes, Canty-Yes, Golden-Yes, Keohan-Yes Recorded by: Kenzy Philabaum, Executive Assistant Page 2 of 2 PLYMOUTH SELECT BOARD Wednesday, July 28, 2026 | 6:00 p.m. MEETING MINUTES 6:00 PM Call to Order Present: Deb Iaquinto (Chair) — Present Bill Keohan (Member) — Present David Golden Jr. (Member) — Present Kevin Canty (Member) — Present Richard Quintal Jr. (Vice Chair) —Present Derek Brindisi (Town Manager) 6:00 p.m. Open Session The meeting was held in the 1820 courtroom due to technical difficulties. RECITALS WHEREAS, the TOWN is the owner of record of a certain parcel of land situated on 83 Court Street, specifically Memorial Hall, in Plymouth, Massachusetts, shown on Assessor’s Map 17, as Parcel No.017000-100-000. For Grantor’s title, see deed recorded with the Plymouth County Registry of Deeds in Book 1320, Page 173. WHEREAS, THE PHIL shall be recognized as the Orchestra in Residence for the term of this Memorandum of Agreement and shall be part of the ongoing conversations and planning as it relates to the future of Memorial Hall and THE PHIL shall partner with the TOWN in supporting and promoting community support for the refurbishment of Memorial Hall as a community asset through its ongoing marketing, programming, outreach and community engagement efforts. WHEREAS, both the TOWN and THE PHIL desire to strengthen the partnership between the two parties and THE PHIL shall promote its partnership with the TOWN through marketing materials, advertisements and publications; NOW, THEREFORE, in consideration of the mutual promises set forth herein and of other good and valuable considerations, the receipt and sufficiency of which are hereby acknowledged, the parties agree to as follows: I. USE, PURPOSE, FEES, CONDITIONS Effective on the date of execution hereof by the TOWN, the TOWN hereby grants to THE PHIL, its successors and assigns, and its contractors, agents, representatives, employees, invitees, permittees and licensees, the use of Memorial Hall, specifically the Main Hall, the Green Room and the Blue Room, according to the terms and conditions set forth herein. THE PHIL shall be recognized as the Orchestra in Residence for the term of this MEMORANDUM OF AGREEMENT. THE PHIL shall have a 12-month right of first refusal to prioritize concert dates and THE PHIL shall inform the TOWN of the dates that THE PHIL wishes to exercise their Right of First Refusal twelve months in advance of their annual schedule. THE PHIL shall have Memorial Hall the second weekend of every December for the Holiday Pops concert. THE PHIL shall be limited to 100 complimentary tickets per event. THE PHIL agrees to pay fees and costs associated with their use of Memorial Hall for their events as follows: THE PHIL shall be granted a 30% reduction from the standard fees, resulting in a fee of $2,450.00 per day and $1,225.00 for one half day for loading. THE PHIL shall be responsible for all Department of Public Works (“DPW”) fees for each event. THE PHIL shall be responsible for all security fees for each event. THE PHIL agrees to charge and collect a fee of $1/ticket, exclusive of complimentary tickets, and to provide those monies and an accounting of that fee to the TOWN at the end of each event. Should this fee increase as part of the Memorial Hall management, THE PHIL agrees to abide by any and all increases. THE PHIL agrees that 20% of the gross Concession and Liquor sales are due at the end of the event without exception. THE PHIL acknowledges that Memorial Hall Policies must be abided by. Those policies are attached hereto as Exhibit A and will be updated on an annual basis. II. TERM The initial term of this MEMORANDUM OF AGREEMENT shall be three years (the “Term”) and shall terminate three years after the execution date of the agreement unless otherwise terminated as provided in this MEMORANDUM OF AGREEMENT. Provided THE PHIL has not defaulted under the provisions of this MEMORANDUM OF AGREEMENT during the initial term or any additional term provided by this MEMORANDUM OF AGREEMENT, the PARTIES may mutually agree to extend the term of this MEMORANDUM OF AGREEMENT for an additional two-year period upon the terms set forth herein and/or such terms and conditions as the TOWN and THE PHIL may otherwise agree upon in writing. THE PHIL shall give written notice to THE TOWN of its election to exercise the extension options provided herein not less than ninety (90) days prior to the end of the initial term for any additional term. In the event of a material breach of the terms and provisions of this Agreement, the TOWN may revoke this MEMORANDUM OF AGREEMENT if such breach is not cured within ten (10) days of THE PHIL’S receipt of written notice of such breach. The rights granted to THE PHIL, its contractors, agents, representatives, employees, invitees, permittees hereunder shall be exercised from the date of the execution of this MEMORANDUM OF AGREEMENT until three years from the date of execution of this MEMORANDUM OF AGREEMENT, unless sooner terminated in accordance with the provisions of Section IX below. Approval by the TOWN shall not waive THE PHIL’S obligation to comply with all applicable laws, bylaws, rules and regulations including, but not limited to, the obligations and requirements contained in other documents applicable to THE PHIL. III. CONSIDERATION The consideration for this MEMORANDUM OF AGREEMENT shall be $1.00 together with the observation and performance by THE PHIL of all the obligations and covenants set forth within this MEMORANDUM OF AGREEMENT to the reasonable satisfaction of the TOWN. IV. INSURANCE Prior to occupancy and at all times during this MEMORANDUM OF AGREEMENT, THE PHIL and/or its contractors shall, at its sole cost and expense, maintain the following insurance: a. Liquor Liability of at least $1,000,000 each occurrence/$1,000,000 aggregate with the Town named as an “Additional Insured”. (This coverage is to be only required when there is liquor served on the premises.) c. The insurances listed above shall be on file with the Town prior to the date of your event evidencing insurance in the amounts as noted above, with the Town of Plymouth listed as additionally insured on all required policies. KOCH CITY OF QUINCY IN COUNCIL ORDER NO. 2026-122 ORDERED: September 22 2026 WHEREAS, the City of Quincy is constructing two new parking garages in the downtown as part of its urban renewal efforts; one garage located at 86 Parkingway a/k/a 25-55 General McConville Way, and the second located at 119 Parkingway a/k/a 101 General McConville Way, each in the City of Quincy; and WHEREAS, the City of Quincy seeks to reduce the financial burden on the tax payers of Quincy related to the operating costs of all city-owned buildings; seeks to reduce its carbon footprint from municipal operations; and seeks to otherwise promote clean energy goals; and WHEREAS, the City of Quincy is a member of PowerOptions, Inc., a non-profit entity that, in association with the MassCEC which is the Commonwealth of Massachusetts’ economic development agency for accelerating clean energy, competitively procured renewable energy development services; and WHEREAS, as a result of that competitive process and pursuant to Massachusetts General Law Chapter 164 Section 137, PowerOptions selected Solect Energy Development, LLC, to provide solar energy development and other services; and WHEREAS, Solect Energy and PowerOptions have entered into an agreement governing the terms and conditions of Solect’s participation in the PowerOptions Solar Programs; and WHEREAS, the City of Quincy Department of Public Buildings has been engaged with and working in conjunction with Solect Energy for the design, installation and operation of a solar photovoltaic system to be installed by Solect Energy on structural canopies located above the top-level parking deck of each of these new parking garages; and WHEREAS, pursuant to Massachusetts General Law Chapter 164 Section 137, after having complied with the provisions of said Chapter 164 Section 137, the City of Quincy is exempt from further procurement provisions of any other Massachusetts law relative to the procurement of these solar energy development services and/or the solicitation of bids for the disposition of the City’s real estate interest in these parking garages for the development of these solar energy generation facilities; and ORDER NO. 2026 – 122 Page 2 of 2 WHEREAS, Solect Energy and the Department of Public Buildings acknowledge and agree that mandate of prevailing wages pursuant to Massachusetts General Law chapter 149 is in force and applicable for the installation of these solar electric energy generation facilities. WHEREAS, the installation and operation of the solar photovoltaic system at each of these new parking garages requires a disposition of a real estate interest of the City by the City per the terms of Massachusetts General Law Chapter 30B; NOW THEREFORE at the request of, and upon the recommendation of, the Commissioner of the Department of Public Buildings, the City Council does Order as follows: That pursuant to Massachusetts General Law Chapter 30B, the real property interest of the City of Quincy above the top level parking decks of each of these two new parking garages and other defined space within each said garage for associated equipment and interconnections are hereby declared to be available for disposition solely for the purpose of the installation, maintenance, renewal, replacement, interconnection, and operation of a solar photovoltaic system and the utilities and equipment related thereto; and Further, that the Mayor is hereby authorized to enter into and execute Lease and Easement agreements with Solect Energy Development, LLC, related to the above described real estate interests for the purpose of the development and operation as stated of solar electric energy generation, upon the terms and conditions that the Mayor deems to be in the best interest of the City; Further, that the Mayor is hereby authorized to enter into and execute a Power Purchase Agreement with Solect Energy Development, LLC, its successors and assigns, for each of these two parking garages, for a term not to exceed twenty-five years, for the purpose of the development and operation as stated of solar electric energy generation, upon the terms and conditions that the Mayor deems to be in the best interest of the City; Nếu quý vị đã chuyển đến một địa chỉ khác trong thành phố/thị trấn này, thì văn phòng bầu cử tại địa phương sẽ cập nhật địa chỉ của quý vị và gửi thư xác nhận thay đổi cho quý vị qua đường bưu điện. Nếu quý vị đã chuyển đến một thành phố/thị trấn khác, quý vị sẽ được xóa tên khỏi danh sách cử tri sau ngày hôm nay. Hãy bảo đảm đăng ký bỏ phiếu tại địa chỉ mới của quý vị càng sớm càng tốt. KOCH CITY OF QUINCY IN COUNCIL ORDER NO. 2026-122 ORDERED: September 22 2026 WHEREAS, the City of Quincy is constructing two new parking garages in the downtown as part of its urban renewal efforts; one garage located at 86 Parkingway a/k/a 25-55 General McConville Way, and the second located at 119 Parkingway a/k/a 101 General McConville Way, each in the City of Quincy; and WHEREAS, the City of Quincy seeks to reduce the financial burden on the tax payers of Quincy related to the operating costs of all city-owned buildings; seeks to reduce its carbon footprint from municipal operations; and seeks to otherwise promote clean energy goals; and WHEREAS, the City of Quincy is a member of PowerOptions, Inc., a non-profit entity that, in association with the MassCEC which is the Commonwealth of Massachusetts’ economic development agency for accelerating clean energy, competitively procured renewable energy development services; and WHEREAS, as a result of that competitive process and pursuant to Massachusetts General Law Chapter 164 Section 137, PowerOptions selected Solect Energy Development, LLC, to provide solar energy development and other services; and WHEREAS, Solect Energy and PowerOptions have entered into an agreement governing the terms and conditions of Solect’s participation in the PowerOptions Solar Programs; and WHEREAS, the City of Quincy Department of Public Buildings has been engaged with and working in conjunction with Solect Energy for the design, installation and operation of a solar photovoltaic system to be installed by Solect Energy on structural canopies located above the top-level parking deck of each of these new parking garages; and WHEREAS, pursuant to Massachusetts General Law Chapter 164 Section 137, after having complied with the provisions of said Chapter 164 Section 137, the City of Quincy is exempt from further procurement provisions of any other Massachusetts law relative to the procurement of these solar energy development services and/or the solicitation of bids for the disposition of the City’s real estate interest in these parking garages for the development of these solar energy generation facilities; and ORDER NO. 2026 – 122 Page 2 of 2 WHEREAS, Solect Energy and the Department of Public Buildings acknowledge and agree that mandate of prevailing wages pursuant to Massachusetts General Law chapter 149 is in force and applicable for the installation of these solar electric energy generation facilities. WHEREAS, the installation and operation of the solar photovoltaic system at each of these new parking garages requires a disposition of a real estate interest of the City by the City per the terms of Massachusetts General Law Chapter 30B; NOW THEREFORE at the request of, and upon the recommendation of, the Commissioner of the Department of Public Buildings, the City Council does Order as follows: That pursuant to Massachusetts General Law Chapter 30B, the real property interest of the City of Quincy above the top level parking decks of each of these two new parking garages and other defined space within each said garage for associated equipment and interconnections are hereby declared to be available for disposition solely for the purpose of the installation, maintenance, renewal, replacement, interconnection, and operation of a solar photovoltaic system and the utilities and equipment related thereto; and Further, that the Mayor is hereby authorized to enter into and execute Lease and Easement agreements with Solect Energy Development, LLC, related to the above described real estate interests for the purpose of the development and operation as stated of solar electric energy generation, upon the terms and conditions that the Mayor deems to be in the best interest of the City; Further, that the Mayor is hereby authorized to enter into and execute a Power Purchase Agreement with Solect Energy Development, LLC, its successors and assigns, for each of these two parking garages, for a term not to exceed twenty-five years, for the purpose of the development and operation as stated of solar electric energy generation, upon the terms and conditions that the Mayor deems to be in the best interest of the City; title: FTM Warrant 9-14-2026 True Copy
text: Essex, ss. TOWN OF ROCKPORT WARRANT FOR FALL TOWN MEETING Monday, September 14, 2026 The Commonwealth of Massachusetts To: One of the Constables of the Town of Rockport, Massachusetts in said County of Essex in the Commonwealth of Massachusetts. GREETINGS: In the name of the Commonwealth of Massachusetts, you are hereby directed to notify and warn the inhabitants of said Town qualified to vote in Town affairs to meet and assemble at the Rockport High School at 24 Jerden’s Lane in said Rockport on Monday, the fourteenth day of September, 2026 A.D., at 5:30 in the evening, then and there to act on the following articles, to wit: ARTICLE A. ARTICLE B. ARTICLE C. ARTICLE D. To see if the Town will vote to raise and appropriate, or appropriate and transfer, a sum of money to pay unpaid bills of previous fiscal years; or act on anything relative thereto. (Select Board) (Requires 9/10 vote) To see if the Town will vote to raise and appropriate, or appropriate and transfer, a sum or sums of money to add to the appropriations made under Articles 5, 5A, 5B, 5C, 6, 6A and/or 6B of the April 11, 2026 Annual Town Meeting or to reduce appropriations made thereunder; or act on anything relative thereto. (Select Board) (Requires majority vote) To see if the Town will vote to hear and receive the annual report and recommendations of the Community Preservation Committee pursuant to Section 5 of Chapter 44B of the General Laws and Chapter 27 of the Code of By-laws; or act on anything relative thereto. (Community Preservation Committee) (Requires majority vote) To see if the Town will vote, pursuant to Section 6 of Chapter 44B of the General Laws, to set aside in the Community Preservation Fund sums of money from Community Preservation Fund FY2027 estimated annual revenues for later spending for the respective purposes indicated: First, a sum of money to be deposited in the Community Housing Reserve Account; Second, a sum of money to be deposited in the Open Space/Recreation Reserve Account; ARTICLE E. Third, a sum of money to be deposited in the Historic Preservation Reserve Account; or act on anything relative thereto. (Community Preservation Committee) (Requires majority vote) To see if the Town will vote to appropriate and transfer from the Community Preservation Fund or by borrowing the following amounts for the respective purposes indicated: ' First, $200,000 to be expended under the direction of the Thacher & Straitsmouth Islands Town Committee, working with the Community Preservation Committee, for the restoration, rehabilitation, and preservation of the historic South Tower on Thacher Island and to enhance the safety, historic integrity, and appearance of the tower; Second, $87,800 as a grant to the Sandy Bay Historical Society, to be expended under the oversight of the Select Board and DPW Commissioners and Director working with the Community Preservation Committee, for the restoration, repair, and historical preservation of the First Parish Cemetery historic Hearse House on Beach Street, in Rockport; Third, $238,000 to be placed in the Rockport Affordable Housing Trust Fund, to be administered by the Rockport Affordable Housing Trust Board of Trustees in compliance with the Code of By-Laws, to be used for community housing purposes consistent with the Community Preservation Act; Fourth, $100,000 to be expended under the direction of the Select Board, DPW Commissioners, and Director, working with the Community Preservation Committee, for treescape restoration at several municipal park and open space locations in Rockport; Fifth, $30,000 to be expended under the direction of the Select Board and Historical Commission, working with the Community Preservation Committee, for the restoration, rehabilitation, replacement, and repair of the historic Tercentenary Markers in Rockport; Sixth, $8,500 as a grant to the Rockport Rotary, to be expended under the oversight of the DPW Commissioners and Director, working with the Community Preservation Committee, for the restoration, rehabilitation, and repair of the historic Pigeon Cove Veterans Memorial; Seventh, $115,000 to be expended under the direction of the DPW Commissioners and Director, working with the Community Preservation Committee, for the installation of a handicapped accessible ramp at Cape ARTICLE F. ARTICLE G. Hedge Beach and for the purchase of three Beach Wheelchairs and storage units for beaches in Rockport; Eighth, $193,200 as a grant to The Pigeon Cove Chapel, to be expended under the direction of the Select Board, working with the Community Preservation Committee, for the restoration, rehabilitation, and preservation of the historic building located at 155 Granite Street, Rockport, as outlined in the application filed with the Committee; Ninth, $70,000 to be expended under the oversight of the Town Clerk, working with the Community Preservation Committee, for the restoration and preservation of historic Town records; or act on anything relative thereto. (Community Preservation Committee) (Requires majority vote) To see if the Town will vote to appropriate a sum of money to pay additional costs of the Town Hall remediation, renovation and modernization project, so called; to determine whether this appropriation shall be raised by borrowing or otherwise, or to take any other action relative thereto. (Select Board) (Requires 2/3 vote). To see if the Town will vote to rescind, amend, or revise any one or more of the authorizations previously given to borrow funds for municipal purposes, excluding always, any and all authorizations that have been executed by a borrowing; or act on anything relative thereto. (Town Treasurer) (requires majority vote) And you are directed to serve this Warrant by posting attested copies of the same at each of the Post Offices, the Town Bulletin Board and in other public places in each village of the Town, fourteen days at least before the day of the holding of said FALL TOWN MEETING. Hereof fail not and make due return of this Warrant, with your doings thereon to the Town Clerk, three days at least before Monday, September 14, 2026. Given under our hands and seal of the Town this 18th day of August 2026 A.D. SELECT BOARD TOWN OF ROCKPORT Paul F. “ hy, Chair Donal A uthard, Vice Chair Ross C. Brackett, Member Laura F. Action Contemplated Councillor King Moved Adoption for first passage Voted Resolution Supporting Assistance for Salem SNAP Participants WHEREAS, the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, also known as SNAP, is the largest and most effective anti-hunger assistance program in the nation, serving more than 900,000 Massachusetts residents in 2026; and WHEREAS, since the start of 2026, 77 percent of calls trying to reach a SNAP worker on the statewide SNAP phone line were automatically disconnected because the Massachusetts Department of Transitional Assistance (DTA) does not have enough staff to answer the phones; and WHEREAS, since H.R.1, otherwise known as the One Big Beautiful Bill, was signed into law, the SNAP caseload has declined statewide by nearly 175,000 people, including 62,000 children, and resulted in a loss of more than $360 million federal food dollars per year; and WHEREAS, participation in SNAP in the City of Salem has declined by 1251 participants, nearly 15%, as residents are losing SNAP due to H.R.1’s cruel eligibility cuts, and because they can’t reach DTA for help; and WHEREAS, while the federal government is focused on cutting programs that have served our Page 10 of 171 11 CITY OF SALEM September 10, 2026 REGULAR MEETING residents well for decades, we know Massachusetts can choose differently by investing in SNAP and DTA’s workforce. NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED, the Salem City Council urges the Healey-Driscoll Administration and the Massachusetts General Court to prioritize ending a SNAP access crisis in Massachusetts that is preventing members of our community from tapping into this powerful resource. BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED, the Salem City Council requests the hiring of additional DTA case workers to ensure those eligible for SNAP are able to receive and maintain benefits. BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED that the City Clerk respectfully forward this resolution to Governor. Healey and Lt. RECEIVED & RECORDED MINUTES SANDWICH SELECT BOARD AUGUST 20, 2026 SAND HILL SCHOOL COMMUNITY CENTER, DEWEY AVENUE 6:00 p.m. Present: D. Sampson, S. Hector, C. Holden, D. Sullivan G. Dunham, Town Manager; H. Harper, Assistant Town Manager Mr. Sampson opened the meeting at 6:00 PM. PLEDGE OF ALLEGIANCE PUBLIC COMMENT Sue Dangle from Mashpee - addressing the pond situation at Ryder. Modifications for the jet skis tie up worked for a couple of weeks but a lot of non-residents continue to tie up. There is an opportunity for an intermunicipal agreement with Mashpee, with the Mashpee harbormaster overseeing Ryder. She also addressed clear cutting at the Village Green construction site despite the restrictions the Town has placed for the site. It is causing nitrogen stormwater runoff and other adverse effects, and there is concern that the developers will continue to ignore the restrictions. Brian Wallace - addressing the situation at the pickle-ball courts. He would like to see the reservation system eliminated. He has been involved for many years when the play was at Oak Crest Cove and was open. There was no problem at all there. The reservation system does more harm than good and does not help the sport grow. Part of the problem is that there must be four players to make a reservation and singles finding others is difficult. Having open play with sign-up on a board would work better. Or he suggests maybe having two shifts a week be open or one full day a week. Mr. Dunham said there is going to be a special meeting about pickleball in September. Sue Carrai is here to complain that the Village Green developers are showing no accountability and have ruined the land. The Town should realize that they appear to be doing whatever they want and don't care about water or other issues. She hopes the Town will hold the developers accountable for their actions. Andy Davis - is here because the pickleball reservation system doesn't work. Other towns have open systems, and the Sandwich pickle-ballers have been going elsewhere to play. The reservation system goes one month out and often the courts are empty; they are not used half the time. They are actively discouraging people from playing pickleball. A Freeman Ave Resident- speaking about supporting the pickleball reservation system. There are lots of positives but there are lots of times that the courts are empty, especially at mid-day. The Recreation Department is amazing serving kids to seniors and Trish and Heather listen and try to resolve issues. Reservations are used widely elsewhere. The courts are closed in winter; indoor pickleball courts are differentiated according to skill level. There is a large pickleball community, and the reservation system gives predictability. REVIEW AND APPROVAL OF MINUTES Mr. Hoctor moved to approve the minutes of August 6, 2026. Seconded by Mr. Sullivan. Approved with one abstention (Holden} (3-0-1 ). • • • • • • • TOWN MANAGER REPORT The next Board meeting is September 10th . The Town Hall restoration is progressing really well. All windows have been replaced on the first and second floors. The exterior is being painted. The process should end in September. The beach attendants and guards are finished after tomorrow. The restrooms are available until September 8th and the large restroom building has been removed. The Recreation Department is planning an open forum about pickleball on September 16th at 5:00 PM at the CAL. The Department has facilitated pickleball, and Mr. Dunham hopes people recognize what the Department went through to provide the courts, including striping Oak Crest Cove. The courts are overseen by the Recreation Committee, which needs members. Eversource is in the process of converting old electric meters and replacing them with smart meters all over town. The Town has had a slowdown in the public outreach for signage. We are working through the DPW and Public Safety Departments about small signage that if people are interested, they can put on their property to encourage people to slow down. The Military/Civilian Community Council met, and it was reported that the VA is providing a new VA clinic at the main entrance to the Base. It will provide multiple services and will assist those currently having to go to Providence or Boston for care. It will be complete in 2027. CORRESPONDENCE/STATEMENTS/ANNOUNCEMENTS/FUTURE ITEMS/FOLLOW-UP None. STAFF MEETING JERA Americas - Update on Canal Station Development Plans • Randy Bell, Vice-President, Government & Regulatory Affairs • Wyatt Metzger, Senior Manager of Science and Advanced Technology • Amy Magee, General Manager, Independent system Operator New England (ISONE) • Kyle Farrell, Maintenance Manager, Canal Generation Mr. Dunham started by reminding everyone that the power plant is the largest taxpayer in the Town. It has been through different owners, and the Town has had a positive relationship to all. Working with JERA has been at a whole new level with open communication. Some of the facilities are outdated and JERA is being open-minded and thinking ahead. Mr. Bell then provided a review of who JERA is. They provide 30% of all power in Japan and the U.S. has the largest footprint outside of Japan. The canal plant has been powered by fossil fuel, but it is time to think about other approaches to providing power. Mr. Bell then addressed a slide show summarizing important aspects of current and future plans. The company owns several operations in various parts of the country; some of the plants have provided an opportunity to lower emissions and reduce infrastructure. There are seven plants in New England; all are either, oil, gas or dual. JERA is looking at reducing emissions through solar, low carbon ammonia, and all electric motor drivers, all to keep power at an affordable price. He then talked about the canal generating plant - Units 1&2 have been online since 1968 and Unit 3 since 2019. These provide grid support during periods of adverse weather and are rarely run unless the system is in crisis. Since JERA has taken ownership in 2022, they have deepened their investment in the Sandwich community with investments in town organizations and non-profits, STEM education, workforce development and other efforts. Their proposal for the canal plant is for a Battery Energy Storage System (BESS), and they are willing to explore additional community investment as well as develop an associated PILOT and community benefits agreement. The batteries would be on 5 ½ acres of property (maps included in the presentation), have more powerful charge and discharge and be more cost effective. They can turn on instantaneously when needed and connect directly to the grid. The batteries would be in shipping containers, and their Site Suitability Report looks at effects of climate change on the equipment, carbon storage, biodiversity and social/environmental burdens. They believe they have addressed all of these issues, and the Report will be submitted in September. Subsequently, there will be another public meeting, and they encourage everyone to attend that meeting. The construction would happen in association with the bridge project to minimize construction impacts. They have provided a list of potential impacts and mitigation and addressed potential safety issues, including emergency response and plans that address what to do in case of fire. The project lifespan is 20 years, and they have developed plans for decommissioning. They then provided a potential timeline with construction beginning in early 2029. Mr. Wyatt then spoke briefly. He said that safety is very important and that the company has an excellent track record for safety. There are a number of compliance codes they address, and a number of codes associated with safety of batteries. Every battery is continuously monitored, and controls automatically disconnect if any factors are outside safe limits. To mitigate fire, containers contain detection, alarm and fire suppression systems. Clear lanes support emergency access. Emergency response training will be in the Community Benefits Agreement. Questions/Comments Mr. Sampson thinks this is a very exciting project, especially seeing the plant using new technology in a small, localized area, as technology is moving fast. Mr. Hoctor appreciated that safety is an important factor, how much risk is addressed, and plans for Fire Department training. Mr. Holden thanks the company for the outreach. Mr. Sullivan thinks it is exciting and low impact and there is potential for new revenue. Mr. Dunham said that said there will be better economic opportunities for the Town and the Town should support projects that improve quality. There will be a great third-party review, and he is confident the work will happen. OLD BUSINESS Other Matters Not Reasonably Anticipated for Old Business None. NEW BUSINESS Request to Declare Suicide Prevention Month - September 2026 The Proclamation is in the agenda packet. Mr. Hoctor moved to declare the month of September (9/20 to 9/26) Suicide Prevention Month as presented. Seconded by Mr. Holden. Approved unanimously. Other Matters Not Reasonably Anticipated for New Business None. PUBLIC COMMENT Joe Silva - here to talk about Village Green. He says that the Town didn't want the development to be built. The developers have done everything they could with the property without any notification. The financial aspect might not matter but the Town needs to find a way to stop its effect on the environment. Chris Dennis - expresses frustration at the lack of immediate action to prevent further damage to the land at Village Green. She looked up the fines for violating conditions and the Building Commissioner needs to give notice. Apparently, the Town would need to go to the state court to collect non-compliance fines. Chapter 40 B projects are fully bound by the conditions put on the permit. The Town needs to know its rights before the next violation occurs. Peter Hartman - is complaining again about the "illegal" HOA in his neighborhood. There is nothing on his deed that says there are dues. There must be signed documents through Massachusetts. Also, there are large campers parked in people's yards. There should be community standards about this. There should be a report to the Postmaster that the postal service cannot deliver illegal requests for money. Mr. Sampson responded that there have been some contacts regarding the safety issues. The Board does not have jurisdiction over the HOA issue. CLOSING REMARKS Mr. Holden says to continue to pray for peace, restraint among leaders, and protection of innocent life with justice guided by wisdom. ADJOURNMENT The meeting adjourned at 7:30 PM. Next meeting: Thursday. QUESTION 1: LAW PROPOSED BY INITIATIVE PETITION Do you approve of a law summarized below, on which no vote was taken by the Senate or the House of Representatives before May 6, 2026? SUMMARY This proposed law would make most records held by the Legislature and the Office of the Governor public records under the Massachusetts Public Records Law. This proposed law would exempt documents related to the development of public policy and communications between legislators and their constituents, if those communications are reasonably related to a constituent's request for assistance in obtaining government-provided benefits or services or interacting with a government agency. A YES VOTE would make most records held by the Legislature and the Office of the Governor public records under the Massachusetts Public Records Law. A NO VOTE would make no change to the Massachusetts Public Records Law. QUESTION 2: LAW PROPOSED BY INITIATIVE PETITION Do you approve of a law summarized below, on which no vote was taken by the Senate or the House of Representatives before May 6, 2026? SUMMARY This proposed law would specify that employees of the Committee for Public Counse] Services ("CPCS") are permitted to engage in collective bargaining with their employer. It would also require CPCS, after executing a collective bargaining agreement, to request the appropriation necessary to fund such agreement from the Governor. A YES VOTE would specify that Committee for Public Counsel Services employees may form a union to collectively bargain with their employer. A NO VOTE would make no change to the law governing labor relations for Committee for Public Counsel Service employees. QUESTION 3: LAW PROPOSED BY INITIATIVE PETITION Do you approve of a law summarized below, on which no vote was taken by the Senate or the House of Representatives before May 6, 2026? SUMMARY This proposed law would eliminate political party primaries for state elections and instead establish a system where there would be a single, all-party primary in which all candidates, regardless of their party affiliation, would be listed on one ballot, and voters could vote for any candidate on the ballot. The two candidates receiving the most votes in the primary would advance to the general election ballot. This proposed law would require candidates for governor and lieutenant governor to run and be listed jointly on the ballot in the primary. This proposed law would provide political party status to any group whose candidates for any statewide office received at least 3% of the ballots cast in the state primary. A YES VOTE would eliminate separate party primaries for state elections and require a single primary in which all candidates appear on one ballot, voters could vote for any candidate, and the top two candidates would advance to the general election. A NO VOTE would make no change to the laws governing primary elections. QUESTION 4: LAWPROPOSED BY INITIATIVE PETITION Do you approve of a law summarized below, on which no vote was taken by the Senate or the House of Representatives before May 6, 2026? SUMMARY This proposed law would permit eligible individuals to register to vote or update their voter registration address on Election Day. An individual who is eligible to vote could register to vote on Election Day by going to the polling place in the precinct where they live during voting hours and presenting proof of residency and signing a written oath. Proof of residency could be a valid photo identification, or documentation showing the individual's name and the address where the individua] 2 resides, such as a current utility bill, bank statement, government check, residential lease, wireless telephone statement, paycheck, current student fee statement or other document from a post-secondary school, or another government document or correspondence. The written oath would require the individual to certify that they are a citizen of the United • States, are at least 18 years old, are not legally prohibited from voting, and have not and will not vote in the same election at another location. The oath would require the individual to acknowledge that providing false information is a felony punishable by not more than 5 years imprisonment or a fine of not more than $10,000, or both. If an individual did not present proof of residency, they would be allowed to cast a provisional ballot, which would be counted only if the individual returned to provide the required information before the close of polls for a municipal election; within two days after a state primary; or within six days after a state election. Individuals who register to vote on Election Day would be registered to vote in future elections as well as in the election taking place that day. Individuals who are already registered to vote would not be able to change their political party affiliation on Election Day. The proposed law would take effect on January 1, 2028. A YES VOTE would permit eligible citizens to register to vote or to update their voter registration address at their polling place on Election Day. A NO VOTE would make no change to the laws governing voter registration. QUESTION 5: LAW PROPOSED BY INITIATIVE PETITION Do you approve of a law summarized below, on which no vote was taken by the Senate or the House of Representatives before May 6, 2026? SUMMARY This proposed law would change the limit on how much revenue the state can collect in a given year. The proposal would limit state revenue in a given year to the net amount of state revenue from the year before, increased by a rate equal to the average growth of wages and salaries in Massachusetts over the most recent three years. If revenue collected by the state in a given year exceeds the limit, the excess amount would be refunded to taxpayers the following year. The proposed . law would include all revenue from the surtax on incomes over $1 million when calculating the revenue limit and when determining whether state revenue exceeds the limit. The provisions of the proposed law would all be effective as of July 1, 2027. The proposed law states that, if any of its parts were declared invalid, the other parts would stay in effect. A YES VOTE would change the limit on state revenue collection, tying it to prior year collections plus average wage and salary growth, and provide for a rebate of revenue exceeding that limit. A NO VOTE would make no change in the law relative to state revenue collection. QUESTION 6: LAW PROPOSED BY INITIATIVE PETITION Do you approve of a law summarized below, on which no vote was taken by the Senate or the House of Representatives before May 6, 2026? SUMMARY This proposed law would establish a Nature for All Fund that, subject to appropriation by the Legislature, would receive 50% of state taxes collected from the sale and use of sporting goods, recreational vehicles, and golf courses for the first year of its operation. After July 1, 2028, the Nature for All Fund would begin receiving, subject to appropriation by the Legislature, 100% of state taxes collected on the sale and use of sporting goods, recreational vehicles, and golf courses. 3 The sales tax revenue received by the Nature for All Fund would exclude sales tax revenue transferred to the Massachusetts BayTransportation Authority State and Local Contribution Fund and the School Modernization and Reconstruction Trust Fund. The proposed law would allow the state Executive Office of Energy and Environmental Affairs to spend the money in the Nature for All Fund for natural resource conservation. The proposed law would allow public and private donations to the Nature for All Fund. The proposed law would prevent the state comptroller from transferring surplus funds in the Nature for All Fund at the end of the fiscal year. It would also allow state agencies, municipalities, public charities involved in natural resource conservation, tribal governments, and other regional public entities to receive money from the Nature for All Fund. Natural resource conservation would include the conservation or restoration of land to protect drinking water, streams, rivers, lakes, coasts, farms, forests, connectivity between open spaces, and lands and natural resources of indigenous cultural significance. Natural resource conservation would also include the creation, improvement, and management of parks, trails, greenspaces or outdoor recreation access.
